div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

" Tms is a sponging breeze," said the old sailor as he fanned his unruly boy with his hand. THE hen that sets on a porcelain egg, may not accomplish much, but she has on-nest intentions. IT is possible for an orator to use 213 words per minute, but it isn't possible for any of them to amount to anything. A MAN said to his aged mother, speaking of his wife, "I do wish I could keep Mary from exagger- ating so." Get her to talk about her age," responded the shrewd old lady. "DID yen see many tandems while you were in Boston, Chawles "Not many, Gus. They mostly ride hobbies there, you know." A MAN being accused of tieing so mean that he would quarrel about a c'ent retorted:—" I know I would, and I'm proud of it, for everybody knows the less one quarrels about the better." ASKING a lady what her accomplishments are is, generally speaking, harmless enough. Still, in these days, it might in some cases cause embarrassment to put the qUestion, "Do you paint ?" A LITTLE boy went to his first tea-party when four years and three months old. Upon his hostess asking hini how he liked his tea, he replied:—" It is very nice, but it tastes very much of the water." "Pa, who was Shylock "? Pater, loquitur—" Great goodness, boy? You attend dhurch and Sunday school every week, and don't know who Shylock was ? Go and read your bible, sir." "Is the sun blue?" is the question which now agitates scientists. If you see him when his girl has gone on an excursion with another fellow be- cause he hadn't money enough to take her you'd think the son was blue, and justly so.

Pretty girl to Charles (her betrothed)—" Charles, how far is it round the world 7 Isn't it twenty-four thousand---" Charles (putting both arms around her)—"That's all a mistake, my love; it is only about twenty-four inches." "Mother, don't the angels wear any clothes 1" asked a little girl of her mother. "No, my daughter." "None at all, mother 2" "None at all.' There was a pause, and the little cherub asked, "Where do the angels put their pocket handker- chiefs."

JONES asks his wife:—" Why is a husband like dough?" He expected she would give it up, and was going to tell her it was because a woman needs him; but she said it was because it was hard to get off her hands.

WIFE—John, dear, if it should be my misfortune to die before you do, do You think you would marry again? Husband—Well, I dunno, my love. Until it comes to him, no man can tell how he would be able to stand prosperity. "So, you've got married, old man, while I have been away 7 " "Yes." "Well, I congratulate you on having shaken off that she-dragon of a house- keeper of yours at last." "Oh, don't make any mistake, dear boy—l have married her 1 " JUDGE—" How old are you 7" Witnesa (a lady) —"Thirty." Judge—" Thirty I have beard you give the same age in this court for the last three years!" Witness—" Yes. I am not one of those persons who say one thing to-day and another to-morrow?'

"OH 1" exclaimed Miss Daubwell, "what a clever man that Mr. Fogg is? He is really quite a physi- ognomist. I was telling him last evening that I had become quite proficient in painting, and he said I was sure of it madame, your face shows it.'" Chorus—" Indeed." A WELL-KNOWN New York artist and his wife made their appearance at an evening party last winter. , As they entered the drawing-room the dhostess hastened to greet them with effusion, and exclaimed—" I'm so glad.to see you! We 've been ransacking the very highways and byways to get people to come here to-night." DUMLEY (who has sold a watch)—You told me, Robinson, that if I would let you have tliq watch you would pay me in thirty days. It's a good deal more than thirty days now. Robinson—Not by the watch; that watch loses twelve hours out of the twenty-four.

RURAL Boy—" Say, Pop, that new summer boarder from Philadelphia has been fishin' in the pond for 'most a week, and I'm 'fraid he's gettin' discouraged." Pop—" That won't do. You drive over to town to-night and buy another fish. Maybe the one we put in last week is dead."

PHILADELPHIA AUNT (severely)—" As I glanced Into the parlour last evening I saw you with a young man's arm around you." Chicago -Niece (calm)—" Yes, aunty. I was waiting for you to pass the door to see us. Young men are very slippery now-a-days, and one can't have too many witnesses."

"GOOD-BYE, my dear friend, I am going to leave you. lam going to Australia, and I will probably never come back'," said an ingenious youth. i` Will I never see you again 7" "Never." "I say, do me one last favour. Lend me five pounds." "Oh, no, don't let us do anything to increase the pangs of our parting."

To cure-snoring an exchange advises that a piece of soap be dropped into the mouth or the snorer. The oil in the soap will lui.ricate the pharynx and other Latin parts of the throat. It strikes us that this remedy had better be applied with caution, else the snorer might arise and lubricate the floor with the man who dropped in the soap.

"THIS is my last; birthday," said a handsome girl to her adorer on the 29ch of August. "What do you mean 7" he exclaimed, clutching at his heart. You are not going to die, are you ?" "Well, I should hope not. I'm twenty-one to-day, and a woman never has a birthday after that, you know." He remembered then that they didn't. SAYS DUMLEY—" The lady in the other part of the house is learning to play the piano, her husband is struggling with the violin, I have a daughter who is studying the organ, and a boy who is learning the banjo, and—" "What are you learning ? " asked a hearer. "Oh, I'm learning to get used to it," was the prompt reply. A WELL-KNOWN statesman recently happened to meet the Bishop of Peterborough. "I hear, my lord," observed he, "that you don't quite approve of my dealing with the Irish question." "Oh, dear, no," quietly answered the Bishop; "it is not your 'dealing' that I mind—it is your shuffling that I object to!" WIFE—" Be sure to advertise for Fido in the newspapers." Husband— "Never fear. I'll tie a knot in my handkerchief." prcxt day the wife reads in the morning newspapers :—" Ten Dollars Reward.—Lost, a measly yellow cur, with one eye 1.12L1 no tail. Too fat to walk. Answers to name Tido. Smells like a cheap perfumery shop after a -fire. If returned stuffed 10 dollars reward." She faints.

"LOOK here, waiter, quick," called out a gentle- man in a restaurant. "What is it, sir ?" " Here is a dead fly in my soup." "So, I see. It seems to be quite dead." "Well, by thunder, I want you to understand that I consider it an outrage." "I am sorry, sir, but if you are opposed to eating dead animals, you should patronise one of the vegetarian restaurants." CUSTOMER (indignantly)—" See here, you 've swindled rae ! You said that chicken was young, and it's tough as leather 1" Young woman (pertly) —" Can you guess how old I am?" Customer (bewildered)—" Eh—what? 'Well—l should say 16." Young woman (triumphantly)—" Just 16! You wouldn't call me old, would you? Well, I raised that chicken myself, and I know that it isn't half as old as I am!"

A CLERGYMAN called on a poor parishioner whom he found bitterly lamenting the loss of an only son —a boy about four of five years old. In the hope of consoling the afflicted woman, he remarked to her that one so young could not have committed any very grievous sin, and that no doubt the child was gone to heaven. "Al), sir," said the simple. hearted creature, "but Tommy was too shy—and they are aU strangers there."

JOHN BROWN (flab), who was a warm personal friend of Dr. Cairns, was speaking on one occasion in his characteristic way of Cairns. Some one adverting to his big body, warmth of heart, and childlike simplicity of nature, Dr. Brown remarked —"He is just a great big evangelical Newfound- land dog." "Did you ever remark," said another, "his extraordinary grasp when he shakes hands? His hand is just like a vice." "Well," replied flab, "it's the only vice he has." CORONER—" You seem very sure tilint the deceased was killed by some accident. Could he not have committed suicide'? " Witness—" No, sir; no man ever committed suicide with a full bottle of whisky in his inside pocket."

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

A London correspondent gives currency to the report that the action for divorce in which a sub- ordinate member of the Government was cited as co-respondent has been settled by the aggrieved husband accepting a sum of £5,000.

The Hon. W. Carrington, the Queen's Equerry, visited the Foreign Office, on Monday afternoon, with reference to the Queen's departure for the Continent. B.er Majesty will leave England on the forenoon of the 22nd inst., and will reach Grasse on the 25th. The Prince of Wales will be abroad at the same time as her Majesty.

The Grand Hotel at Grasse lips been taken for the Queen for four weeks, but her Majesty's stay will not much exceed three weeks, as, according to pre- sent arrangements, she will leave Grasse late on the night of Thursday, April 16, arrive at Cherbourg early on the morning of Saturday, the 18th, and reach Windsor on the evening of that day.

Considerable irritation is felt,both at Windsor and Berlin, at the intelligence that the Princess Eliza- beth of Hesse (the Queen's grand-daughter) has joined the Greek Church. The Princess protests that she takes the step of her own free will, but when she married the Grand Duke Sergius it was specially agreed that she should not give up the faith in which she was brought up.

Univers' ty-extension is moving along. The Bikhop of Durham,better known as Canon Westcott,blessebl it at the Mansion House, on Saturday, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer stood up -for it. They may well do so, for it is a great success, and answers one of the real needs of the times. It gives a chance to the poorest of securing a bit of the best.

Lord Egerton of Tatton, chairman of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company, the Mayor of Man- chester, and. the Town Clerk were in the lobby of the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, inter- viewing members on behalf of the proposed Loan Bill. They had no difficulty in securing the support of most of the Lancashire representatives, and it is understood that they were also very favourably. received by important members of the Government.

A story is being told which, if it has any founda- tion, shows what Nilihism has done for the nerves of Russian Royalty and its entourage: During a banquet given to the: Czarewitch, at the Govern- ment House, Madras, a loud explosion was sud- denly heard outside the window. At the sound, the Czarewitch and his suit instantly sprangto their feet, with hands on their swords and consternation on their faces. It turned out that a soda water bottle had burst on the verandah.

The Duke of Devonshire has now formally made over Compton-place, his residence near Eastbourne, to Lord .11artington, who will live there a great deal in the future,especially after his marriage with the Dowager Duchess of Manchester, which,. I am informed,will shortly be celebrated. Owing to cer- tain family considerations, it is probable that the ceremony will take place abroad. Compton-place is being thoroughly overhauled, and even the grounds are being remodelled.

Mr. F. W. Broughton, whose bright, witty little comediettas brought him fame and pelf, formerly wrote chatty columns for one of the Bradford papers under the nom de plume of" Rapier," which were widely read. He is, like many brilliant writers, most erratic in his literary work, and has been known, after a period of idleness, to commence and finish a play in a couple of days. In appearance he is tall, thin, and youthful-looking. His conversation has not the brilliancy of his stage talk. His father Is a prosperous Bradford merchant. His" Withered Leaves" is his freshest and best play."

The abolition of betting in Paris has had a disas- trous effect on the nice meetings. As there were no bookmakers allowed at Auteuil on Sunday there were few spectators. It was a day of " mournful dreariness." The police present almost outnum- bered the people. The few spectators who were present took very little interest in the races. This raises the most serious question—does racing enst for the benefit of horse-breeding or for the encour- agementof betting? It is very evident that horse- racing without betting would not pay. This aspect of the question will come before the French Chamber again.

The new knight, Sir Wm. Pink, is a retail pour in a big way in Portsmouth. He commenced life with Fortnum and Mason, and when the Crimean war broke out, was entrusted by them with the superintendence of the execution of large Govern- ment orders for military and naval positions. This he did with so much success that when, a few years later, he commenced business in Portsmouth,. his old firm helped him with strong recommendations to the wholesale provision houses. He has now. half i a dozen large establishments n Portsmouth,.and a big business in Winchester as well, and is locally said to have feathered his nest.

With reference to Mr. Stanhope's account of the advantages of a soldier's life in respect of daily provision made for him, it is interesting to learn from the schedule of the Army Act what money allowance is authorised for the soldier when he is billeted. For lodging and attendance, where a hot meal is furnished, a maximum sum of 2lyd. is al- lowed for the night. Where no hot meal is fur- nished, but together with lodging and attendance are thrown in candles, vinegar, salt, the use of fire, and the necessary utensils for dressing and eating his meat,,4d. a day is allowed. For the hot meal, the broad outlines of which are solemnly fixed by Act of Parliament, the maximum price paid is is. lid.

Mr. Healy's forecast of the political situation in Ireland is worth noting. The hon. memi)er thinks it possible that out of his thirty-three followers Mr. Parnell may return eight at a general election, but that he will certainly not return a dozen. The re- mainder of the seats, except those that will be pre- sented to the Tories, will go to the majority. The Tory gains will be either five or six votes, and the Irish party will return to Parliament over seventy strong, the exact estimate being seventy-three. In other words,according to the estimate of the member for North Longford, the opponents of Mr. Parnell in Ireland will sweep the country, while Mr. Parnell and his followers will be in a hopeless minority.

Miss Edna Lyall, the popular authoress, has a strength of conviction and bravery in expressing it which some public men might envy. It was not long ago that she had to repudiate an insinuation that she had agnostic leanings, but the death of Mr. Bradlaugh has drawn from her a most kindly worded letter to his daughter, Mrs. Bradlaugh Bon- ner. It appears that on three occasions Miss Lyall had subscribed to Mr. Bradlaugh's election expenses and she has followed this up on learning of dip state of the late member's finances by a personal gift to Mrs. Bradlaugh Bonner,with the proviso that it shall not be used for any freethought purposes. The present is accompanied by a very high tribute to Mr. Bradlaugh's character as the result of per- sonal aCquaintance with him,
CHARLES WESLEY'S DESCENDANTS.

John Wesley left no one to bear his name, but it was not so with his famous brother Charles, the poet of Methodism, author of many beautiful hymns which are sung to this day in thousands of churches and chapels every Sunday. Charles died three years before his elder brother John, and his son Samuel became a distinguished composer, liv- ing till 1837. At the age of six he composed an or- atorio, and was evidently the original of the pro- digies so common now. Samuel's son, Sebastian, became the distinguished organist of Gloucester Cathedral, and lived much esteemed as a musician and composer till a few years ago. His sister a granddaughter of the poet of Methodism, was or- ganist of St. Bride's, Fleet-st., till her death, in 1885. Thus for three generations poetry and Music ran in the Wesleys and are still running in the fourth. One of Charles Wesley's great wand-sons is at the present moment organist of Edinburgh Cathedral, while a great granddaughter, Miss Eva Wesley, is the authoress of tales with a religious bias in the " Christian World," " Family Circle edition."

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 14, 1891.

Mr. Burt has determined on the second reading' of the Mines (Eight Hours) Bill,to move an amend- ment declaring that it is not desirable that the hours of labour to Pe worked by adults in mines should be fixed by Parliament.

Mr. F. Wilkinson is ?le —heaviest and also the lengthiest member of this year's Oxford eight. He has been awarded his " blue " none too soon, and deserved it last year. It was mainly owing to him- self and the present Dark Blue stroke—C. W. Kent —that his college boat—Brasenose—was able to attain to the position of head of the river at Oxford last summer. To the same pair of oarsmen may be attributed much of the success which fell to the lot of the Brasenose boat at Henley, last year, the sensational victory in the Steward's being quite the feature of the regatta. Mr. Wilkinson, who is an Australian by birth, stands six feet three inches in height, has a rowing weight of thirteen and a half stone, and is rowing at "number six.'

Within the last few days I have read that Sir William Gordon has left England4for Japan, for America, and for Spain. These statements are as erroneous as they are discordant. Sir William is in London, where, and in Yorkshire, he will remain for some weeks to eome. It is true that he had intended going to Malaga, whowi his purpose was baulked. by his lawyers, who for the present require his presence at home. The military authorities—to put it mildly—did not facilitate his departure. Along with his application for "foreign leave" on •the ground of ill-health, he forwarded in accordance with the prescribed injunction, a medical certifi- cate. This, although their own requirement, did not satisfy the authorities, who demanded his appearance before the medical 'board, on whose report would turn the question of his obtaining the leave for which he had asked.

The" Star " says :—A few weeks ago we referred in this column to Dr. Julius, Bishop of Christchurch, New Zealand, formerly a rector in Islington, as the most Radical Anglican prelate alive, and mentioned the consternation he caused by refusing to be ad- dressed as "your lordship" and by preaching a scathing sermon on "The Greed of Capitalism." Since then Bishop Julius has been giving a further proof of his independence of the episcopal conven- tionalities. On a recent Sunday he was walking to his cathedral to preach—he always walks and is a magnificent athletic pedestrian—when suddenly, looking at his watch, he discovered he was behind time. No conveyance was at hand, but a friendly fish-cart opportunely hove in sight, and to the hor- ror of a shocked and scandalised community, the Bishop was then driven to his cathedral, and en- abled to ascend the pulpit at the proper time.

div.head: TOBACCO QUESTION.
div.p: THE TOBACCO QUESTION.
BY COUNT TOLSTOI.

"The Review of Reviews " says:— In the "Contemporary Review" there is a, very characteristic article by Count Tolstoi on "Wine Drinking and Tobacco Smoking." Upon both those subjects he is well qualified to speak. Few men have been more given to wine and cigarettes than Count Tolstoi, and the conclusions at which he ar- rived from a lengthy experience are full of interest and not lacking in, characteristic originality. Me thesis is that-7

' People drink and smoke, net merely for something better to do to while away the time, or to raise their spirits; not because of the pleasure they receive, but simply and solely in order to drown the warning voiceof conscience.

Considering that one of the special objects of our Association of Helpers is to secure tobacco for the old people in our workhouses, it is rather hard to come upon the Count's demonstration of the per 4.- nicious influence of tobacco upon the moral sense.. He asks :

To what extent can smoking stifle tbe voice of con.- science? We have noneed to seek for the materials for a solution of this question in exceptional cases of crime and remorse; it is amply sufficient to observe the be- haviour of the ordinary—one might almost say of any-- smoker. Every smoker abandoning himself to his pas- - sion, loses sight of, or rides roughshod over, certain the most elementary rules of social life, the observance of which he demands from others, and which he himself. respects in all other cases, whenever his conscience is not completely silenced by tobacco. Every person of mode- rately good breeding in our social sphere holds it to be unseemly, ill-mannered:. churlish, merely for his own pleasure to interfere with the peace and comfort of others. and a fortiori to injure-their health. No one would take the liberty to flood with water a room in which peopie were sitting; to scream and yell in it ; to turn on hot or cold, or fcetid air, or to perform any other acts, tending- to disturb or injure others ; and yet out of a thousand smokers scarcely one will hesitate to fill with noxious fumes a room, the atmosphere of which is being breathsa% by women and children who do not smoke.

div.p: NrAr BOOKS, &c.

A second edition,is issued by Messrs. Mcamillan and Co., of "Natural Religion," by the author of " Ecce Homo." At the present day, when ques- tions of religion are occupying so much of the pub- lic mind, the work is one which men of all creeds might read with profit. The writer believes that religion is something greater than the creeds which sometimes impede it, that it grows with the spirit- ual growth z of humanity, and that there is develop- ment and evolution in religion as in other things. He does not see why there should be any antagon- ism between science and religion, for he regards scientific investigation as in itself religious, in- asmuch as it is an interpretation of the work 'of the "Power which makes for righteousness." In the same way he holds art to be religious in so far as it is inspired with enthusiasm and honestly expresses a love of beauty. "The higher life in whatever form it expresses itself is to him religion. Looking forward to the development of natural religion, he says—" such a reform must rest upon the principle that, as Christianity was wider than Judaism, so the religion of the present age must be wider than Christianity, but at the same time, as Christianity did not renounce Judaism, so our religion must not renounce Christianity." Again, "as described here, religion does not brood over the future life, but is intensely occupied with the present; it does not surmise something behind Nature, but contemplates Nature itself; it does not worship a Pouter which suspends natural laws, but the power which is exhibited in those laws.' There is a good deal to set people thinking in this volume, which will be widely read, even if it should not be- come as popular as" Ecce Homo." "A Ogarette-Maker's Romance" is the title of the latest novel from the pen of F. Marion Crawford, author of "Mr. Isaacs," "Dr. Claudius,"&c. The scene is laid in Munich, and the materials are for the most part of the simplest kind. The characters are not numerous, but they are drawn with vigour and with loving care. That of" the Count," who is reduced to cigarette-making and becomes mildly mad one day in each week, is portrayed with exceptional finish and delicacy;' also that of Vjera, who is in love with him. It might be objected that there is a considerable amount of prosy detail in the beginning of the story, but it is seen, as the plot de- velopes, that it all tends to heighten the final climax, which is described with rare beauty and pathos. The novel is as healthful as it is stimulating, and well calcu- lated to add to the repute of the eminent writer. The work is published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co:, price is. " Whittaker's Almanac" for 1891 is, like its predecessors, in standing unrivalled as a shilling publication for the amount and variety of the information which it supplies. Broadly speaking, it gives particulars "respecting the government, finance, population, commerce, and general statistics of the British Empire throughout the world," with considerable notice of other countries. Account is always taken of astronomical and other phenomena,with special articles relating to matters of more than ordinary public interest. In the supplement this year, there are articles relating to the forthcoming census, the revenue and expenditure of the Great Powers, the partition ot Africa,. tniversity extension, and applied electricity. But with a volume of over 700 pages, the difficulty is not to say what it contains, but what it does not con- tain. "Whittaker" to those who have ever used it is in- dispensable..

lia the Canterbury poets series, published by Mr. Wal- ter Scott, we have "English Love Lyrics, selected and edited with an. introduction by Percy Hulburd." The period covered ranges from 1500 to 1800, thus excluding living writers,, and steering clear, of course, of copy- right. As might be supposed,the selection is a truly de- lightful one. It embraces muck with which all students of poetry are familiar, and many admirable things,. which in all probability they will not have previously seen. The daintiness of expression which characterises some of the older lyrics, is certainly not surpassed by anything that is written to-day. What can be finer, for. instance, than this by Herrick ?--

"1 dare not cake kiss, I dare not beg a smile;, 'Lest, haying that or this. I might grow proud the while No, no, the-utmost share Of my desire shall be, Only to kiss, that air. . That lately kissed thee."

The same firm publishes in its Camelot Series "-The Plays of Richard Brinsley Sheridan, edited with an intro- duction by Rudolph Dirks." It is a treat of no small kind to obtain 'these masterpieces of dramatic art in a single volume for one shilling. The plays are "The Rivals," " St. Patrick's Day," "The Duenna," "The School for Scandal," " The Critica,"and "Pizarro." The epilogues written by Sheridan are also included. Mr. Dirks in.-his introduction gives a brief but interesting account of the life and character of Sheridan. Concluding he says—"lf one leaves Sheridan with a feeling that there was a want of wholesomeness about his life, that there was some- thing of tinsel in all the glitter, one nevertheless is impressed by the genius, vigour, and, above all, the wonderful humanity of the man." We have had occasion. ere now in this journal to criti- cise Professor Huxley aa-a critic of General Booth, ani ,we have now to hand a shilling work on "General Booth and his critics, being an analysis of the scheme and an inquiry into the value of the criticism of Professor Huxley, Mr. C. S. Loch, the 'Times' newspaper, and other critics." It iafrom the pen of Dr. H. Green- wood, M.A., who makes a good stand in defence of General Booth. Amongst the matters di,scussed are "Objections to the central scheme," "The Salvation Army," " Tz ust in the General," " Separate suggestious.." and "Whether the scheme should be tried." An outline is Oven of the new trust deed, and the conclusion come to may be summed up in , the sentence—"the Salvation Army, in spite of its peculiarities and shortcomings:, is eminently fitted to carry the scheme into effect" The /publishers are Messrs. Howe and Co., London. "Cassell's Magazine of, Art "for March has for frontis- piece a Charming photogravure of J. M. Swan's picture of the "Prodigal Son." The first paper is by Mr. X. H. •Spielmann, and is a memorial notice of the late Charles Keen Of "Punch" fame. An article on Lord Arm- strong's collection of modern pictures is splendidlyillus- trated,-,and the same may be said of the paper on the "English School of Miniature Art," by Mr. J. L..Propert. The other illustrated articles are "The Modern Sultools Of Painting and Sculpture." "Studies in Journalism," " Untramelled Art," and "The Life and Work of Barye." The current issue of the "Cabinet Portrait Gallery " contains photographs and letterpress descriptions of, the Duke of Clarence and Avondale, Miss Agnes Hunting- don;and Herr Antorianbinstein. We have previously had occasion to speak\in the highest terms of this highclasS 'Work, and have only to add that the reputation it has acquired is fully maintained. - -

, " Ca'ssell's Magaiine "loses nothing of its interest as one of the most popular and best edited periodicals of: the day. The current t number contains two serial stories, anwo complete stories, besides numerous miscellane— ous illustrated papers, including "Famous. Naval •Figurehead Relics,""" Suggestions for fashionable ern, broideries," "Eyes- and no eyes," "The Garden• March," &c. "The Quiver," Maintains its high level, both in tezd ,and illustration. Amongst the contents we have "Rough days in March," "-The fall of Jericho," "A. cordial for care," "The shielch the sword and the battle," " In,the mission boat," "'Short arrows" and " Sweettharmony." "Little Folks !'-has a bright frontispiece illustrating a short poem entitled "Kitty's pony.' There • areS two continued stories, of great interest, besides numerous sketches and stories in prose awd. verse, amply and ad- mirably illustrated. A publication which is likely to prove of great inrest and therefore- be in great demand is " Zassell's-Store- house of General Information." As the name implies, it will give information of a general kind which willbe the work of specialists in every branch of knowledge, and thus keep the reader up to date. It is being_ fully illus- trated with, high-class wood engravings ,and with maps and coloured plates arranged in alphabetical order. The information is easy for refesence, and the wort may be looked upon as a comprehensive and popular- encyclo- pedia. It is being published in parts-at 7el, each, and after seeing the two parts-Issued we can strongly recom- mend the publication. Pare 4to hand of " Fiier's Popular Scientific Works" completes the series. It deals with the world :before the deluce''e,. concluding withithe "appearance of man and the Asiatic deluge." Tables of strata are given ;: ' there-is a full index, and the illustrations, are numerous. and well finished.

Ninnber three of the fine-art publication of " Robin- sopecrusoe " is as attractive as its predece,ssors in illua• traraon, and it is noteworthy that the type of feature adopted for the hero. is carefully preserved by the artist in every illustration,. thus preserving a sense of reality which is in harmony with the text. , Wehave also to hand the current members of ". gas- sell's Dore Gallery,' "Science for " Natural History," "British Battles," "The world of adventure," ana '6 Familar wild Flowers." " The Ladies' Gazette of Fashion," for March has for frontispiece, a coloured place of the latest fashions, be- sides several other coloured. plates and special' illustra- Wins of Danish lacework. The articles include" Parisian novelties," "Indoor and walking dresses," "Society and Fashion," " With pencil and needle," "Fashionable weddings,"" Round theshops," " Afternoon ca!ls," and "A few words •on furnishing," &c. It is published, price sixpence, by Messrs. Houlston and Sons, London.

div.head: PERCIVAI_ GORDO N,
div.p: PERCIVAI_ GORDO N,
OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT. BY SYLVANUS COBB
CHAPTER. H.
LIFE-STORY OF THE DYING HUSSAR-A NEW SHADOW.

While the messengers were gone in quest of the colonel the dying• man asked that the cot of Tom Crawford might be moved to his side. Said he: "I feel it in my heart that Tom will eventually be as a father to my boy. Old Jack,—God bless him I—is not long for this life. He looks strong and rugged, but he will not get up from another serious wound. At all events I want Tom to hear my, story, and I have a sacred charge to give him." Crawford's cot was not far away, and it was very easily removed to Robert's side, as they, lay for a long time with hands clasped. Tom had thought his hours were surely num- bered, but the surgeon had told him if he would strictly obey orders, he might pull through all right, without losing a limb. Col. Harry Maxwell was the eldest son of the Earl of Wenham, and bore the title of Lord Clayburn. He was five-and-thirty years of age, a born soldier, tall, and splendidly formed, brave as the bravest, always cool and collected in the season of greatest danger, making the good and the comfort of his men his chief care, quick and sure to recognise and reward merit, and as sure to detect and punish wickedness. He never inflicted punishment in anger, nor did he refuse to listen to the sincere pleading of the erring. So he was beloved by his soldiers, and he knew that there were many in the regiment who would have laid down life for him willingly and heartily. Both the sergeant and the boy were admitted to the colonel's presence, in a poor, blackened room of a miserable cot, where they found him nursing a woundod foot, but not wounded badly, only a scratch, he said, which would be all well in four-and-twenty hours. The old man pushed his grandson ahead to do the errand, and it was done unflinchingly, and modestly. "Sergeant Robert ! dying! 0, no! We tnust not let the surgeon have his way in this. Of course, I'll go." He called to an orderly, and having procured a soft, easy moccasin for his "scratched" foot, he drew on an undress frock, and was ready to set forth. It was but a few steps to the barn where the wounded of the--th Hussars lay, and Max- well walked without difficulty, but not so our good old sergeant In spite of all his efforts to the contrary he limped badly. The colonel saw, and spoke of it, but the sufferer declared it to be "only a scratch." "No, grandpa,!' spoke up the boy, emphatically. is a deep out, as you know; and you ought to.let the-surgeon•see it." The old man.peolvpooh'd; but the-colonelshook his head, and looked seriousi though he said no more at the time.

"God bless you, Colonel I" fervently ejaculated the dying hussar, ,as Maxwell stood by the low cot. "I am glad you- come. 0, very glad." "I am glad to be able to please you, my dear seargeant, but• sorry to find you in this plight. Doctor, can you give me a grain of hope?" He understood the significant shake of the' head but too well, and he said no more in that direction, but the sufferer himself took up the theme. "No, no, my lord. - I am very near the end, and I know that what I would do in life I must do. quickly. I have a story to tell, and the time may come when my boy will want a friend to speak for him—a friend who knows the truth. Good Old. Jack is here, the boy's grandfather ; . but he is not . young, and he may not live to see my sons man- hood. Tom Crawford is also here, but he is sorely - wounded, and we cannot tell how he may come • out, though I give him a long life to come. So, my• noble, true-hearted commander, you will not wonder - that I wanted you to be here." "I came gladly, my brave comrade, and you. may lay away in your heart the assurance that I will never fail your son, while life is mine, and mine the opportunita to serve him." ' At this point, when Robert had once more , breathed a fervent prayer of blessing, the surgeon signified to him that time was swiftly passing, and that he had . better -tell his story while strength was at his command. Half-a-dozen knapsacks were so arranged at his back as to support him in a sitting posture, . then he was given a generous , draught of diluted brandy, the colonel and the old sergeant eat by his side, the latter holding Percival in a loving embrace, while the surgeon seated him- self where he could mark the throbbing of the weakening pulse. Tom Crawford also sat up, so near his comrade's cot. that he could reach.him with, his hand.,
The dying man addressed the friends assembled, but he seemed to direct his speech chiefly to his commander and to Tom Crawford.

"Colimel," he said, bestowing upon Lord Clay-. burn a look of deep affection,"before I say, another word I want to bear witness with my dying breath to the grand nobility of your., character and to your goodness of heart. 0.! that more of our commanders knew how to win the love and esteem of their men as do you. You .wii believe that this comes from my heart." "Bless you, my dear boy, I 'do believe you, ana I sincerely thank you for your kind words. You may know that I shall remember Ahem gratefully while I live." Robert brushed this band across his eyes, an.d having taken a sip of the cordial, he went on.: "My lord, and you, Tom, mark what I say. Old Jack already.wows much that I have to tell, but it will bo new to you. In the first place, I have a legal right to the name I bear, because when I married I.took the namtl, of my w'f-te but the name by which you have known me is not the name that was given me at the christening font. I surrendered my true family name for myself 'but I' did not surrender it away. from my boy>, and is is my desire, when I ara- no more on,earth, that my sonzhauld assume the name of hie.- fore- fath ei s.

"I come- at- gentle bloodPoit both sick& My mother was. Mary Patten, . daughter of: George Patten; and. George was.. younger sonc, of Sir William Patten, of Ambleton, in Devonshire. The elder brother took the title and the estate, and left sons enough behind him to hold the title in that line for all.time." "That elder brother was Sir Cherie.% Patten?' interrupted the colonel.

"Ye, sire" "Bless. me I knew: him well, and know several of-his sons. Aye, and I knew your mother. I met hal- two or three times at her Uncle Charles's, though loxes but a child,at the time.. But go on. What of your father? A cloud. settled upon die face of the•clymg soldior and a looks of tender compassion. "Eh!. my father was more to. be pitied than blamad. He was brave and generous, noble at heart-,,and full to tho, brim of 10/e and good-will.. He, too,, was a younger son—the youngest of five,. Three of the elder brothers married, and I know- that twc. of them had children. My father was, Captain. Archiball Gordon, q the First Life: Guards."

"Wbat 1" cried) Maxwell, starting as thank ballad: been struck. "Tell me again. Was Archy •&.ordol, of the Guards, at Windsor, your fathex?! He was, sir. Did you know him ?.' ":11)oor Arch 3.7., 1 I knew him well," said the colonel, deeply. affected. "My own father- was second in command of the regiment before ha came to his title. Aye, I knew Ulna. And you---yon— are his son 4"

"His son and only child," returned Robert, wiping a tea-from his cheek. "If you kilew him, sir, you kn,4w his sad fate. It was a hard place that troop—for a poor man of his terepers.ment. He drank„ and drink became his master. And he _gambled. 0! there should be compassion in heaven for my nether, for her lot was cast in sore trial and tribulation. Her, father died in what should have been the prima of his life, his health broken with driuk and his purse emptied at the gaming- table. "rut enough of this. As you probably know, the family seat was at Gordoncroft, in Devonshire. The elder brother, David, had succeeded to the title when I was born. My father died when I was five years oil He had sold his commission during the previous year, and ray mother was left in absolute poverty. The baronet, Sir David, gave her help meanly and grudgingly; but at length the officers of the Life Guards learned of her situation, and they made the remainder of her days comfortable; ,but her bodily powers had been overtaxed, and she knew nothing of health in my remembrance. I was ten years old when she died.

"Shortly before the death of my mother„ Sir David, who was at that time a member of Parlia- ment, was informed that in the event of the expected death her child would be, in all probe. bility, adopted by the Life Guards. The, baronet did not like it. At the time we thought,that he had found a warm corner in his heart, but I was uot log in dinevering *ALIN 11414rea4ed the

iiromidelee which ail—adoption 15Sr- the Guards would give to his poor brother's child. However, he came to see my mother and begged of her that she would allow him to be a father to her son in case she should be taken away. His manner impressed her favourably, and she gave her con- sent.

"Two of my uncles attended my mother's funeral—the baronet, David, and the second brother, Amos, a rector, settled at Gordon. croft. On the following day my mother's scanty effects were disposed of, and my uncles took me away, but not to Gordon Hall. No, it was the rector who was to adopt me. Sir David had told my mother that I should be educated by the churchman, but he had not told her that I was to be made the rector's drudge, his cow boy and turnspit.

"Two weary, miserable years I remained with my uncle, the rector; and then I ran away, resolved to go to sea. After a long and tiresome jaunt— but a blessed relief it was from the life at the rectory—l fund myself in Liverpool, where I found a berth its cabin-boy on board an Indiama.n. -I told the captain the truth—told him my story from beginning to end just as it was,—and he took a liking for me at the outset; and with Captain John Romaine, in the ship Antwerp, I sailed thirteen years, advancing during that time from cabin-boy to second officer. In seventeen-ninety- eight, when I was five-and-twenty years of age. Captain Romaine, on account of broken health and age, retired from the service, and I lay for a time upon my oars, making my home in London with a family where Sergeant John Coverly and his daughter Bessie were boarders. "To fall in love with sweet Bessie Coverly was the result of but a few days' intimacy. And she, at the same time, fell in love with me •; but when I spoke with the sergeant on the subject of marriage he declared emphatically that he would never con- sent that his dear. chi id should marry with a man who followed the sea for a livelihood. For a time I was perplexed, for to give up 'Bessie was not to be thought of; but what could I do for a living ? " tt this point the failing man stopped a third time for rest, and for a draught of cordial, where- upon the old sergeant took up the thread of the story. " Let me give the boy a rest." he said, with a bow trthe colonel: **.l knew that my- danghter Loved this brave fellow, and that she would be unhappy if she did.- not become his wife • but I could not bear the thought of her having a husband who.was to be on the other side of the earth the greater part of the time. However, I fancied I could find a way out of the difficulty. Our regi- ment—l had then been admitted to your troop, my lord—wanted good men, and I did not believe a better than Robert. Gordon could be found. I spoke to him, and he said he would gladly enlist if it could be in our hussars. So he enlisted • and, when he had gained the rank of corporal he and Bessie were married; but not under the name of' Gordon." _

"."No," said Robert, with renewed strength.. '93ut yon have got ahead of the story, old man."' Then to the colonel he continued:. ".Shortly before my enlistment in your troop,, my lord, I received a very polite letter from my uncle, the rector. He had been informed that I was in London, and he wished very much to see me; so to Devonshire I went, and to the rector of Gordoneroft. Never mind the hollow, fulsome, hypocritical reception. First, the reverend uncle had a packet of papers which belonged of right to me, they having been placed in his hands by my mother, he promising most solemnly to keep them sacredly, and to give them to me when I should• have attained my manhood. What might have been the fate of those papers had there not been two living witnesses of their delivery to him, can- not be told. I think he would have kept them from me had he dared; but two officers of the Life Guards had been present when he took them, one of whom, as I afterward learned, had asked him how he had kept faith with his brother's dead wife. Those papers were the marriage certificates of my parents, and of my mother's parents, together with various copies of old church Registers and ancient family records. "Father," he said, turning to old Coverly, "you have that packet now in your keeping. Remember—it is my son's, for him to take in charge when he shall have reached the age of eighteen; or, he may -have it before that, should he earnestly desire it, or should the need arise of referring to thers4 And mark this: Should the ' hand of death be laid upon you while Tom Craw- ford lives, you will turn it over to him. This you promise." "Yes, my son, "And you, Tom, will accept the eharge, and be true to the trust" "If I am spared—yes." And Col. Maxwel promised that, should the need arise, he would accept the trust. "Bless you, my lord! And my boy will .bless you, I know." "I shall ask God to bless our good colonel. He can bless more, than I can," said the boy, , with earnest, heartfelt faith. _ _

"And I will, ask God to bless you, my noble boy. Be sure I will not forget," Maxwell added, as he Aviped the moisture from his eyes. "There is but little more," resumed the failing, hussar, when. he had once again raised the cup of cordial to bin. lips. The rector learned from me that I was planning to enlist in the English army,. and that I was engaged to marry with the daughter of a ergeaut of hussars. He did not seriously • object, but he conferred with the elder brother, , the baronet,, and the latter sent me fifty pounds,. together with a request that I would enlist, under another name thr.as that of - Gordon. IL did not realize at the time the full significance of - the proposition. They knew that my marriage was to follow my enliqment, so if I should enlist under a new name, of course, my wife and children would bear it. I did not love the name,of Gordon ;- I did not even respect itsince my parents had died;. and I threw it off willingly, at the same time. feeling !that I was shaking the drat of Gordoncrofti. from my. feet. "Bat,. mark you, I lid no% take the fifty pouncloi, The thought came to me that it was meant as an inducement to the change of name, and I cast it from me. I simply,- took whet was righteously mine., own, and left: the place, leaving with my unelos. the assurance that my fellows should know me no more as of the family of Gordon, "On my way bank to London I thought. the ma.tter over, and a thrill of satisfaction went through me as thshAhought came to. me that my wife should retain,her own name, and that I would assume the same.. So as Robert Covarly I enlisted, and Robert Coveirly I have been ever since. "But"—and t.he failin3 life seemed to flash up. anew—" I never promised that my son should not bear the name to, which he was entitled: and since entering upon the cam- paign there haebeen an understanding between my father-in•law and myself that, in the event of my death, my boy should assume the name of his sires, and stand before the world, as he has a right to stand, a GOIRDON GORDONCIEOFT. And that shall be done, Whatever name he must bear upon regimental roster, before the. world he shall be known as a Gordon.'

test between us, and you were cocsen betore me." "And I before both of you," put in the old ser- geant, as his commander 'ceased speaking. "Certainly," responded Maxwell, kindly. "You shall not be robbed of a grandsire's sacred right." "And I shall sit here with Percival through the night," the old man continued. "I cannot sleep; so I will watch." "My good sergeant," interposed the surgeon, with an ominous shake of the head, "1 think I will have a word here. Before you commence your watch I will take a look at that thigh of yours. I don't quite like the flush of your face. Let me feel your pulse. -Ah ! I thought so!"

Leaving the colonel to return to his quarters and the boy to keep watch by the side of his dead father, the surgeon took the old sergeant by the arm and led him to another part of the barn, where other surgeons were busy by the light of a large hospital lamp. For a brief space Coverly had thought of objecting, but a moment's serious reflec- tion told him that his wound was growing more and more painful,, and he went along willingly. Upon stripping the sergeant's leg, the surgeon found an ugly wound. It was upon the inside of the thigh, and though it had not reached the great artery it had come very near it, and many impor- tant nerves had been torn and severed. The cut had been made by a ragged, rusty lance, and pieces of clothing had been carried deeply into the wound. A severe inflammation had already set in, and the surgeon saw very plainly that suppuration must follow. The weather was hot, the climate bad, the opportunities for nursing scant, and, last but not least, the patient's age and temperament were against him. " Well, doctor, what think you ?' the old man asked, after the wound had been thoroughly leansed and while an assistant was applying the bandage. "Keep up a good heart, Sergeant.. I'll do the best I can for you." "Pooh! my heart won't fail. Old Jack Cover— ley is too tough to be taken down 'lv such a scratch." "AU right," naded the surgeon; "but you must have a care. I tell yon plainly your wound is a bad one, and you cannot be too careful. An hour later, as the surgeon stopped to take a look at Tom Crawford, the latter asked him in a whisper, so that the boy might not hear, what of old jack. Was he seriously hurt? A glance at Percival, whose face was buried in the clothing of the bed whereon his father's body lay, and the sur- geon replied without hesitation : "The old man's days are numbered. He may live a few days, but a poison is in his blood which no skill on earth cannvezcome.!' "Poor boy !" "Nay, Tom. You shall' get well, and lead the boy up to a bright and worthy life." "God helping me, I will do it 1" spoke the stout Hussar, with soul-sent fervour. (To be continued),
"THE Y DROPPED OFF-POISONED BY MY BLOOD."

There is more or less of an impression upon the minds of some people that statements as to the merits and effects of popular medicines should be received with a 'degree of allowance. That is to say, people are apt to think the proprietors of these articles often enlarge upon and exaggerate the real facts in order to create a de- mand for what they have to sell. We are inclined to believe this is seldom the case, as the intelligent persons who own these medicines are aware that any sort of over-statement tends to injure their sa,les rather than to increase them. The public are sure to form a correct judgment as to the value of an advertised article, and any false claims for it are certain to he recognised and denounced. Honesty is the best policy in this as in all other cases.•
Therefore the reader need not hesitate to accept as true any announcements of which the following is an example : [coin% ]

"1,. Thirza Daniels, of Wrafton, near Barnstaple, do solemnly and sincerely declare, as follows : "-I was always a strong, healthy woman up to the early part of 1879, when I began to.be troubled with my liver and stomach. In July of that year I took a chill from sitting on some wet grass,, and this brought on sciatica and rheumatism. I had, dreadful pain in my hips and legs; it was like knives cutting through me. My.appetite left me, and what little I did eat gave me great pain in the stomach and chest. I had a bad taste in my mouth and pains in the sides and between the shoulders. Finally I- got so weak I had to bring home my eldest daughter from service to look after the house . and my four children. For several months I went on in ; this way. At first Idoetoredmyself, rubbing my joints with a rubbing bottle and: poulticing. Then I sent for - the doctor and he said my blood was poisoned. He blis- tered me and gave me medicine. I was under his care • for. rive months, but I got weaker all the time and went. thitas a skeleton. The pain whilst in bed was very severe. I could scarcely bear it; and I turned and turned,. but I could not find an easy place. Sometimes _I was lifted to the floor and lay there to see if any ease could be got. I became so bad ,I; soot for a doctor from Braunton, but as I ?got no better, \my husband got a recommendation. from the late Colonel Flarding, of•Upcott, and I attended at the dispensary att. Barnstaple four months and then went as an indoor patient in the Barnstaple Infirmary. and was treated by two doctors. They agreed 1 was• blood poisoning, and talked of performing an operation on my thigh, .but concluded not to dolt, saying I was too- weak. ThGy blistered, me again, and no relief from. this,. they applied leeches, but as fast as the leeches were put on they dropped off.„ poisoned by my blood. I was so, low-spirited in.the. hospital that I felt if I clld ,not got- home I should dia-soon, so they made arrangements.to. take me away. When I got in the open air my senses left me, and they- thought I was dying. After reaching home I was-in great agony, and sent my husband for our doctor. His. said he would come, but it was of, no use, as he coulado no more than he had done. klag for weeks, and was so bad that when people speke to me I had not the strength to reply. At this time,iny nepbeWt Robert Daniels, of Pontypridd, sent MS word te trY Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, as it had worked wonderful mres in the district where he lived. So mY husband went to Mr. Farley's, the grocer,, Barnstaple; and bought a. bottle. Before I had taken all of that bottle I could oat, and my food seemed to do me good. By degrees I got stronger and stronger, and after taking fourteen bottles I was strong and healthy. My flesh came-on and all pain, left my thighs and legs, and I have never ailed anything to speak of since. I thank God for making Seigel's Syrup known to me. I owe my life to. it, and I wish ethers to know what I say. I consider it the Lord's doing,, and I will lie Oct to answer any inquiries.

div.head: IMPERIAL PABLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PABLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. THE EASTERN ,QUESTION.LOrdS STRATHENDEN and CAMPBELL having called attention to the correspondence on Turkey, moved for further papers in connection with the Eastern Question. Lord SALISBURY said that papers were in preparation, and if moved for would be laid on the table. The motion was agreed to. The House adjourned at 5.15. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE JUDICIAL BINCH.—Mr. W. H. SMITH informed Mr. Cobb, who drew attention to a newspaper article refer- ring to the inability of one of her Majesty's .judges to per- form his judicial duties, that the Government had no authority over the judges of the land. If the hon. mem- ber had reason to believe there was failure of justice he could present an address to the Crown praying for the removal of the judge complained of. EGYPT AND TOKAR.—Sir J. FERGUSSON told hon. mem- bers that the Egyptian Government had resumed its au- thority in the district about Tokar, that a proclamation i had been issued granting an amnesty to all except some notorious slave dealers, that-of the prisoners taken '231 had been released, but that 300 who were considered dangerous are still detained. '4 EDUCATION IN BIRKENHEAD AND RUNCORN.—Mr. MUN- DELLA asked the Vice-President of the Committee of Council on Education if his attention had been called to the statement of Mr. Kynnersley., her Majesty's Inspector, published in the last general report of Mr. Blandford, her Majesty's Inspector, that `• it is now only in Birkenhead and Runcorn that we have really objectionable build- ings," and to the statement recently made by the chair- man of the School Attendance Committee of that borough that the number of school places in the public elemen- tary schools of the borough of Birkenhead, measured at Bft. per child, is 15,665."—5ir W. HART-DYE: I have seen Mr. Kynnersley's statement to which the right hon. gentleman refers. If the right hon. gentleman had pur- sued his investigation a little further he might have ob- served that the Inspector goes on to notice the extraordi- nary fluctuations to which the population of Birkenhead is liable. That being so, I prefer to await the result of the forthcoming census before expressing an opinion as to the accuracy of the Registrar-General's estimate. The number of school places in Birkenhead is 15,688, but the highest weekly average during any part of last year was only 14,389. SUPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of Supply, when the supplementary vote of £350,000 for the navy was, after some discussion, agreed to, as was one of £2OO for the London and Sheriffs' Police Courts. The supplementary vote of £11,484 for West and South Africa gave rise to a long debate, chiefly concerning the liquor traffic in Swaizland and the treatment .of the natives. _
The House adjourned at 12 28. HOUSE OF LORDS.--TuilveY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at half-past five. FIRST READING, &c.—The Seed Potatoes Supply (Ire- land) Bill was read a first time. The report of amend- ments to the Elementary Education (Blind and Deaf) Bill "was received and agreed to. The House adjourned at a quarter to six. HOUSE OF COMMONS,---Ittrasnev.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE RECTOR OF ASIITON-IN-MABERFLELD.—Mr. CALEB WRIGHT asked the Home Secretary whether he was - aware that, notwithstanding his expression of opinion to • the Rev. W. J. Melville rector of Holy Trinity, Ashton- . in-Makerfield, that such an instruction was contrary to the spirit of the Burial Act, 1880, the bills issued in con- nection with interments in the churchyard still contain • the instruction that breadths or graves were appropri- ated only on condithon that no other than the Church of :England service is used; and whether, in view of the fact that the inhabitants of theparish were deterred from availing themselves of the provisions of the Act of 1880, ,steps would be taken to prevent such imitation of the rights of parishioners ? Mr. MirraEws.—The opinion which I expressed to the Rector on a former occasion was -to the effect that it appeared contrary to the spirit of • the Act to stipulate beforehand that a grave where a Church service is usea chall be in any respect superior to other graves. The Led then assured me this is not the case, and he now repe.cs this assurance. The Rector, however, still insists upon his right to select the part of the churchyard where any interment shall take place, and denies any obligation to sell or appropriate graves to any families or individuals to the exclusion of others. This is a question of law as to which I have stated before it is not my duty to express an opinion. The Rector informs Me that no dissatisfaction has been expressed among his parishioners, and that the provisions of the Act .of 1880 are always loyally carried out by him. REMOVAL OF CATTLIC.—Mr. CHAPLIN, in reply to Dr. Tanner, said he was unable to remove the resttictions affecting the cattle trade in Lancashire so as to allow the free movement of Irish fat cattle. They were subject to the usual inspection under the English Pleuro-Pneumonia Order, and there appeared to be no reason for making an -exception. in their case. ECCLESIASTICAL COMMISSIONERS AND LICENSED PRE- MisEs.—Afr. W. H. Sums told Mr. Winterbothan2 that the Ecclesiastical Commissioners were the owners of a /lumber of licensed premises, but they were reducingthe

-number as far as pos.sible. FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.—MT. HOWARD VINCENT called Attention to the condition of friendly societies in the United .Kingdom, and moved that the encour- agement of more general voluntary provision for ' •aNkness and old age should engage the atten- tion of het Majesty's Government, and that the • Sound principles of provident insurance should be in- Chided in the subjects prescribed by the Education Code for instructionin elementary schools. The hon. member urged that the efforts of friendly societies should be seconded by a capitation grant of ss. or 10s. per mem- ber per annum, the amount to be capitalised as a provi- sion against the old age of the member.—Sir R. PAGET •seconded the motion, which was characterized by Mr. Broadhurst as socialist.—The discussion was being con- tinued when attention was drawn to the fact that there 'were not 40 members present,and the House was counted out at 7.55.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock, but the House was not made.through the medium of a count) until twenty-five minutes past twelve o'clock, when business was proceeded with. THE SMALL HOLDINGS BILL.—MT. JESSE COLLINGS moved the second reading of the Small Holdings Bill, the object of which is to provide facilities for the acquisition of land by the rural population. Sir H. SELWIN-IBBET- SON and Mr:Cusr supported the measure' and Sir W. Foster, while sympathising with its objects, thoughtthat some of its provisions required amendment. Mr. CHAP- LIN said the Government were prepared to assent to the Principle of the bill and support its second reading, but at the same time he could not approve of all its provi- Aims. Sir W. HAnconwr warmly supported the measure but declared that it would be inoperative unless the Government choose to create a capable and willing authority armed with compulsory powers, and unless cheap transfer7of land was secured. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN tarmly supported the Bill and ridiculed the tone of Sir LY. Harcourt's warning. The Bill was read a second ume. GAmp BILL.—The second reading of the Possession of Game Bill was carried by 1.47 to 95 votes. Other bills 'Were advanced. COMPENSATION FOR SUBSIDENCE. —Mr. ACKERS-DOUGLAS 'toyed that the Select Committee on Brine Pumping (Compensation for Subsidence) consist of Mr. Gainsford Bruce, Colonel Hill, Mr. Lyell, and Mr. Mather, with three members added by the Committee of Selection. This was agreed •to. TOWN HOLDINGS COMMITTEE .—The Committee 011 OW Holdings was then reappointed, on the under- 'standing that on a future day two new members should U e added. The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Lord Chanceller took his seat on the woolsack at half-past four o'clock. birscELLANHous.—The Clergy DiScipline (Immorality) t'aitdh been through Committee after some amendments T o made. On the report of amendments to the Rent Charge Recovery Bill, Lord BRABOURNE COP- PLaei ed of so little time having been given to the con- thourration of the Standing Committee's amendments.— t'LLue d SALISBURY defended the course he had taken, and **Port 'was received. The Elementary Education (8/iild and Deaf) Bill wasread a third time and passed.

div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three. QUESTIONS &c.—Mr. RITCHIE replied to Mr. Herbert Gladstone regarding a prosecution at Barrow, on the, strength of the borough analyst's certificate, for selling vinegar alleged to have been adulterated with 33-4 per cent of water, but which was found to be genuine com- mercial vinegar of low quality. Dr. Cameron called atten- tion to certain statements by Dr. Rentoul, of Liverpool, as to the great number of interments of stillborn Chil- dren, and Mr. Ritchie promised to consider the practica- bility of obtaining figures. Mr. Marrumws informed Mr. Broadhurst that he intended to introduce the Employers' Liability Bill as soon as the state of public business per- mitted. Mr. Surni replied to Mr. Gladstone and others on the course of public business, indicating that the ad- journment would propably be from March 25th to April Bth. Sir JAMES FERGUSSON informed Sir G. Baden- Powell that a reference to arbitration of the dispute with France regarding the Newfoundland fisheries had been signed. A new writ was issued for Aston Manor. 'ma LIGHT RAILWAYS.—The House went into Com- mittee of Supply, and on the vote of £55,831 for certain expenditure connected with the relief of distress in Ire- land, Mr. Balfour explained in great detail what had been done in this direction by the building of light railways, which, although, not originally intended for the relief of distress, were eventually hurried on with that effect. About 8,000 men had been employed in the West, and £40,000 spent in wages. -Mr. J. Morley, Colonel Nolan, and SirJ. Pope Hennessy criticised Mr. Balfour's state- ment. \' ment. The discussion was continued `until midnight, when Mr. SMITH moved the closure. This was agreed to on a division. The House ran through the remaining orders, and adjourned at ten minutes to one o'clock.
ABDUCTING HIS OWN WIFE.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY CASE.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY CASE.

A Clitheroe corresplondent says: As the congregation were leaving the Parish Church, on Sunday, after morn- ing service, a carriage drove up containing three gentle- men, one of whom seized Mrs. H. H. Jackson at the church gate, and, with the assistance of the others. carried her into the carriage, and drove off to Blackburn. The chief abductor was Mr. Jackson, the husband, who had obtained a decree for the restitution of conjugal rights, his wife having refused to live with him since their marriage in 1887. When the carriage reached Blackburn, it pulled up at the residence of Mr. Jackson, into which Mrs. Jackson was quickly carried. The doorsand windows were then barricaded, and the blinds drawn. An hour later, a carriage, containing a number of excited friends of Mrs. Jackson' dashed up, and, headed by Mr. Baldwin, the family lawyer, demanded admittance, which was refused. A great crowd gathered, and the lady's friends threatened to storm the house, but the police arrived and prevented them. Mrs. Jackson was a Miss Hale, of Clitheroe, and pos- sessed a fortune of £47,000. She married Mr. Jackson privately, unknown to her friends, and on the day of the wedding the bridegroom left for Australia. When he returned inlBB9 his wife refused to cohabit with him. He obtained a judge's order for the restoration of con- jugal rights, and forcibly executed it on Sunday. The crowd remained round the house all night, and the excitement continued.

div.head: CHARGE OF ASSAULT.
div.p: CHARGE OF ASSAULT.

A special Sitting of the Clitheroe magistrates was held on Wednesday, to hear a charge of assault which had been made against Mr. Jackson, Dr. Robinson, and Mr. D. Robinson in connection with the carrying off of Mrs. Jackson from Clitheroe, on Sunday. By arrangement with the police, the three defendants were present in the precincts of the court, but on the case be- ing called,Mx.Waugh, who appeared for them, said they were awaiting arrest under the warrants which had been issued. He said the issue of warrants under such circumstances was illegal and unjustifiable. The magistrates, in view of an undertaking given by the de- fendants to be in attendance, declined to order the exe- cution of the warrants, and Mr. Waugh thereupon sub- mitted that there was nothing before the ,court. Mr. M'Connell, who represented the complainant (a sister of Mrs. Jackson), applied for summonses against the three defendants. The application was granted, and the in- struments, having been prepared, were served upon the defendants outside the court.. Upon the attendance of the defendants, Mr. M'Connell applied for an adjourn- ment of the case, on the grounds that he had not received his brief, and that access to Mrs. Jackson, whom the complainant desired to call as a witness, had been denied to them. Mr. Waugh urged that the case should proceed, but after discussion it was adjourned till Mon- day, the 23rd inst. The defendants were lotnlly cheered on their appearance in the streets. Intense excitement ,was created in Blackburn on Thurs- day afternoon by the publication of report that Mr. Jackson intended to carry his wife out of the country. Large numbers of people in consequence again visited the houseat West-view, where they found doors and windows still barricaded, and the pickets of both forces on the .alest. Interviewed by telephone, both Mr. Jackson and his solicitors utterly repudiate any intention to abandon their position. Mr. Jackson's friends are highly indig- ant that such a statement has been made.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.
THE NATIONALIST SPLIT.

Messrs. John O'Connor, °Welly, W. Redmond, and Harrison, Parnellite members of Parliament, left Queens- town on Tuesday, on board the Cunard steamer Etruria, for New York, Mr. O'Connor and Mr. O'Kelly joined the steamer at Liverpool, and on Mr. O'Connor disembark- ing at,Queenstown, to await the arrival of Messrs. Red- mond and Harrison, who travelled by train from Dublin, he met with a hostile reception. Messrs. Redmond and Harrison reached the terminus at Queenstown shortly before mid-day. They were accompanied by the Mayor of Cork, and some members of the Cork Town Council. On their alighting from the train there was a good deal of groaning and hissing., and afterwards several ineffect- ual attempts were made to present the hon. members with an address. The hon. members afterwards em- barked amidst cheers and hisses. Meetings of Mr. Parnell's supporters and opponents respectively were held in Mitchelstown on Sunday. At one of the meetings the Rev. T. Morrison, chairman, declared that the resolutions published in Mr. Parnell's favour, along with other manifestations of sympathy, were manufactured by paid agents of Mr. Parnell.

MR. PARNELL AT NEWRY. Mr. Parnell left Dublin on Saturday for Newry, and, addressing a gathering at :the station, said he was confi- dent that Ulster was as sound on his side as other pro- vinces in Ireland. At Newry, Mr, Pullen was received by a large crowd, and accompanied to his hotel by a torchlight procession. On Sunday Mr. Parnell was pre- sented with addresses from various bodies, and in reply, said that the assurances given to Mr. M'Carthy, who claimed to be the leader of the Irish party, left the solu- tion of the land question in the hands of the Imperial Parliament, which was an important matter for the men of Ulster. He added that his party did not desire to trespass upon any prerogative of the Crown, but they would accept no settlement as final that would not secure to them the control ef their own business. NEW NATIONAL FEDERATION. Under the presidency of Mr. Justin McCarthy, a large and representative company of Irish Nationalists assem- bled in the Ancient Concert Rooms in Dublin, on Tues- day, for the purpose of establishing the National Federa- tion—the new party erganisation. Letters warmly ap- proving the object of the meeting were read from the Raman Catholic Archbishops and most of the Bishops of the various dioceses. Mr. McCarthy in his speech re- ferred to the negotiations at Boulogne, and said it was only when they found union impossible that they in- vited their countrymen to come together in support of the Parliamentary party. They stood there on principle, determined that no personal ambition should come be- tween them and national liberty. They would shave no more fetish worship and no more dictatorship. Mr. Sexton and Mr. Healy also spoke. A motion formally establishing the Federation was passed. Mr. Davitt, moving the appointment of the executive, strongly con- demned Mr. Parnell's late indefinite appeal to the hill- side men and the party of force. They would refuse to believe in Mr. Parnell's capacity to win for Ireland by any means,legal or revolutionary, what Ireland demanded for her contentment and prosperity. The "Star "says :—A strong meeting of Nationalists was held in Dublin on Tuesday, and a National organis- ation established. Mr, Parnell taking advantage of the delay caused by the Nationalists from their desire to pro- mote peace—a desire in which he never shared—got possession of the National League machinery. In order to avoid unnecessary friction, the Nationalists did not attempt to cease the organisation. They have created the National Federation, which will take all the old Leaguers away from Mr. Parnell and leave him with a skeleton. ,
