div.head: TUE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 14. 1891.
div.p: TUE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 14. 1891.
TERRIBLE WEATHER.
GALE AND SNOWSTORM. MANY TRAINS BLOCKED. SHIPPING DISASTERS AND GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

A snowstorm of great severity, accompanied by a tar- rific gale of wind from the north-east, passed over the south, south-east, and south-west of England and Wales on Monday afternoon and during Tuesday night, and ac- cording to telegrams, there has been no storm which has approached it in severity since the memorable blizzard, which occurred in January, 1881. The two Englisb counties which have suffered the most by the storm are I Kent and Sussex, on the coasts of which the wind seems to have centred its fury thereby causing a sad loss of life. SIX LIFEBOATMEN DROWNED. The Press Association's Sandgate correspondent tele- graphs that during the storm on Monday night, three vessels were observed off the Littlestone in distress, one of them being on fire. The coastguard lifeboat from Lynd,in response to the signals of distress, went out,but was capsized, and six of her crew were drowned. Five of the bodies have been recovered.

INQUEST. The inquest on the six bodies of the coastguardsmen and seamen who perished in the gale off Dungeness was held at Littlestone. on Wednesday. In the case of the seamen death resulted from exposure. The coastguards' men, Thomas Sullivan, Samuel Hart, and another whose body has not yet been recovered, were rowned by the capsizing of the lifeboat. The evidence showedthat the lifeboat was launched in a very heavy sea with a crew of eleven instead of 13 hands, Sullivan, the chief boat- man, being a volunteer. All the men behaved nobly. showing no hesitation in going out, but they could not get the boat clear of the surf, and, being broadside on, she was constantly swept by heavy seas and eventually capsized.—A verdict of" Accidentally &owned " was returned, and the jury expressed admiration of the con- ctuct of the crew, and suggested a public subscription for the benefit of the bereaved families.

VENTNOR. No such weather has been experienced in Ventnor since H.M,S. Eurydice sank in March, 1878. The storm. was also very severe at Ryde and Pickfords. The luggage vessel Midge had her stern stove in, and was wrecked. The yacht Semphore was wrecked on the Black Knolls, Walton-on-Maze, early on Tuesday morning, and the owner named M'Laren was drowned. A schooner also stranded on Gunfleet Sands, Walton-on-Maze, and the crew took to the rigging pending the arriva lof a life- boat.

BRIDGWATER. The Great Western mail train from Plymouth was snowed up near Newton Abbott, and two up trains were locked between Exeter and Taunton. A train was snowed up at Dunster, and another train at Watrlet, traffic being entirely suspended. The same condition of things prevailed on the North Devonbranch, a tram be- ing snowed up at South Molton.

CARDIFF. The snowstorm throughout the Rhondda Valley has been very severe, and nearly 40 large collieries were practically at a standstill, about 20,000 colliers being idle. Engine drivers who have worked on the Taff Vale , Railway for forty years declare that they have never ex- perienced such a blizzard. The French schoonei St. Anne, Captain Coire, went ashore at Penarth, but the crew were saved. A chimney fell at Cwmavon killing two children. The mail drievr had to bring the mails from Lydney to Monmouth on horseback, the cart having stuck fast in the snow Two sloops passed Sandgate on Tuesdayoheipless, with their sails torn to shreds. The club boat Victoria, which left Dover at five o'clock on Monday evening with the Duchess of 'Edinburgh and Lady Rothschild on board, had a terribly rough passage, and did not arrive at Calais until nine o'clock on Tuesday morning. The scenes at Hastings on Monday night during the attempt to 'bring the fishing fleet into harbour were most exciting. There were a number of accidents, and five smacks were broken to pieces, but it was not known until Tuesday morning how many lives had been lost. It was then ascertained that three poor fellows were missing, having been drowned. The damage to the fishermen's boats is esti- mated at £l,OOO. _

board early on Tuesday morning. The steamer left Guernsey on Monday, and after being at sea a. few hours met the full force of the bizzard in the English Channel. Sea after sea swept her decks, partially dis- mantling her, and eventually extinguishing the fires. when on the verge of foundering, the vessel was taken in tow to Portland by the steamer Headworth. A telegram from Chard on Wednesday night, says that snew had fallen for 48 hours and there was no commu- nication with the villages in the district, the drifts being from ten to 20 feet deep. Several personsare missing. There was a renewal of the snowstorm on the north- east coast of Yorkshire on Wednesday. Largedrifts have accumulated in the neighbourhood of Scarborough, and traffic is seriously impeded. Several fishingboats which returned to port owing to stress of weather, have again put to sea. Lloyd's report that the schooner Lizzie Ellen has been totally wrecked in Start Bay. Two hands were drowned. The schooner Lunesdale, of Barrow-in-Furnesss has been totally wrecked in Start Bay, four hands being drowned. The captain was saved. The full extent of the storm in the west is now be- coming known on the partial resumption of the tele- graphic service. Just outside Falmouth, the steamer Dundelia, of Beltast,sfrom St. Michael's, with fruit went ashore at Portloe, and will become a total wreck. One life was lost. Not far distant a German steamer, the T. Carl Heneberg, in ballast from Cardiff, drove ashore in Portscathe Creek. On the other sideof the bay a large vessel, called the Bay of Panama, of London, on a voy- age from Calcutta to Dundee, with jute, drove on the rocks when the hurricane was at its height. Most of the crew were saved by the rocket apparatus, but the captain, his wife, and officers perished. Close to this terrible disaster two small vessels are supposed to have gone down with all hands. The snowstorm was renewed in various parts of the Principality, on Wednesday, greatly impeding railway and vehicular traffic. A married woman named Derby, endeavouring to cross the uplands near Llynpia, was overtaken by the storm and perished in the snow. An old man named Bennett, an inmate of Merthyr Work- house, was also found dead in a gulley at Penydaren. Two miners, named John Lewis and Alfred Price. were likewise found in an e4hausted condition ou the hills near Cwmthlary. Lewis succumbed shortly afterwards, and Price is not expected to recover. Another death from exposure is reported from Llansamlet. Snow has drifted to great depths on the mountain ranges, and the upland farmers report heavy losses of ewes and lambs. - - - - • -

The following were wrecked in Start Bay :—Barque Dryad, of Liverpool, losing all hands; schooner Lunes- dale, of Barrow, captain only saved; schooner Lizzie Ellen, of Chester, two drowned. CLEARING THE LINES. The Press Association says ,the great railway blocks in the west and south-west of England caused by the snow- drifts are gradually being removed, but some districts are still cut off from railway communication. Trains are running between Bath and Bournemouth with fair punc- tuality. One line has been cleared on the South-Western Railway between Exeter and Plymouth. The Great Western main line from Exeter to Totnes is cleared, and on Monday night's express from London to Plymouth passed Totnes on Thursday morning, but is now stopped at Brent, beyond Totnes. Passengers had terrible experiences. A foreign steamer was wrecked during the off Start, with all hands. A LIVERPOOL SHIP AND 24 LIVES LOST. It was ascertained on Thursday, that several lives were lost as a consequence of the wreck of the ship Bay, of Panama. The captain was David Wright, of Liver- pool, and he, along with his wife, the chief officer, and eleven of the crew, was drowned. The Liverpool barque Dryad has been wrecked off the Start, and it is believed that all on board, numberingtwenty-four, have perished.

ACCIDENT IN AN IRONWORKS. Early on. Wednesday morning, while a tube was being heated at a furnace at Blochairn Ironworks and Steel Company, of Scotland, the metal exploded with terrible force. One of the workmen, John Singleton was disem- bowelled by the flying metal and died, and Singleton, others were terribly burned. It is supposed that moisture in the tube caused the explosion.

div.head: DEAL.
div.p: DEAL.

The gale raged over Deal and the Downs all Monday night, and there was a tremendous sea in the Downs. A lifebuoy was picked up on. Tuesday morning with the name " Niagara " upon it, and a large quantity of wreck- age has since been recovered. The Niagara is a schooner belonging to•Fowey, and the wreckage corresponds to a vessel of her description. It is believed that she foun- dered snddenly, and that her crew were lost, as no boat could haverlived in such a sea. Up to a late hour on Tuesday no train had arrived at Deal from London.

div.head: RAMSGATE,
div.p: RAMSGATE,

The lifeboat .men were on the alert, and at 2 a.m. a flare was seen in the Channel, as if from a vessel drifting before the wind. The snow squalls were blinding, and it was utterly impossible to find the vessel. The maiicart from Dover to Ramsgate could not get through because of the depth of snow upon the roads, and owing to the fact that the London, Chatham, and Dover line was blocked, the town was without letters until about noon.
NEWHAVEN,

Five men belonging to the fishing vessel Welcome Home, of Folkestone, walked here from Beachy Head on Tuesday morning, their vessel having run ashore at one a.m. The men were exposed to the severity of the storm the whole night,and are suffering from the effects of their exposure. The tidal-train from London due at Newhaven at 10.30 on Monday night, was snowed up about a mile from Newhaven until 6.50 on Tuesday morning, the pas- sengers being compelled to remain in the train.

div.head: FAVERSHAM.
div.p: FAVERSHAM.

The local down train, hich should have reached Faversham at 10 30 on Monday evening, was snowed up in Beacon Hill cutting, and the passengers were im- prisoned all night. The passengers were taken to their destination on Tuesday morning by a special train. THE STORM CONIINUED. MORE SHIPPING CASUALTIES. FURTHER LOSS OF LIFE.

The two Lowestoft colliers the Lord Exmouth and ,the Advance have been lost in the North sea, the former off Flamborough Head, and the latter near Blakeney, but the,crews were saved. The Duke of _Edinburgh, who was snowbound at Taunton On Tuesday night, was able on Wednesday to proceed, with about 200 other delayed passengers, as far as Exeter, but there was little prospect of his Royal Highness proceeding further. Reports from the west of England yesterday state that great loss has been experi- enced among cattle and sheep. A Weymouth correspondent telegraphs that seven survivors of the steamer Neptune, of Newcastle, on being landed at Weymouth on Wednesday afternoon, reported the loss of the captain and first mate, named respec- tively Eastwood and Green, who were washed over-

div.head: TILE LABOUR COMMISSION.
div.p: TILE LABOUR COMMISSION.

A Cabinet Council was held,on Saturday at the Foreign Office. Ministers were reticent as to the chairmanship of the Royal Commission on Labour, but unofficial members believe this position will be filled by Mr. .Goschen. The' Observer" says the Committee of the Cabinet charged with the duty of nominating the Labour Com- mission have had under their consideration a proposal, urged from various quarters,to include in the commission one or more women having special knowledge of ques- tions affecting working women and children. They have, we understand, decided that the suggestion is practicable.

div.head: BREACH OF PROMISE CASES.
div.p: BREACH OF PROMISE CASES.

At Chester Assizes, on Tuesday, Benjamin Bennett, a butcher and cattle dealer in a large way of business at Flint, of which borough he is an ex-town Councillor, was the defendant in an extraordinary ,ction for breach of promise brought by Hannah Ede Maddocks, widow of a ship's cook. The defendant, who is a married man, stoutly denied that he had ever courted the plaintiff or passed her off as his wife at an hotel where they had sojourned a night. Bennett's counsel retired from the case, and a verdict was given for the plaintiff, damages £275. In the same court Mary Jones, a domestic ser- vant atLlangollen, was awarded £5 damages against a brewer's traveller named Robert Lloyd for breach of promise. At Chester Assizes, on Wednesday, a Macclesfield widow named Emma Clarke brought an action against Joseph Dentithe, aged seventy-seven, a retired provi- sion merchant, to recover damagcs for breach of pro- mise. The plaintiff, who had already buried two hus- bands, was sought in marriage by a man who had thrice .previously entered into tnatrnnonal bonds. Theplaintiff was more than 50 years of age.; the defendant had reached the mature age of 'l7. He is nearly blind, and suffers much from asthma ; but even with this complica- tion of disabilities weighing upon him he had the cour- age, after seeing his third wife comfortably interred last May, to" commission "a friend to provide him with another. The friend's choice fell upon Mrs. Clarke, who was then drowning her grief for the loss of her" second" in the busy distractions of a muffin shop at Macclesfield. A wedding was arranged for, but on the fatal day the asthmatic bridegroom changed his mind,and Mrs. Clarke, who had given up the muffin business, is compelled to rely for her maintenance upon the profits she derives from the sale of old clothes. The defendant acknow- ledged the " breach " and paid £5O into court ; and the Jury intimated that in their opinion that amount was " enough and too much "—a verdict with which the .Judge was able to agree.

div.head: SIR EDGAR BOEHM'S WILL.
div.p: SIR EDGAR BOEHM'S WILL.

Mr. Justice Jeune delivered judgment on Tuesday in reference to the will of the late Sir Edgar Boehm. The testator, it was said, had inter.ded to leave £lO,OOO each to his daughters lieorgiana and Florence, but by the mistake of a conveyancer the name of Georgiana had been inserted twice, and that of Florence omitted. Pro- bate of the will was now granted, with the name of Georgiana struck out in the second instance.
THE ALLEGED JUDICIAL SCANDAL

Correspondence between Mr. Cobb, M.P., and Mr. W. H. Smith regarding the alleged judicial scandal is pub- lished. Mr. Cobb says he no longer hesitates, in answer to the challenge thrown out, to state that the Judge indi- cated is Mr. Justice Stephen. Mr. Smith complains that no specific allegation as to a failure of justice has been made, and says that any member of Parliament is equally entitled with the Government to move an address to the Crown.
, THE ASTON MANOR. ELECTION.

There is a " deadlock " in regard to the Aston election. It seems that the " Whips " have been unable to aszertain definitely whether Mr. Kynoch is dead. The Unionist leaders state that the" Whips" have communicated with Johannesburg, and have received a reply saying that no information can be obtlined as to Mr. Kynoch's death, and it is expected that a question on the subject will be asked in the House of Commons. _
On Thursday evening the difficulty was got over,a new writ for Aston Manor, for the election of a member in room of the late Mr. Kynoch, being ordered in the House of Commons.

div.head: SHOCKING MURDER AND SUICIDE AT
div.p: SHOCKING MURDER AND SUICIDE AT
BURY.

At six o'clock. on Thursday night, a horrible tragedy took place in High-street, Bury, a bucher named James Chadwick murdering his paramour, named Mary Stott, and then committing suicide. Chadwick, who appears to have borne a bad character, was 35 years of age, and although he had a wife living in the adjoining town of Radcliffe, he had lived with Stott for seven years. Re- cently sheleft him, went to work at some mills, and lived with a Mrs. Manock, near the High-st. Chadwick had been persistent in his endeavours to bring about a recon- ciliation, but the woman resolutely refused to return to him. On Thursday night he followed her home, and, having obtained a butcher's knife, drew it across her face, inflicting terrible wounds from ear to ear. He then stabbed her to the heart. Following up his act, he in- flicted severe wounds on his own throat.and had renewed the attack on his victim when Mrs. Manock took the knife from him. He then seized a table knife ,and with it nearly severed his head from his body.

div.head: EARL SPENCER ON IRELAND.
div.p: EARL SPENCER ON IRELAND.

Earl Spencer was the principal speaker at a Liberal meeting on Wednesday night at Rochdale. His speech was largely devoted to Ireland. It had, he said, been his lot during nearly the whole of his political career to be intimately connected with that country. For eight years he had the honout of representing Her Majesty there, and not only did that give him the greatest attachment to the Irish people, but it also created in him a deep interest in the remedies for removing the defects of Irish government which he knew so well existed. Referring to the Parnell episode and the attitude of the late Irish leader towards Mr. Gladstone, Earl Spencer denied that there had been any attempt at dictation on the part of the latter. Events had shown that he had taken a just and wise course. Thetentinuance of Mr. Parnell as Irish leader would not have been accepted by this conntry, and the cause of Home Rule would have been thrown back many years. In spite of what had taken place, the Liberal party would ask the country at the next election whether it was in favour of Lord Salisbury and coercion or Mr. Gladstone and local self-government for Ireland. Lord Spencer also referred to free education, Fair Trade, and reform of the registration laws.

div.head: WA:RIAGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WA:RIAGTON COUNTY COURT.

A sitting of this court was held on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. The cause list comprised 5 adjourned plaint summonses, 1 default summons, 210 original plaint summonses, and 27 original judgment summonses. There were no causes of public interest. AN ABSCONDING BANKRUPT.—Mr. Forshaw, solicitor Otfessrs. Davies and Forshaw), made applica- tion to his Honour Judge Ffoulkes for a warrant for the arrest of John Blumenay, a banlcrupt, formerly carrying on business as a furniture aealer, in Win- wick-street, Warrington. The application was made on behalf of the trustee, Mr. George Graham Poppleton, chartered accountant, Birmingham, and in support of it Mr. Forshaw said that a receiving order was made against Blumenay on the 28th January last, and pro- duced affidavits setting forth that there was every reason to believe that the bankrupt had absconded, in order to avoid payment of his debts. One of the affidavits, sworn by a former assistant of Blumenay's, stated that Blum- enay had told him he was about to go either to Vussia or America. He made over his book debts to his two assist- ants in lieu of paying them a considerable sum that he owed as wages. In the other affidavits it was pointed out that Blumenay had realised on his furniture and stock.—His Honour said that a warrant would be granted on the ground that Blumenay had absconded.

div.head: ARPLEY DROWNING CASE.
div.p: THE ARPLEY DROWNING CASE.

An inquest was held by Mr. Coroner Brighouse at the Higher Seven Stars, Bridge-st., on Saturday afternoon, touching the death of a man who was found drowned in the three cornered pit in Arpley Meadows, the previous morning,as already recorded. Thos. Holcroft, a boy living in Speakman's Yard, Latchford, said he saw the deceased going under the iron bridge one night last week—he thbouglA it was Wednesday.—Police-Sergeant Bowen said the lad had told him it was Thursday night, and the man could not have lain in the pit all Thursday without being discovered by the numerous passers by.—The boy adhered to the statement he now made, and further said that the deceased seemed to be walking steadily.—Sergeant Bowen said the the place where the boy saw him would be about 500 yards from the pit.—Stephen Cook deposed to find- ing the body about 7 o'clock on Friday morning eight feet irom the side, and said the deceased could not have walked from the footway straight into the water as there were some railings. It was not a likely place for him to be drowned in accidentally. There were no marks on the body. He Lad on him a knife, a purse, a lead pencil, a halfpenny, and a ticket for Dutton Workhouse.—The Coroner read the ticket, which had on it .the name of William Chard.and he pointed out that as this was not proof of his identity he must be considered as unknown, there being no one present to identify him.—The jury returned a verdict that the deceased, being a man unknown, was found drowned in the pit, but that how he got into the water there was no evi- dence to show.—The Coroner said in case the man's identity was subsequently proved he had the authority to have the register altered by the inser- tion of the deceased's name. SIR CHARLES DILBE AND THE FOREST I NAVVIES MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON. • OF DEAN. Sir Charles Dunce, who has been asked to come forward as the candidate for the Forest of Dean division, visited Cinderford on Monday and addressed ,the Liberal Four Hundred. Mr. Provost, the vice-president of the Liberal Four Hundred, moved, and the Rev. J. George, a Baptist minister, seconded a resolution expressing confidence in the moral integrity and distinguished ability of Sir Charles Dilke, the belief that that confidence was shared by the constituency and the mass of the English pevie, who heartily welcoming him as the only candidate who could unite the constituency. Replying to questions which had been asked in various quarters, Sir Charles said he had been dismissed from the first trial with costs, and that the issue of the second trial was not whether he had been guilty of adultery, but whether the intervention of the Queen's Proctor was justified. He complained that at this trial he was not allowed to be represented by ccunsel, and said the "Pall Mall Gazette' had grossly mis-stated the verdict. The jury did not find that he had committed adultery. They simply found that the Queen's Proctor had not succeeded in showing that the verdict was against the weight of evidence. After he had stated that the declarations attesting his innocence would undoubtedly be published later, the resolution was adopted amid great enthusiasm. Sir Charles, in reply, said he was touched and inspirited by the resolu- tion, and was sanguine that he should return to public life strengthened and not weakened by suffefing. But they must await his final acceptance of the invitation until the constituency had had time to ratify the choice, and then it would be his proud duty to accept the position of candidate.

On Sunday morning an outdoor meeting in con- nection with the Navvies', Bricklayers' Labourers, and General Labourers' Union, was held at Bridge Foot, Warrington. Some 200 working men were present, including a considerable proportion of the navvy class. Mr. John Ward, president of the Union, first addressed the meeting. Ile said that he had come now that the approach of spring was awakening up and reviving thino.''s, to try to revive a sentiment of enthusiasm in favour of the Union. The branch of the Union in Warrington numbered about 90, and had he not been prevented by business.in London from attending to this part of the country as he would have liked to do, the number would no doubt have been much larger. He was anxious to jo something to instil into the navvies and labourers of the district the spirit of unity which had been so wanting amongst them. They must not imagine their condition was too bad to be remedied. In modern days, there were none so crushed down that could not have a spirit of indepen- dence instilled into them if there still remained a spark of manhood in their breasts. It was true that the navy was despised ,• and that even by their own classes. The aristocrats of labour, among toe working-men, despised them. The way to make themselves respected was to do as other working-men had.done, that was by combining. They must help themselves, for the masters seldom helped their men. The majority of employers were actu- ated by but one motive, that of buying their workmen's labour as cheaply as they could. They showed the men the way: they knew that isolated they fell to the ground; that they must stand shoulder to shoulder to prevent labour from assorting its rights. They did not drink their beer and smoke their pipes and expect the millen- nium to come: they formed themselves into a union, and the workers who had no union to contend against i the masters were unfairly dealt with, as though outside the pale of civilisation. No one could deny that work- men were paid in proportion not to the amount of work they did, but to the extent to which they were organised. The most highly paid trades were the best organised. The trade of the lithographic printers was the best organised, and it had the highest wages; the London Society of Compositors was the next best organ- ised and commanded the next best wages; the Society of Engineers was the next best organised, and commanded the third best wages. There was plenty of work at present for all classes of workmen, and now was their opportunity to demand fair wages. Extreme fiepressions of trade took place about every seven years, and if the opportunity of asserting their rights and ob- taining fair wages were not embraced by workmen now they might never have another in their lifetime like that they had at present. If men asked him what a union would do for them, he answered them by asking them what unions had done for other trades. A man who could not do with a pint of ale a week less to pro- tect his interests—for that was the cost of membership of the Union—was not worth the snap of a linger. He urged the non-unionist men present to join the Union that they might demand from *their masters in the future the fair play they had not had in the past. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Leonard Hall, of Eccles, publisher of "The Navvy's and Labourer's Guide," and the dis- trict organiser, then addressr.el the meeting. At the head ot the posters announcing the meetinghe said were the words " Union is strength." In them lay the whole case for unionism. Union was not only strength to the labourers, but it was their only weapon. The masters had wealth, the professional classes had education, and the aristocracy had birth and influence ; all that the lanourers nad to rely upon was combination. They had no wealth and very little education, under the present system, which made a point of keeping the workers as ignorant as possible in order that they might remain content. The Union in London had not been in existence twelvemonths, and yet it had succeeded in establishing 6d. an hour there as the rate of pay fpr navvies and labourers, and if that could be done in London where the works in which such men were em- ployed were much smaller than in the provinces surely it could be done here where the navvies were massed by thousands on such works as the Ship Canal. There were two causes why the Warrington branch of the Union had got the dry-rot into it of late. The frost had caused a good many who had belonged to it to go away from the district, and Mr. Ward's services had been required in London for two months after Christmas becauseof the frightful state of misery and the lack of work which existed there at that time. Now the district council had been formed,with a local organiser,who would visit the Warrington branch regularly ; and right through the summer speakers would be coming down. (Applause.) A second meeting was held in the afternoon in the same place and was well attended,it also being addressed by Messrs. Ward and Hall, who in the evening held a meeting in Runcorn. On Monday evening they had another meeting at Warrinton, in the club room of the Seven Stars, but it was hot largely attended.

of the China Inland Mission), said that, while strong drink had slain thousands and tens of thousands, opium had slain hundreds of thou- sands and even millions. This is an appalling statement to make—appalling because there is every reason to believe that it is true. India and China suffer frightfully from the use of opium, and the evidence goes to show that there is an increase in the number of the slaves to the life-destroying drug. It is worse than even alcohol in its demora- lising effects. Mr. BRUCE, Superintendent of tea plantations in Assam, says of the opium smoker: —" He will steal, sell his property, his children, the mother of his children, and finally even com- mit murder for it." Similar testimony is given by other European observers in India and also in China. But it may be asked—Why should we in England concern ourselves about the folly and madness of the natives in these far-away countries? The answer is because England is responsible for the growth of opium in India, and for forcing it upon the Chinese as an article of commerce. The records of our opium wars with China in 1840 and 1857 form the blackest pages of English history, and, if we had nothing better to show for our character as a nation, we should deserve to be swept from the face of the earth. It is repulsive to read of the persistent attempts of the Foreign Office to legalise the traffic in opium after the treaty of Nankin, which was signed in 1842. The Chinese Emperor held out, and sought to sup- press the smuggling in of the drug. On one occasion when he was pressed he nobly answered: —" It is true I cannot prevent the introduction of the flowing poison: gain-seeking and corrupt men will, for profit and sensuality, defeat my wishes ; but nothing will induce me to derive a revenu e from the vice and misery of my people." Another war ensued, "profit-seeking and corrupt men" triumphed, and China has since been given over to the horrors of the opium traffic.

The guilt—for guilt there is—rests upon the English Government and the English people. It is a question of revenue—a matter of money, not of morals. The Indian Government have set up a monoply in the manufacture of opium, and it is because it brings in a large return that no attempt is made to reduce or abolish the evil. Thus that which can only be sold in this country as a drug labelled "poison" is constituted a profitable article of commerce in India and China. The Government thrives, or seeks to thrive, on the misery and degradation of the people. It is in the Presidency of Bengal that the poppy is grown and the licenses are granted. In 1881 there was a pro- posal from the Supreme Government to intro- duce the growth of the poppy into the Presidency of Bombay ; but it was success- fully resisted. The answer of the authorities was that it had been tried in Gujerat, and "the result was wide-spread corruption and demoralisa- tion." But why, if the traffic is too bad for the Bombay Presidency, is it not too bad for the rest of India? The only answer that can be given is —Revenue, Revenue, Revenue. It is galling to think that as Rulers of India we are all being made Party to a deadly traffic, which is at this moment ruining thousands and tens of thousands both in mind and in body. Englishmen are, for the most part, living in sheer ignorance of the ravages of the drug, or they would, before the year is over, insist on the trade being abolished. If sold at all, it should be sold as in England—under the restric- tions which attach to it as a poison. It is time We realised that our present traffic in opium is a crime againist humanity.

St H IT is satisfactory to see that the . elens miners of St. Helens and district miners. are alive to their own interests. They had a tea party and concert in the Volunteer Hall, on Saturday, and, what was more to the purpose, they had addresses on labour questions from Mr. SETON-KARR, the sitting member, and Mr. KENNEDY, Q. 0., who is expected to take Mr. KARR'S place when the constituency has another opportunity of selecting a representative. In 83- conding a motion in favour of an eight hours day for miners, Mr. GEORGE DIXON, who is himself a miner, expressed the opinion that three-fourths of the miners of the kingdom were in favour of the restriction. This is an important point, and one which is not as yet satisfactorily settled. Mr. C. M. PERcY, who is regarded as an authority on mining questions, holds that the voice of the majority has not yet been heard. It would scarcely be prudent to legislate until all doubt upon the subject has been removed ; and such gatherings as that held at St. Helens render a service by eliciting definite expressions of opinion. The meeting was unanimous in its approval of the motion. It Was supported, too, by Mr. SETON-KARR, who evi- dently had much more regard for catching votes that for consistency. He said he thought "Par- liamentary interference with the adult hours of labour would be very dangerous " ; but he finally intimated that he should support the Eight Hours 13111 for miners! What he probably means is that be is altogether opposed to introducing what he regards as a " very dangerous" element in legis- lation; but, recognising that there is a very large number of miners in St. Helens, he will run the risk by committing himself to carrying out their Wishes. How far the miners can trust a represen- tative who thus blows hot and cold, it is for them- selves to decide. If they watch the signs of the times, they cannot but observe that the Govern- ment, which the member for St. ^Helens says he would support if he had forty votes, exercises all its energy and skill, not in dealing with, but in shelving, labour questions. They do not face difficulties: they get rid of them by refer- ring them to Select Committees and Royal Commissions. Mr. SETON-KARR supported the Government in disposing of Railway Servants in this way. It is notorious that railway men work very much longer hours than miners—many of them twice as long—and yet Mr. KARR decides off-hand in favour of reducing the hours of miners, Whilst railway servants are " shunted " for an in- definite period as "empties," or " goods " of no Moment. Where is the justice—to say nothing of consistency—of such conduct? And how is it to be explained? Is it that railway servants com- Inand few votes, whilst miners command many? Alr. KENNEDY as the Liberal candidate showed that he stood on firmer ground. He not only ex- pressed himself in favour of the Eight Hours Bill for miners; but pointed with great effect to the need there is of amending the Employers' Liability Act in various ways, and especially in the direction of making it compulsory. Let the working-men Of St. Helens ask themselves how it is that the Present Government have not effected this reform, although they have been in office over four years; 4/10721 they will then have no difficulty about voting at the next election.

"TOUCH AND GO."
"A Voice from the Wilderness :"—lf you will send your name and address, we will insert your letter next week.

The brutal weather of March is in shivering contrast to the genial mildness of February. It was a matter of course to expect a change; but, with hard frost, snow storms, wrecks and loss of life, it is natural to exclaim—" Something too much of this !"

Sir James Fergusson, in answer to Mr. Morley, stated in the House of Commons the other night, that, having got to Tokar, there is no intention of retiring. This means an extension of Egyptian occupation, the expenditure of more money, and probably more fighting.

Sir John Macdonald is returned to power as Canadian Premier, but with a small majority—too small, it may prove, for working purposes. It is evident that the Dominion is in a very unsettled state,and, if the mother country doesn't mind what she is about, there will be a " ruction " which may result in annexation to the United States.

In a case heard at the Liverpool Assizes, on Wed- nesday, it was stated that Dr. Hill, of Liverpool, is a believer in faith-healing. Odd if it should be so. And of what use can he be as a doctor? II everybody believed in healing by faith, there would be no room for the doctor: his occupation would be gone.

Well done Mr. George Woods. He has been ex- erting himself to some purpose on behalf of the Warrington Musical Society, of which he is an active member. Starting last autumn with the burden of a debt of something like .tl2O, the Society is now, owing mainly to Mr. Woods' efforts in collecting subscriptions, practically out of debt, and out of difficulty. This achievement is one of good augury. More power to the fiddler's and very other elbow.
- During the extension of Thelwall Church, it has been necessary to remove temporarily, the gravestone over the remains of Dr. J. T. Heath, with its suggestive epitaph which runs as follows :
He always was a neighbour's friend; Deny it, if you can; He never paid a lawyer's bill, Or caused another man. Dr. Heath died in 1826, aged 83 years.

During the week, Mr. Justice Day, sitting at the Liverpool Assizes, has sentenced two men from this district to imprisonment for eighteen months. One of the offenders hailed from Widnes, and had been guilty of using the knife in a most cowardly fashion. The other was a Ship Canal labourer, of Latchford, who while excited by drink had shame- fully rrialtreated another labourer—without the slightest provocation. Both culprits richly deserve the punishment they will receive.

The Health Committee of the St. Helens Cor- poration are showing themselves thoroughly in earnest in their effort; to secure an abatement of the nuisance arising from noxious vapours. They are not content to continue a waiting policy, and have passed a resolution which is in the nature of a warning to offenders. As Alderman Pilkingt,n said on Wednesday, it is the duty of a Health Committee to preserve, if possible, the health of the town.

There is a scheme on foot to erect a new church —St. Mary's—as an offshoot of Holy Trinity, War- rington. At a preliminary meet;ng, on Monday evening, Mr. John White remarked that church- building had not kept pace with the increase of population. "Warrington had increased during the past 50 years by 35,000 inhabitants, and only four churches had been built." How this came to be thus was not stated. Can it be that some of the 35,000 prefer Dissenting places of worship? And is it possible that others don't go to church at all?

There is certainly room for an explanation of some kind. As Sir Gilbert Greenall was referred to as a "noble example" in Church matters, and as a "venerable and beloved gentleman," it wottla be interesting to know how many of the Sixty- two licenses held by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., in Warrington,, have been obtained dur- ing the past 50 years, and how many new public- houses they have erected during the same period. Pursuing the inquiry, it might be useful to ascer- tain how far the growth of public-houses has inter- fered with the growth of churches, and whether the example set is really a " noble " one.

In the spring, the poet tells us, " a.young man's fancy lightly turns to thoughts of love " ; but witk the navvies and labouring class generally fancy is turning, this year, to thoughts of higher wages. And quite right, too, for when poverty comes in at the door love sometimes flies out at the window. On Sunday there were two public meetings, at Warrington Bridge,with the object of adding mem- bers to the General Labourers' Union. There was some pretty plain speaking; and, if the men organise as they are advised to do, there is no doubt that combination will be a benefit to them.

At a meeting, on Tuesday, of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority there was further dis- cussion on the effects of the noxious fumes from Widnes. As bearing upon the admitted fact that the death-rate of Widnes is lower than many other towns, the Inspector to the Authority said "he had made inquiries about the death-rate, and had ascertained that there was a fluctuating population, the people standing the fumes as long as they could, then going away dying." As this is an im- portant statement to make, the matter should be investigated. What has the Medical Officer of Health for Widnes to say of this new and startling theory ? Is there anything in it?

Can a person who commits suicide be regarded under any circumstances as sane? It would seem not, for at an inquest held at Richmond,on Tuesday, on the body of a physician who had shot himself with a revolver, it transpired that he had left a note behind him affirming that he had for years suffered excruciating pain, but that when about to take his life he was "as collected as the most sober man in the world." He begged that a verdict should not be brought in of "unsound mind or temporary insanity " ; but that is exactly the verdict which the jury did bring in: Men who will take their lives cannot prevent those who still live from hav- ing doubts as to their sanity.

The London Liberal and Radical Union, at a well-attended meeting, onMonday evening, passed an important resolution calling ior a revaluation of the land, with the view of charging it with a tax of at least four shillings in the pound. This will strike some landlords who know something about history as vory shocking ; but if they will go back 200 years, they will find that four shillings in the pound was the sum originally levied upon land by a landlords' Parliament. This was in place of the irregular levies for the maintenance of the army, provision for which was the original condition upon which land was held. In so Far as the 4s. tax has not been kept up the nation has ' been defrauded. It is time somebody moved in the matter.

Mr. Coningsby Disraeli aired his juvenile politics at Warburton, on Tuesday. He tries to come up smiling after being so severely punished in the wordy war with Mr. Leadam, the Liberal candi- date. His idea of a reply is to repeat absurd statements without offering the slightest proof. He still sticks to it that "the Board of Agriculture, when they have time, will cope with the distress- ing fall in prices of agricultural produce." When they have time! How childish! If they can do this thing, they ought to set about it at once. be- cause anything else they are doing—or professing to do—is, as compared with it, "as moonlight is to sunlight, and as water is to wine." If the Juvenile Plunger really ha 4 "no more off" than this, he ought to be sent back to his primer; and if he does no better, what are we to think of him?
UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. SUTTON'S Sankey-St., Warrington.—Advt.
THE RETURN OF WINTER.
A severe snowstorn visited the Runcorn and Widnes districts on Friday, and the weather has Since been very cold and winterly-.
THE MERSEY MISSION' INSTITUTE RUNCORN.

The Committee of the pruposed Institute have accepted the tender of Mr. H. Coward, contractor and builder, to construct the building for the sum of £1,045. It is expected that the foundation stones will be laid in May.
UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.

The fifth of a series of lectures on " The political Systems of Europe "was delivered last evening week, by Mr. H. J. Mac Kinder M.A., who dealt with the subject of " France." Views were shown by means of the lime light lantern. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. Durrox's Sankey-st., Warrington.—.Advt. THE CARPENTERS' STRME AT RUNCORN.

The Carpenters of the Ship Canal Company,after being onstrike nearly a fortnight, returned to work on Thurs- day on the terms offered by the Company. The men asked for 711. per hour, and the Company offered 7d., which has been accepted. They were formerly paid 30s. per week.
WIDNES BICYCLE CLUB.

The members of this club are anticipating a healthy and vigorous existence during the cowling season. The rule making the adoption of the club uniform compul- sory has been withdrawn and a large accession of mem- bers is expected as a result, while several medals will be offered for competition. Mr. H. Wade Deacon is the president, Mr. H. Haigh, the sec., Mr. T. Jones the captain. _ .

WIDNES AND THE DISTRICT VETO BILLS

At a public meeting held in Hutchinson-st., Cocoa- rooms on Tuesday evening, resolutions were passed in favour of the English and Welsh Direct Veto Bills now before Parliament. Mr. Ecroyd, of the Liverpool Direct Veto League,gave an address on the objects of the league, and pointeeout that both candidates for Widnes were opposed to the Veto. Mr. Richard Kean, of Warrington, presided. SUDDEN DEATH OF A HALEBANK CYULIST.

Whilst returning home, from Little Woolton, on Mon- day night, Arthur Tomlinson, 18 years of age, son of the late Mr. James Tomlinson, of Halebank, fell from his safety bicycle, and expired immediately. The sad event has cast a gloom amongst the friends of his much re- spected family. The cause of death is believed to be heart disease. An inquest was held on Wednesday. and a verdict of death from natural causes returned.
UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W, DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COM3IITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday after- noon under the presidency of Dr. O'Keeffe, the chair- man (Mr. H. Wade Deacon) being absent through indis- position. The Librarian (Miss Proctor) reported that during February the total attendance at the reading room was 11,534, giving the average of 493 for the 24 days on which the Library was open. In the correspond- ing month last year the average was 497. There had been 4,414 books issued during the same period. There was no business of public interest.
RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.

From our ad;;;tl;in-g. columns it will be seen that this society intends on Tuesday evening to perform Mendels- sohn's Elijah in the Drill Hall, Greenway-road. In the past the chorus have proved themselves equal to all the demands made upon them, and we are confident their reputation will not suffer by their rendition of the beau- tiful music of the Elijah. The principals are etght in ntunber, the professionals being Madame Conway, Miss Emilie Lloyd, Mr. Henry Guy, and Mr. Bantock Pier- point. There will be a full band, and altogether the con- cert is expected to be of the highest class. DEATH OF MR. JOSEPH WILLIAMS, OF RUNCORN.

Our readers will regret to learn of the death of Mr. Joseph Williams, of Irwell-lane. For some months past he had suffered acutely from asthma, and, despite the attentions of Dr. Robinson, he died on Wednesday. Mr. Williams, who had attained the age of 76 years, had amasseda competency as a tailor and draper, which business he carried on in Bridge-st. for many years. He retired about ten years ago. At one time he took an active interest in the affairs of the town as a Commis- sioner and a Guardian, and he was generally respected for his genial disposition and charitable spirit. The flag at the Town Hall was hoisted half mast high out of re- spect to his memory.
UmRELLAs RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTONYI, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. DITTON WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

With the object of raising funds in order to renovate this chapel and provide more accomodation, a bazaar was held in Lacey-st. School on Thursday afternoon. A sum of £l5O is needed, and there were five stalls well stocked with attractive articles and attended by the ladies of the congregation. Mr, Thomas Robinson per- formed the opening ceremony, and the sales commenced. A variety of entertainments were provided for visitors, and in the evening there was a large number of persons present. The receipts for the first day amotrited to over £BO. The bazaar was continued yesterday, when the proceedings were opened at four o'clock by Mr. W Clarke, of Rough Green. There was a good company present.

EiMlGßATlON.—lntencling emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Cana, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Union, American. and other lines.— John Walker. agent. " Examiner" Office, Bewsey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. CLAIM FOR WAGES AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Samuel Jones. brought an action under the Emol.vers and Workmens' Act, 1875, to recover from the Liverpool Silver and Copper Company £1 2s. 6d. wages which he alleged to be due to him. Mr. Knowles appeared for the complain- ant and Mr. Husband defended.—The complainant said while in the employ of the defendants he heard of a vacancy at other works and he asked the foreman to allow him to take the place. Permission was granted, and he left his check at the office and went away. On 'the following Friday, he went to the office for his money but it was refused. William Howell, the foreman, was called, and admitted that he gave the man permission to leave at the time stated. The defence was that it was a rule of the works that every man leaving should give a week's notice or forfeit his pay, and this rule was posted in the works. Mr. Husband produced a copy, and the case was dismissed. BASSINETTES.—J .S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING AT WIDNES. On Thursday,at Widnes Petty Sessions,Brian Evers,of Marsh-st., was charged with unlawfully wounding John Flaward, of Peel-st., by kicking him on the head. On Saturday night, the two men were together at the prisoners lodgings, and they had some drink together. Howard had a few;words with a woman in the house, and it was alleged that the prisoner, without provocation, knocked him down, and kicked him about the head and body. Dr. Flutchinsou said there was a severe wound on the top of the head, several contusions about the fore- head, the right oye being much swollen, aud ceveral dis- colourations on the back. The wound on the top of the. head could not have been caused by a fall. The defence was a total denial of the charge, and it was sought to ' prove that Howard injured himself by falling and coming in contact with a chair and the fender. After hearing a number of witnesses, the Bench dismissed the case.— Thomas Cruise, of Water-st., was again remanded on a charge of unlawfully wounding Samuel Eyes, lodging- ! house keeper, Lugsdale-road, on the 14th February. Dr. McLennan said the man was now out of danger, but was not in a condition to appear in court.
THE EXAMINER, SATLRDAY, MARCH 14, 1891.
RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOL EVENING CLASSES.

On Thdrsday evening Dr. McDougall delivered a lec- ture to the students at these classes on the subject of physiology of the human frame. There was a capital at- tendance, a number of persons not connected with the classes being present. By the aid of diagrams and lan- tern slides, the doctor gave an interesting and instructive description of the skeleton and internal organism of a man, dwelling at length upon the structure of the heart and lungs and the important part they played in the circulation of the blood, which the lecturer traced with considerable minuteness. The attention of the boys never wandered from the subject in hand, and at the close they acCorded a vote of thanks to Dr. McDougall with much heartiness, the motion having been made by Mr. James Pritchard and seconded by Mr. S. Coventry. A number of views of Irish scenery were then thrown on the screen and described by Mr. Moulton, the head mas- ter. Mr. Bowyer manipulated the lantern. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt.

naittee approved plans of 15 houses in Cross-st for Mr. E. Wood, and recommended that as Messrs. Sayce and Randle had failed to remedy the defect ia the drains at the Baptist Chapel, instructions be given to press for- ward the legal proceedings. The Committee recom- mended that legal proceedings be taken against Messrs. Sayce and Randle for non-compliance with bye-laws in erecting two villas in Deacon-road.—On the motion of Mr. Sadler, seconded by Mr. Houghton,the minutes were adopted with the withdrawal of the item as to the Baptist Chapel. "
HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The Medical Officer's report, read to' this Committee, showed that for the month of February the births had been 94, equalling 36.3 per 1,000, and the deaths 46, equalling 17.8 per 1,000. The Committee recom- mended that the tender, £2lB 17s. Bd., of Sayce and Randle be accepted for the erection of laundry, &c., and that the tender, £BO, of E. Connor be accepted for the supply of an ambulance for the fever hospital. The Committee's report also contained the following items among others: " Letters,2sth and 28th Feb., from the Clerk to the Huyton and Roby Local Board, complain- ing of the nuisance caused by noxious gases from Wid- nes."—The Chairman reported that the deputation ap pointed at the last Board meeting had had an interview with the Chairman of the Directors and the Secretary of the United Alkali Co. Ld., and that they had promised everything possible should be done to prevent any nuis- anCe. Canal Boats—Recommended that the owner and master of the boat "Active " be prosecuted for noncom- pliance with the Act. —Mr. Wright moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Neil seconded.—Mr. Heyes said he thought the Board had placed themselves in a ridiculous position by sending a deputation to the United Alkali Co. after having decided by a large majority not to take legal proceedings to compel them to abate the nuisance, and would better have consulted their dignity under the circumstances by taking no further notice of the matter. Be pored an amendment that the paragraphs on the subject in the Committee's report be struck out.— Dr. O'Keefe said the Board not haying control over the inspectors appointed by the Company could not place confidence as a Board in the statements made by the directors, and the Board were not bound to believe them when day after day and night after night these poisonous gases continued to emanate from the works. He was sorry to say that, very little courtesy had been shown to Dean Finegan as, to 'his statement read at last meeting in regard to these gases or to a military gentleman at Rainhill who had written complaining about the same matter. He (Dr. O'Keefe) had heard complaints from gentlemen of position in the neighbourhood of Warring- ton that when the " South-westers " were blowing these gases came into their places and destroyed the incipient flowers that were springing up in their gardens. He had heard gentlemen from Stockport say that the gases from sulphuretted hydrogen at Widnes were almost powerful enough to kill people who inhaled them. People in the suburbs of Liverpool and at Birkenhead complained years ago that sulphuretted hydrogen gases were deleterious to foliage. The gentlemen whe were carrying out this diance- Claus process, said it was not paying. Why, then, did they not devote their works to something that would pay, and not be poisoning people as they were? He said, as a medical man, and as having a knowledge of chemistry not inferior to that of any- body in Widnes, that these gases were a slow and gradual poison, and that the lives of the people were en- dangered by them; and the laws of England would not allow any number of manufacturers to poison human beings for their own aggrandiseinent—for the purpose of making a lot of money.—After some appeals by the Chairman to Dr. O'Keefe as to what he proposed, the doctor moved that the paragraphs in question be re- ferred back to the Health Committee. He remarked that there was not a particle of truth in what the directors said. They believed their inspector's reports,but he (Dr. O'Keefe) knew better by his eyes and nose.—Mr. Heyes accepted and seconded Dr. O'Keefe's amendment.—The minutes were, however, adopted as they stood.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee reported that Mr. Carey had desired to be relieved of the chairmanship uf the committee, and Dr. O'Keefe had been unanimously appointed in his place. The committee also reported that the Hon. T. H. W. Pelham had given the Board the choice ot a day for the holding of his inquiry as to the proposed incorporation of Widnes, and the committee had fixed it for March 25th.—The minutes were adopted. The Board then went into committee.

div.head: ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE AT WIDNES.
div.p: ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE AT WIDNES.

Assaults on the police at Widnes have of late become more frequent than is customary, and on Monday, at Widnes Police Court, the magistrates marked their sense of the seriousness of this kind of offence by sending William Kinchley, of Elizabeth-street, to gaol for three weeks without the option of a 'fine. On Saturday night the prisoner was drunk and disorderly in the street, and P.C. Lord, finding mild measures of no avail, took him into custody. In a very violent fashion, Kinchley then kicked the officer, who was obliged to allow his prisoner to go, but P.C. Hargreaves was at hand, and prevented his escape.—Michael Costello, of Marsh-st.,,was charged with a similar offence. About 11 p.m.on Sunday, Cos- tello was drunk and making a disturbance in Waterloo- road. He refused to go 'home, and on P.C. Tweddle attempting to take him into custody, he placed himself in a fighting attitude. A struggle ensued, during which both fell to the ground, and the constable was wounded on the hand by a kick. The prisoner was fined ss. and costs for each offence, or in default 14 days with hard labour. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland. 51. Bridge-st., Warrington, and at Earlestown.—Advt.

THE WOOLTON WILL CASE. The hearing of counsel on the application of the defendants for a new trial of the action Hampson v. Guy, known as the Woolton or convent will case was continued on Saturday before Lords justices Lindley, Lopes, and Kay. Mr. Willis Q.C., who appeared for the defendants (appellants), con- cluded his address, which had occupied three days; and Mr. Murphy, Q.C., proceeded with his address for the plaintiff in the action, but had not con- cluded when the court adjourned to a date beyond the present week, to be afterwards fixed for re- sumption of the bearing. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.---J. Sc W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Ada.

MR. GLADSTONE AND Mn. H. SETON-KARR, M.P. The attention of Mr. Gladstone having been called to a letter from Mr. H. Seton-Karr, M.P. for St. Helens in regard to his vote on the Religious Disabilities Removal Bill, the right honourable gen- tleman has forwarded the following communication to a St. Helens correspondent :—" The observations of Mr. Seton-Karr on the Bill and on me call, I think for no reply, though I presume he believes them to be arguments. But in regard to the debate I must correct him. The Attorney-General spoke in it, ,summing up, in fact, against the Bill; and stated that while the loyalty of our Roman Catholic fellow subjects was unquestionably perfect, they ware governed by another principle higher than loyalty, which disabled them from 'duly exercising, and therefore from holding these offices. You are at liberty to publish this letter." Now OPEN FOR Tnit SEASON.—Smart and Co.'s private Writing and Commercial Academy for ladies and gentle- men, at Mr. Chantry's, 13, Sankey-st., Warrington. div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs. B. Brown (in the chair), E. Carey, D. Wright, J. Mid- wood, G. J. Neil, .J. iloughton, J. Taylor, W. J. Mar- greaves, H. S. Timmis, and V. lleyes ; Dr. O'Keefe, Messrs. S. Hoyle (assistant clerk),J. S. Sinclair (sur- veyo:), and I. Carr (engineer). THE SMELLS FROM THE WORK& _

Mr. Wright reported that hp as Chairman of the Health Committee, had, with; the Chairman of the Board, waited as a deputation from thq Board, upon the Directors of the United Alkali Co., with refe- ence to the escape of sulphuretted hydrogen from the Widnes Works. The directors confessed that a serious nuisance had been caused through the emission of these gases, and that the company had no right to emit them. They had premised to do all they could to remedy the nuisance and had taken steps with that object. It was now agreed upon all hands that the nuisance had been considerably less during the last fortnight than pre- viously. He did not think there was now much cause for complaint.—lt was agreed that discussion on the subject be deferred till the Health Committee's minutes had been read.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE,
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE,

This Committee's minutes stated that the engineWs report had been submitted. This contained the follow- ing item :—" Increased. Consumption of Water—l beg again to direct your attention to the continued increase in the consumption of water. The 79 millions delivered during the four weeks ending the 25th ult. averages 2,820,000 gallons per day, including Sundays. The total pumping capacity, exclusive of the " Swan " engine, is only three million gallons per diem, so that the mar- gin for stoppages and repairs is already altogether in- sufficient, and in the event of a serious breakdown the water supply to the town would at once be in jeopardy. Should there be no further increase in the consumption of water over that of the present time it is absolutely necessary if a constant supply is to be maintained to proceed at onee with the erection of additional pumping plant." In accordance with the engineer's recommenda- tion, the Committee recommended that a coke hoist and siding be provided at a cost of £250, also that the contract with the Stavely Coal and Iron Company be sealed. They further recommended that extra pumping machinery and buildings be provided at Netherley, at an estimated cost of £9,ooo.—The Chairman moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Wright seconded The Chairman as to the last-mentioned recommendation said that for some days more water had been delivered to the town than they had pumping powers for, and the requirements exceeded the supply. The Board would see that if anything happened to their engines they would be in a very great dilemma, and the Committee recom- mended the provision of a new engine. The Chairman also mentioned that by the arrangements it was proposed to make, between £2OO and £3OO a year would be saved in the cost of fuel. It was not proposed to borrow money for the extension. The Committee thought they• would be able to meet the outlay out of the accumulated profits as they went on in two or three years.—Mr. Wright seconded.—Mr. Neil asked whether it was neces- sary to lay out such a sum as £9,000 at Netherley.—Dr. O'Keefe thought this question a very pertinent one, and said he would vote for the adoption of the minutes except as to this expenditure. He thought the profits ought to be utilised for decreasing the rates instead of increasing them; and the Chairman of the Finance Com- mittee would tell them that the rates in the coming year would be 3d. in the £ more than last year. If the Board borrowed the money with the extension of the repay- ment over 30 or 40 years—with the usual terms on which they had been borrowing, he did not object. Moreover if the householders were more favoured as to the price of water as compared with the manufacturers he would prefer it: he should n3t have the slightest objection to equalize them. Considering what had been said in a neighbouring town about the manner in which matters had been manipulated for the benefit of large consumers of gas and water and what had appeared in the daily papers, the Board had sufficient to induce them to keep very quiet in regard to consumption by large consumers. He would rather the proposed works were constructed at Bell Vale than at Netherley, asthe Board would thus be utilising land which was well adapted for the pur- pose and was now a white elephant. He moved an amendment that the subject be referred back to the Com- mittee.—The Chairman thought the best way to decrease the rates was to encourage the development of the place, and if it had not been for the inducements in the way of good and cheap water and of gas and other things Widnes would not have developed as it had done. He denied that Bell Vale was a white elephant to the Board, and they might congratulate themselves on getting the best and cheapest water works in the country, and he thought water could be supplied and produced as cheaply. He did not think £9,000 was a very large sum to expend for the additional machinery, and taking the cost per million gallons he thought at most places the pumping stations were much more costly.—The amendment was not soconded, and the minutes were adopted as they stood, by 7 votes against 5, Dr. O'Keefe giving notice that he would propose at next meeting that the eXpenditure be not incurred.

ITIMIWAY COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended among other things, the I adoption of the following streets as public highways : Terrace-road. Bold-st. for about 55 yards from Victoria- road, Poni-st., Milton-st., We 4 Bank-st.' South-st. , Bunting Terrace Passage, Robert-st. for about 43 yards from Albert-road, passage between Waterloo-road and Wellington-,st., Frederick-st. for about 251 yards from Widnes-road; also several short passages. div.head: PROPOSED COTTAGE HOSPITAL FOR
div.p: PROPOSED COTTAGE HOSPITAL FOR
RUNCORN. TOWN'S MEETING

Acting upon a requisition presented to him, Mr. S. Taylor, the Chairman of the Board of CJMMig- sioners called a town's meeting, on Monday even- ing, for the purpose of considering the advisability of establishing a cottage hospital in Runcorn. The meeting was held in the Board-room at the Town Hall, and Mr. Taylor presided. Amongst those present were the Revs. Canon Wood, J. Holden, G. H. Kingston, H. Burson, Messrs. H. White, J. E. Longshaw, E. Gregory, G. Bellamy. R. H. Posnett, Dr. Robinson, Dr. MaeLennala, J. Prichard, C. Leffler, E. W. Humphreys, W. B. Frith, E. Imison, James Frith, E. Marwoncl, A. Jordan, W. Shaw, A. Salkeld, E. Key, T. Riley, B. Kniveton, J. J. Howitt, F. J. Norman, M. Barker, Worthington, J. Johnson, Jas. Littler, John Littler, J. W. Lightburn, J. K. Digges, F. A. Lake,W. kankinson, B. Bisbrown, T. Nicholls, J. Dutton, J. Sherlock,J. Franklin, D. Garner, J. Clare, Darbyshire, W. Cartwright, F. Wilkinson, J. Plant, William Dudley, J. Lunt, H. Wright, E. Mar- shall (secretary to the Commissioners). The Secretary read the requisition calling the meeting. The Chairman said he was sure the object of the meeting would recommend itself to the sympathy and suppert of all present, as they must all be agreed that a cottage would be a great boon to Runcorn. (Hear, hear.) It would have come under their notice on many occasions that persons injured by accident had had to be con- veyed to Liverpool and Chester, and when, after the annoyances and fatigues of the journey, the case had proved fatal, they could not help feeling that there was a posiibility of those lives being saved had there been effectual help at hand. If the establishment of a Cottage Hospital was the means of savin.; only one life; it would be gratifying to every right-thinking and generous- hearted individual in Runcorn; but he was of opinion that such an institution would do a vast amount of good, not only in accident cases, but in other matters. They could not ge about the town without observing many cripples and deformed persons, probably through carelessness in their younger days,who had thos become paupers for the whole of their lives. He felt sure that establishing a Cottage Hospital where good nourish- ment and proper treatment would be given, would be the means of preventing many fram going through life in ill-health or crippled. (Hear. hear.) Mr. Lake said some time ago the Chairman and he, whilst travelling in the same train, had a conversation as to the need of hospital accommodation in Runcorn, snd Mr. Taylor prorhised that if he would obtain facts and particulars showing that it was feasible to establish and maintain a cottage hospital in the town, he would take the matter in hand and do his best to promote such an institution. (Hear, hear.) He had collected some information, and had consulted a little book of Dr. Sweet, who was an enthusiast on cottage hospitals. Mr. Lake gave a number of particulars showing how similar institutions were managed in various parts of the coun- tryand the cost of establishment and maintenance. Explaining what was meant by a cottage hospital, he pointed out that in Warminster, the hospital was for the accommodation of the poor when suffering from disease or accident, no infectious case being ad- pitted. Mr. Lake was of opinion, .after reading Dr. Sweet's book that a hospital suitable for Run- corn, containing six beds, a matron's bedroom, and servants' bedroom, would cost £125 to furnish,exclusive of surgical appliances, and the annual expenditure in maintenance would be within £2OO a year. The man- agement of these institutions varied, and it would be for that meeting to appoint someone to draw up rules for their guidance. (Applause.)—The Chairman announced that all the medical men of the town were most favour- able to the establishment of a hospital.—Mr. Lightburn described the efforts made in 1883, by a Committee, of which he was hon. sec., to found such an institution by voluntary subscriptions, and said they did not receive sufficient encouragement to proceed with the work. He hoped the present effort would meet with a better fate • and he said he was glad to help all he could.—Mr. W. Shaw said his experience had shown that a cottage hos- pital would be very useful, and he narrated instances where a local hospital would havebeen a great benefit.— Mr. W. Hankinson gave his hearty qupport to the project. —Dr. Robinson said.that for a great many years they had nowhere to put their dead, but now they had a mortu- ary. He did not think it creditable to Runcorn that they had not some place for a poor man to be taken to when injured or sick, without sending him to Dutton Workhouse. There were many cases where removal to Dutton Workhousewas positive inhumanity, and not long ago a man lost his life entirely through being taken all the way to Dutton. Then to go to Liver- pool and Chester asking charity of these neighbouring communities was very humiliating, and he thought Run- corn would be able'to support some sort of plan to meet the requirements, not of the people who had homes, but of tho great number who had no home. He should be glad ta help in the matter.—Dr. MacLennan also sup- ported the proposal. because he thought a cottage hospital was an absolute necessity. He hoped all present would join in bringing the project to a successful issue.— Mr. Lightburn said the necessity for such an institution was self-evident, and he moved that a cottage hospital be founded, and furnished and maintained by volun tary contributions.—The Chairman said the question might be asked how were the funds going to be raised? In all projects of this kind that question forced itself to the front. The Relief Committee had a balance in hand of £Bl, which they had decided, if a cottage hospital was formed, to hand over to that institution. There was also a sum of £4O in the hands of the Aged People's Treat Committee, and he thought there would be no difficulty in persuading that Committee to hand over their balance to so good a pro- ject as the one they were considering. (Hear, hear.) That Committee might feel quite safe in leaving the aged persons' treat to look after itself, for it must hake been

I very gratifying to those who took part in the treat " find so good a response to the request for funds a",/ practical sympathy. So far as the relief fund was is,, cerned,long as he had lived in Runcorn, he was surpr to find how many liberal-minded people they had in town. In a very few days they had £lBB subscribed ff relief. With these two balances, therefore, there wourj be probably £lOO available, and he felt sure there would be no difficulty in raising the funds necessary for the establishment of a cottage hospital, and he heartily seconded Mr. Lightburn's proposition.— The motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. Lake suggested that a committee be appointed to obtain the necessary in- formation and draw up a scheme. Mr. Howitt moved that the medical men, the secretaries of all the sick benefit societies, the clergy of all denominations, and 12 gentlemen selected from that meeting, form the Committee.—A lengthy and animated discussion then took place as to the constitution of this Committee, and numerous suggestions and proposals were made. Ulti- mately those present resolved themselves intoa Com- mittee, and decided to appoint a sub-Committee of , twelve to draw up a scheme. There were 27 gentlemen nominated, and a vote was taken by ballot. While the scrutineers were casting up the votes, it was re- solved, on the proposition of Mr. Humphreys, seconded by Mr. Pritchard, that the duties of the Committee should be to draft a scheme showing, Ist: the pro- bable cost and best means of establishing a hospital: 2nd, the scope of the institute and rules for management thereof; 3rd, collection of funds for establishment and maintenance ; and 4th the constitution of the governing body. The Sub-Committee to report to the General Committee. The result of the ballot was as fol- lows :—Canon Wood 55 votes, E. Imison 55, F. A. Lake 45, S. Taylor 39, A. Jordan 37, Rev. J. Holden 31, W. Towns 31, A. A. Salkeld 28, F. J. Norman 28, W. Mellor 28, E. Marwood 27, and P. Speakman 26. The gentlemen who were unsuccessful in obtaining a seat on the Com- mittee were :—Rev. H. Burson, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Rev. C. Finch, Dr. MacLennan,Messrs. H. White,J. J. Howitt, W. H. Hankinson, Thomas Handley, R. Abel, E. Marshall, J. R. Frith, D. Worthington, E. W. Humphreys, Thomas Riley, W. Timmins. COMMITTEE MEETING.—A SPLIT.

The meeting of the Committee appointed met at the Town Hall on Thursday night and after Mr. S. Taylor had declined to take tile chair, the Rev. Canon Wood was voted to the position. The proceedings were not marked by the unanimity necessary to the success of an undertaking such as the one in hand, and after a heated discussion the meeting was adjourned without any bus- ness being transacted. We understand that on the ground of the unrepresentative character of the Com- mittee, Mr. Taylor, Mr. F. J. Norman, Mr. F. A. Lake, and Mr. E. Marwood have resigned their seats. It is alleged that the meeting on Monday evening was packed, with a purpose, and there is much indignation ex- pressed in the town that religious prejudices should be introduced into a matter that was projected for the good of all, irrespective of creed or faith. The Com- mittee now consists of seven members of the Parish Church and Mr. P. Speakman, who is absent, en route for the Holy Land ; and how this reduced Committee can formulate a scheme that will be acceptable to the general body of the townspeople, it is impossible to say.
