div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SSNITA.RY. AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SSNITA.RY. AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. A. Thomas, J. P. Mclntyre; Aaron, Parr, Brandreth, Foster, and H. G. Linaker (clerk. TIE POLLUTION OF KECKWICK BROOK. MR. BRUNNER EXPLAINS.

The Clerk read the following letter :—House of Com- mons .Library, 26th February, 1891.—Dear Sir.—This morning I received a cutting from yesterday's " Liver- pool Daily Post" containing a report of the meeting of your authority, according to which it appears that some of the members indulged in the use of strong terms with regard to my conduct. Your letter of the 11th Febru- ary came into my hands on the following day. On the 13th I caused a letter to be written to Sir Hugh Owen, secretary to the Local Government Board, a copy of which is hereto appended. It was my wish that you should have had a copy at the same time and Mr. Griffith who wrote the letter has to-day expressed to me his re- gret at having forgotten this part of my instructions. You will perceive, however, that I did not neglect the interests of the Authority. On communication with the Department to-day I learn that the gentleman whose works are alleged to be the cause of pollution of the brook, has brought before the Departmeut anew process the employment of which it is hoped will render the effluent from the works perfectly innocuous. It is, Pam informed, the necessity for testing this new process which is the cause of the seeming inaction of the Depart- ment. An Inspector has been appointed to report on this process, and the Department cannot move until this gentleman's report has been received. I remain, Dear Sir, yours faithfully, John T. Brunner. H. G. Linaker Esq." Mr. Mclntyre said Mr. Aaron would perhaps now apologise for what he said at the last meeting.—Mr. Aaron said he had nothing to apologise for; he would not apologise to the Prince of Wales.—Mr. Parr: If this process does not answer how are we to go on ?—The Clerk : We take it that they will give us authority to take action to close the works.—Mr. Parr: That we don't want to do. We don't want to take severe measures. —Mr. Aaron: Far from that.—He moved that the clerk wrote to the Local Government Board for a copy of the process at the same time pointing out that cattle would soon be turned adrift on the fields and the pollution must be stopped at once.—Mr. Parr said no one wanted to injure Mr. Earp • he had a living to make, but he thought he (Mr. Earl); was rather dilatory in not getting this process in working order before now.—The Chairman suggested that the , clerk should request the Local Government Board to send a report on the process as soon as possible, as the matter was very serious.—Mr. Aaron proposed and Mr. Parr seconded a resolution to that effect, and it was carried unanimously. lIE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. On the proposition of Mr. Mclntyre, seconded by Mr. Aaron ,Dr. Adams was re-appointed medical officer for the ensuing year, at the usual salary of £l2O per annum.— Dr. Adams acknowledged his re-appointment, and re- marked that the work had enormously increased since the Notification Act came into operation. THE CLERK'S SALARY.

The Board then proceeded to fix the Clerk's salary for the past year.—The Clerk said during the late clerk's time the work had enormously increased since the Ship Canal started, and there had been no extra remunera- tion. If the Board thought the late Clerk was entitled to any extra salary, now was the time to decide.—ln answer to a question, he said no statement of the extra work had been prepared.—Mr. Thomas said a great deal of work had been done in connection with the sewerage systems of the Union.—Mr. Parr said he understood whatever expense the Ship Canal caused the company would pay.—The Clerk said the Highway Board voted the Surveyor £3O for extra work through the Ship Canal, and the Ship Canal Company paid the amount.—Mr. Mclntyre suggested that perhaps it would be best to wait until the work was completed, and then have the whole affair se bmitted.—This course was agreed to, and then Mr. Mclntyre moved that the Clerk's salary be fixed at £B5, which was the usual amount. He was sorry to say they had lost the services of a most efficient clerk, and to learn that he was very ill indeed. They had appointed the son in his place, and he hoped that he would prove even a better man than his father.—Mr Parr seconded the motion, which was car- ried. -

THE WIDNES CHEMICAL NUISANCE. Mr. Parr again introduced the subject of the nuisance and injury caused in the neighbourhood of Halton, by the chemical fumes of Widnes, which had been pest- poned for the attendance of the Medical Officer. If that official smelled the fumes oncertain days he would be of opinion that they were injurious, not only to vegetation, but to human health as well.—Dr. Adams said the va- pours were a combination of acid fumes with sulphur fumes. As a matter of fact the particularly noxious fumes were the acid oiaes, and the legislature -had made attempts to limit the percentage of acid fumes which were allowed to be emitted from any smokestack, and this was the reason for building the enormous smoke- stacks in connection with chemical works.—The Act of Parliament failed to determine the percentage of the vapour. The death of vegetation in the neighbourhood was mainly due to these gases, but no one had ever at- tempted seriously to establish the theory that they were detrimental to human health, and that was the , only way in which the Authority could deal with the ' subject. The only present method of dealing with the nuisance was by reference to the Inspector under the Alkali Acts.—The Chairman: The vapours don't come under the denomination of a nuisance injurious to health.—Dr. Adams: No we cannot bring them under that.—The Clerk said that it had been stated that the vapours were reduced on the action of some other public authority.—Dr. Adams said his own impression was that they were less.—Mr. Parr said the gases had not been as bad, but they could be smelt more or less nearly every day. On the third inst. they were something fearful, and on several lakes in the neighbourhood there was a sort of blue and yellow scum, which could not fail to be any- thing than injurious to the cattle that drink the water, and for miles cattle had to eat grass that was possessed by the vapours. If a ditch was offensive, action would- soon be taken, but it appeared to him that those who committed the greatest nuisances could escape scot free. —Mr. Mclntyre said if these fumes were injurious to health the death rate of Widnes must if necessity be very high but he had an impression that the death rate of that town was exceeding low.—Dr. Adams said Widnes was pointed out as having an exceptionally high death rate, but he could not give actual figures.—Mr. Parr said he had heard that people got L. shot" at Widnes and went elsewhere to die. (Laughter.)—lnspector Far- rington said the population was a floating one; they went to Widnes and stood the atmosphere as long as , they could and then went somewhere else to die.—Even- tually, on the proposition of Mr. Parr. seconded by Mr.. Aaron, it was decided that the clerk should communi- cate with Mr. Carey, secretary to the United Alkali Com- pany, on the subject.

div.head: NIIISARCES.
div.p: NIIISARCES.
The Inspector repotted several nuisances in various parts of the Union ano. he was instructed to take the usual measures for ahatem'ent. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

1 The fortnightly meeting was held cm Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. Colonel A,•hton pretsided, and there were present—the Rev. J. \iv. N. Tanner; Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Mclntyre, Taylor, Aaron, Forster, Brandretli, Parr, W. Fishtv, and H. G. lAnaker (assistant clerk).
THE RATING OF MACHINERY. On the recommendation of the Assessment" Committee, the seal of the Board was attached to a petition against the Bill for exempting machinery from rating.

div.head: .THE FORTHCOMING -ELECTION.
div.p: .THE FORTHCOMING -ELECTION.

Dr. Gastaldi said he understood that some time ago it was decided that the Clerk write to the Local Crovern- ment Board with a view to having the forthcoming elec- .tion conducted by ballot instead of by the present system, with which much dissatisfaction had been expressed. Had there been any reply P—The Deputy Clerk replied that nothing had been done, and the election in A mil would be conducted on the same lines as usual. the subject had been before the House of C )mmons, but ner thing had been done.—Dr. Gastaldi asked if any better arrangement could be made.—The Deputy Clerk replied that the only alteration would be to put on one or two extra distributors and collectors.—Mr. Taylor said the chief complaint was that papers were not delivered and not called for.—The Deputy Clerk said the distributors had to endorse every paper not delivered. .They could not be expected to wait at each house ten minutes for their knock to be answered, as they would never get through their work.—Dr. Gastaldi: Supposing a person has not received a paper, where can he get one ?—The Deputy Clerk: He can apply at the Workhouse, on the morning on which the votes are counted, between 10 and 12 o'clock in the forenoon.—Dr. Gastaldi said it was a great hardship to have to travel so far.—Mr. Mclntyre: Cannot they get any voting papers in Runcorn ?—Mr. Taylor: Cannot they be left with the Assistant Over- seer ?—The Deputy Clerk replied that they could not the returning officer was obliged to conduct the election on certain lines.—The Deputy Clerk was then appointed Returning Officer, in place of his father, who is very ill, at a salary of £2O.

div.head: OUTDOOR RELIEF.
div.p: OUTDOOR RELIEF.

Mr. Mclntyre moved that the rules for the distribution of outdoor relief adopted at the recent Poor Law Con- ference at Northwich be adopted. He stated that the only resolution obliterated from the programme was "That outdoor relief shall not be granted, except in urgent and special cases, and then only in kind, to per- sons whose destitution had been caused by intemperance or their own improvidence." Why the Conference oblite- rated that he did not know; perhaps they thought that if it were adopted Othello's occupation would be gone. (Laughter.) That was his opinion. If the whole of the cases of pauperism that could be traced to intemperance could be thrown out, there would be none left. During the 30 years he had been a Guardian as one crop of pau- pers died another crop sprang up, and it would bean im- portant question to ascertain how these paupers were manufactured and try to stop the thing if possible. In reply to Mr. Thomas, the Deputy Clerk said the rules could be modefied to suit circumstances.—Mr. Btandreth seconded the motion, which was carried.

div.head: RUNCORN AND ITS MAIN ROAD.
div.p: RUNCORN AND ITS MAIN ROAD.

Mr. Aaron pointed out that Runcorn Board of Com- missioners were applying to the Cheshire County Council to have the road leading from tile eastern boundary to the Railway Station declared a main road. If that were done, the rural districts, would have to pay for keeping a portim of the streets in order, and he thought that would be anything but right. He understood that Mr. Councillor Speakman said the County Council would adopt the roads if the Commis- sioners pressed the matter. He proposed that the Clerk write to the Council protesting against the proposal.— Mr. Taylor said he would like to know whether the County Council had taken over any rural main roads in Cheshire. —The Chairman : I suppose they have.—Mr. Taylor: Does Runcorn pay any proportiou of the County call upon the Runcorn Union.—The Deputy Clerk : The Call is ftr £3,126, and Runcorn paid one fourth of that amount.—Mr. Taylor said Runcorn therefore paid a large proportion towards maintaining the main roads in the county districts, and was not that township as much en- titled to have its main roads taken over as the county districts ?—The Chairman said this was scarcely a subject with which that Board could deal; and Mr. Mclntyre said they had better not interfere in the matter. There was no seconder to Mr. Aaron's proposition, and it there- fore fell to the ground.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians wat held at Whiston Workhouse on Thursday afternoon, when there were present, Mr. J. W. Wareing (in the chair), Messrs. T. Leatherbarrow, Middlehurst, Marsh, Kenwright, Davies, James Burchall, Ellison, Daine, Mercer, Whalley, Peover, Buckley, Graves, Syder, P. Longton, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). HELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 573 inmates this week, 568 last week, and 604 in the corresponding week last year; 55 vagrants had been re- lieved against 60 in the corresponding period last year. THE ALTERATION OF THE RELIEF DISTRICT.—The Local Government Board wrote acknowledging the receipt of a communication from the Guardians with regard to the proposed alteration of the Widnes, Eccleston, and Pres- cot relief districts and asking, before they further con- sider the matter if the relieving officer consented to the proposed alterations.—The Clerk said he had replied in the affirmative as the relieving officers had consented,_

THE COMPLAINT AGAINST -MEDICAL OFFICERS.—The Clerk read letters from Drs. Casey (Sutton), McNicoll (St. Helens) and Cooper (Widnes) in regard to the com- plain from the Local Government Board. that they had neglected to supply all particulars of cases attended by them in their report books. In each case the medical gentlemen promised to supply the details in future. The WOOLTON MEDICAL OFFICERSHIP.—A letter was read from Dr. S. Jobb Scott, of Woolton resigning his post of medical officer in consequence of the dissolution of his partnership with Dr. Joll. He also asked that the Board would sanction the carrying out of the duties by Dr. Joll during the three months notice he (Dr. Scott) should serve.—The Clerk intimated that Dr. Joll was the assistant medical medical officer, and no resolution was required.

THE BOARD'S CLAIM AGAINST COUNTY AUTHORITIES.— The Clerk reported that the Guardians had received the total amounts claimed by them from the County Coun- cil of Lancashire and the County Borough of St. Helens. St. Helens had paid £2,650 16s. 5d., and• the County Council £4,018 is. 7d., making a total of £6;668 lEls. This was the principal business.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. I. Wigg. GAMING IN PUBLIC PLACES.—James Robinson' Andrew Christie, James Sharkey, James McDonald, and William Chesters, young men, pleaded guilty to having on. Sun- day the Ist inst., played at a game of chance by means of cards on the canal bank near Runcorn Soapand Alkali Works. Each defendant was ordered to pay the costs, ss. 6d., as it was the first case.—Richard Hurst, James Royle, and William Walton, boys, were summoned for having in Ashridge-st.,on the 2nd March, played at pitch and toss.—P.C. Proctor proved the case. The boys said they were only playing for fun, and those who won re- turned the money.—ln answer to Mr. Reynolds the Sup- erintendent said he had had numerous complaintsof this offence and card playing,which was very prevalent.—The defendants were ordered to pay costs and cautioned. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Higgins was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk and disorderly; John Roberts, John Moran, John Rottmell, and Jane Ball were each fined ss. and costs.—John Burke made his 4.lst appearance and was fined 10s. and costs. EVICTING A WATcnastN.--James Shaw, a young fello*, pleaded guilty to being drunk on the previous night.— P.C. Royle stated that at midnight the prisoner turned an old man out of his watchman's hut on Heath-road, and took possession. He was very drunk.---A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed.

BEGGINO.—John Coles, apparently a navvy, was sent to goal for seven days for begging at Halton. oAot BEFORE A TRUCE.—Eleanor Pratt, of Union-st.,: was summoned for using threats towards a neighbour named Mary Bratt. After hearing the evidence, from which it appeared the defendant had burned the prose- cutrix's image the Bench ordered her to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, or go to gaol for four- teen days.—The defendant said she would go to gaol.

Pat- trick McLoughlin was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months for creating a breach of the peace.— Jas. Fallon and Bridget Kenyon, summoned on a similar charge, were dismissed on payment of costs.—Three parents were each fined 55., for not sending their children regularly to school.—Thos. Brady, Frederlck-st. and Catherine Stead, Bold. were each fined 7s. 6d. andicosts for keeping dogs without licenses.—klf red Ward,Water- loo-road, was fined 2s. 6d. for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.-RUGBY.

If there was anybody who fancied the chance of the North of Ireland men against the representatives of the Red Rose, on Monday, they must have been greatly sur- prised at the result, as Lancashire had no difficulty whatever in keeping up their victorious career, and, as usual, by a vast majority of points, as they eventually ran out the winners by 3 goals, 2 tries, and 6 minors to 1 minor. The teams were as advertised, with the excep- tion that J. Roberts (Salford) and J. Bullough (Wigan), filled the places of Craven and Wilson, and B. G.Roscoe, the Manchester half, played instead of Cross, of St. Helens, who was injured in his club match, on Satur- day.

In the first half Lancashire had the wind in their favour, and at once commenced to press, Bullough, Ros- coe,Roberts, and Rome all doing good work, and Walk- fngton did some smart defensive play for the visitors. Valentine had a shot at goal from a free kick, but missed his mark. Berry was next noticeable with some of his usual play, and Pyke, the St.llelens Recreation forward„ made a splendid run in, Valentine landing a goal. Dun- lop,Roscoe, and Berry distinguished themselves by some good play, the latter securing a free kick, but Coop's at- tempt at goal fell short, leaving Lancashire leading at half time by 1 goal and 5 minors to nil.

Lancashire, despite the strong wind against them, soon showed to advantage. They took the ball over the line, Whittaker scoring, but no goal resulted. Coop and Valentine, followed by Myles, all put in smart play, and fine efforts on the part of Gwynn, Berry, and Roscoe added materially to the Lancastrians' offensive tactics. Stevenson, from a free kick, nearly dropped a goal for Ulster, and Dunlop, another Irishman, put in some smart work. From a splendid pass by Roscoe, Whittaker re- gistered another try, no goal being kicked. Pyke was the next to score, Valertine licking the goal. Rome;from a combined rush on the part of the forwards, took the ball over the line and scored. Valentine kicked a goal.

The great Rugby battle of the year is once more thing of the past, and England is humiliated. None o the previous engagements between the representatives of the Rose and the Thistle has ended in such a decisive victory as that of Saturday last. A defeat by three goals to one eclipses anything hitherto accomplished in these annual fixtures. It is cold comfort to calculate what might have happened had this player or that found a place in the English fifteen. The grim fact remains that Scotland scored a glorious success, and on English territory too. To them, therefore, be all the praise. They have evidently profited by last season's reverse at Edinburgh, and have now beaten the Englishmen at their own game.

It was unfortunate that England had to take the field without those sterling forwards Toothill and Bromet, and it was also unfortunate that the elements favoured the visitors, as a dry ground and a dry ball would have been more to the liking of the home side. Still, these are the fortunes of war, and it would be churlish to deny the undoubted superiority of the Scotch team. What effect that goal so early and beautifully dropped by Clauss had on the game it would be difficult to say, but certain it is that the Scottish forwards demonstrated their ability from the first and kept up to the end. It was painful to the thousands of Englishmen present to see the home forwards rushed off their feet time after time, the dash of the Scots being irresistible. It was in this department that they won the day, the English scrimm- ages never shaping like internationals at all. As a con- sequence the back division had few opportunities of showing off, hence the overwhelming disaster. The visitors were quicker on the ball, and never hesitated what to do. The arrangements at the fine ground of the Richmond Athletic Association were admirable.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

There seems to be no limit to surprise in connection with the League. Indeed they crop up almost every week. Two were furnished on Saturday. At Turf Moor the famous North End had to accept a fearful defeat in the shape of six goals to two. In the face of the fact that no team in the League had previously scored more than two goals against the Prestonians in one match the tremendous success of the Burnley players is remarkable. They literally carried the Preston camp by storm. Nichol, a new centre from Scotland, made a sensational debut, as he not only kicked three of the . goals himself but played well in every way. Preston. on the other hand, were completely at sea, the forwards doing badly in the extreme.

Blackburn Rovers bewailed the absence of Southworth and Barton, but the Bolton Wanderers were just as awk- wardly situated, as they had to journey to Ewood Park minus both Gardiner, their crack half back, and Barbour. The game was hotly contested, and terminated in the victory of the Wanderers by two goals to none. This practically extinguishes the chances of the Rovers for the League championship, which once more looks likely to fall to the lot of Everton. The last-named have now only Burnley to meet on Saturday next, and it should be one of the finest matches of the season.

West Bromwlth Albion Football on Monday beat Blackburn Rovers (League) by 1 goal to nil,and Preston North End beat Aston Villa (League) by 1 goal to nil. The match Sheffield Wednesday v. Bootle (Alliance) ended in a draw of 1 goal each. Lancashire beat Ulster by 3:goals, 2 tries, 6 minors, to 1 minor.

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THE CHARGE OF ASSAULT WITH AN AXE.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday Wm Sheldon, aged 16, was brought up on remand charged with inflict- ing grievous bodily harm upon Thomas Rathbone, aged 20, by striking him on the head with an axe, on the 2nd inst. Chief Constable Hunt said the House Surgeon at the Infirmary declared that Rathbone would not be able to leave that institution for a fOrtnight hence, and the prisoner was therefore remanded till rue,sday the 24th inst.
11012 E JUVENILE THIEVING.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, Walter Spencer and Thos. Bailey, boys, were charged with steal- ing a quantity of lemons, value is. from the stall of David Matthews, in the Market Place,on Tuesday night, between seven and eight o'clock. Detective-Inspector Monaghan who had arrested the prisoners on Wednesday night, and Mr. Matthews, who said previous thefts had been committed at his stall, and he had had the lock broken off on one occasion, proved the case. The pri- soners pleaded guilty, and were fined 2s. 6d. each.
THE INCORRIGIBLE JOHN WARRINGTON.

At the Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, John Warrington was charged before Alderman Holmes (chairman) and Mr. Fairclough, with stealing a bottle of porter from the shop of Mr. J. Beacon, St. James's- st., Latchford, the preceding day. P.C. Critchley met the prisoner trying to pull the cork out of the bottle with a,nail ; and, questioning him as to how he came by it, found that it had been stolen from the place men- tioned. Chief Constable Hunt said there were moments when the prisoner did not really know what he was do- ing ; and referred to certain robbefies he had commit- ted as being of such a barefaced character as to show the absence of the ordinary caution of one of perfectly sound mind. The magistrates contented themselves with merely recording the conviction against the prison- er.
ILLEGAL POSSESSION OF A PAWN TICKET.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tnesday, Arthur and Elizabeth Longshaw,husband and wife, were charged with being found in unlawful possession of a paWn ticket for an overcoat supposed to have been stolen. A constable deposed to going to the prisoners' house, Na. 4 Hall-st., about 12 o'clock the previous night and finding them in bed, and charging them with the offence. She passed the ticket to him, and he said it was his, and the constable took it from him and found it was a ticket for an overcoat, value 65., pledged at a pawnbroker's in St. James's-St. The prisoners were remanded tiil Fri- day. Ihe prisoners were again brought up yesterday when the charge against them resolved itself into one of stealing an overcoat from the stall of John Morton, Market-place, and there was an additional charge against them of stealing a pair of boots from the stall of Joseph Frisby. The prisoners were further remanded for the owner of the overcoat, who lives in Manchester, to ap- pear.

div.head: MINOR, CASES.
div.p: MINOR, CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. SLEEPING IN AN OUTBUILDING.—Ann Simpson, for sleeping in an outbuilding in the rear of the premises of Wm. Partington, this morning was sent to jail for seven days. MONDAY. —Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb) and Aldermen Harrison and Sutton. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—SoIomon OUtTalll, Thomas Martin, Albert Cleaver, and John Kilroy for being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on the 7th inst., were each fined ss. and costs. Samuel Beckett, drunk and dis- orderly in Pillar's Brow, on the same date, was fined ss. and costs. John Gillighan, and Charles Collings, drunk and disorderly, the former in Cockhedge-lane on the 27th ult., and the latter in School Brow, on the 2nd Inst., were each fined ss. and costs. Fromm—Wm. Lomax, bricksetter, for fighting in Mersey-st., on the 3rd ult., had to pay the costs, 2s. 6d. BREACHES OF SANITARY REGULATIONS.—The adjourned case of Ellen Musgrove, Dial Court, charged a fortnight since with keeping lodgers in an unregistered house, was new brought up again. Mr. Norman, sanitary in- spector, stated that she had now put the place in proper condition, and her case was withdrawn. John T. Wilkin- son,a similar charge against whom had stood adjourned, had made no attempt to comply with the law, and he was fined 10s. TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Platt (chairman) and Mr. E. M. Crosfield. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Hines and Peter Ward, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., yesterday, the latter being also charged with threatening the life of P.C. Corcoran, were fined, Hines ss. and costs, and Ward 10s. and costs ; James Jordan, drunk and disor- derly in Bank-st., yesterday, was fined ss. and costs, and Wm. Butler, drunk and disorderly in Atherton-st., was fined ss. including costs: INDECENT CONDUCT.—Emma Howard for indecent be- haviour in Wilderspool-road, last night, was sent to pri- son for a month's hard labour. MORE UNSANITARY BUILDINGS.—MaTy Nester and J. Collins, charged by Mr. Norman, sanitary inspector, with occupying bnildings in an unsanitary state, in Great Sankey-st., were fined the costs, 3s. 6d. each. NON-ATTENDANCE AT SCHOOL.—The following parents were convicted, at the instance of Mr. G. Riley, of not sending their children regularly to school :—Richard Badger, forgeman, Howard-street, Matthew Bates, forge- man, Silver-street, Michael Connor, labourer, Oliver-st., M. Towey, labourer, Oliver-street, Thomas Dickinson. hawker, Silver-street, Henry Jewess, forgeman, Bank Quay, fined ss. each • Thomas Taylor, miller, Howley, and Wm. White, labourer, Howard-street, fined 2s. 6d. each. Thomas Jones, labourer, Orford-lane, for non- compliance with an attendance order, was fined 2s. 6d. The cases of Elizabeth Bate, milliner, Cobden-street, and John Kermoy, painter, Mersey-street, were adjourned. THURiDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman), and Captain Ridgway. DRI3NR AND DISORDERLY.—Wm. Dooley, of Latchford drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., last night, and charged also with assaulting P.C. Davies, was fined 10s. and costs.—Mary Carey, charged with being drunk and disorderly last night, in Church-st.,was dismissed.—Geo. Williams and Wm. Bayliss, drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road, last night, were fined, Williams 55. in- cluding costs, and Bayliss 7s. 6d. including costs. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White (chairman), Alderman Harrison, and Dr. Gornall. A QUARREL AMONG WOMEN. Sarah and Catherine O'Donnell., the latter being the formers mother, were charged with assaulting Minnie Bray; Bray was charged with assaulting the O'Donnells ; Charlotte Elizabeth Johnson was charged with assaulting Caroline Davies ; and Patrick Glynn with assaulting the O'Donnells. The assaults were all alleged to have takel place on the 7th inst, and the cases are from Latchford. Mr. A. Browne appeared for Bray and Glynn, and Mr. P. Davies for the O'Donnells. Mr. Davies asked for an adjournment on the ground that Mrs. O'Donnell was ill in bed and could not appear. The cases were adjourned till A.pril 3rd, Mr. Davies's clients to pay costs of adjournment. DAMAGING A WINDOW.—JOIM Burton a boy, was charged with damaging the window of Samuel Thomas Williams, by throwing a stone through it, on Wednesday. He was ordered to pay the damage, is. 6d., and the costs.
The Lord Chief Justice is sal d to be of opinion that there is no ground for the reports as to Mr. Justice Step- hen's health, which have appeared in some of the legal journals.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*** Secretaries of Football. Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

WIDMS ST. MARY'S V. SIITTON.—PIayed at Sutton onl Saturday, before 2,000 spectators. St. Mary's had the best of the game throughout, a,nd won by 1 try to nil. Crewe scored the try. RUNCORN A v. WIGAN A.—This match took place on Saturday, at Runcorn. In the first half there was little to 'record; but after the interval Woods kicked two goals, and Webb before the close added another major point. Runcorn's score was 3 goals, 2 tries, and 3 minors; Wigan's, nil. WIDNES v. MOSSLEY <" A" TEams).—Played at Widnes on Saturday, before a fair attendance. From a drop-out, Rushton obtained possession, and after a good run, scored a try. Half-time score: Widnes, 1 try and 1 minor; Mossley, 3 minors. Final result: Widnes "A," 2 tries and 1 minor ; Mossley "A,,, 4 minors. FRODSHAM V. LITHERLAND.—This match was played at Litherland on Saturday, before about 500 spectators. Play was very even, both teams showing good defence, and at half time neither side had scored. In the second half, Frodsham had considerably the best of the game. Linaker crossed the home line, but the point VMS dis- allowed. From the drop out Linaker again got posses- sion, and, after a good run, scored near the posts,Rogers failing at goal. Frodsham won a good, game by one try and ,five minors to one minor.

'RUNCORN V. WIGAN.-It is some years since these teams met at Wigan, but the Committee of the Runcorn Club succeeded in adding a fixture with the Lancashire team to this season's list, and the match was played on Saturday, on the ground of Wigan. There was a large body of spectators present, numbering about 7,000 to 8,000, and both teams were fairly representative. W. Hughes kicked off for the visitors, and the home team commenced to press their opponents in a determined manner. Houghton, when danger was imminent, did good service. During a scrimmage on the line, Sed- don, in a neat run, passed to Slevin, the latter gaining a try, but Anderton failed to convert. The visitors then attacked the home quarters, but Seddon and Anderton by smart passing, altered this state of things. Cromp- ton relieved the pressure, and the Runcornians com- menced an onslaught on the homesters' quarters; but this state of things was not permitted to continue. W. ' Halliwell broke away from a scrimmage, and Anderton, on receiving a pass, *succeeded in getting over behind the posts, after making a good run. Again the place was missed. Faulkner played remarkably well, and the Runcorn forwards passed in their usual style. At half- time the Wigan team had registered two tries, whilst their opponents had failed to gain a sitgle point. The second half of the game was somewhat similar to the first, and at the close Wigan had added four minors to their score, whilst the visitors were nilled. '

WIDNES v. MOSSLEY.—Widnes journeyed to Mossley on Saturday to play off the return fixture with that club. The sloppy' state of the ground made football proper -quite impracticable. Play amongst thebacks was there- fore out of the question, and the hopes of the respective clubs were centred in the forwards. Though Widnes were far superior to their opponents in the back ranks, they were at a disadvantage in the forwards, hence the reverse which they experienced. Play settled in the centre, where Widnes commenced to attack, and Moss- ley to neutralize had to put in some long kicks. Peters got away, but the state of the ground prevented him getting through. Billings saved by a long kick, and Peters failing to return, the ball was carried in touch near the visitors' line. From a scrimmage at this point, Billings got possession, and running along the touch line, obtained a by. Binns failed at goal. On re-starting,the. game became very rough, Mossley being the aggressors, Widnes attacked, Drummond and Peters carrying the ball into the home quarter, where Poyntonl and Taylor saved. some exciting play followed on the Mossley line where the home half-backs completely disheartened the visitors by their continuous off-side play. This was repeatedly pointed out to the referee, who, from some cause or other,refused to interfere. Half-time was called, with the score as follows :—Mosslsy one try and one minor, to Widnes nil. On changing ends, Binns made his mark opposite the Widnes goal, but Taylor made a miserable attempt at goal. Mossley continued the pres- sure, but the Widnes defevce proved too good for them, Johnson and Whelan saving in turns. Barber also saved at a time when it seemed almost impossible to prevent a try. The game was very even, and shortly after the whistle sounded, the score then being Mossley one try and three minors to Widnes nil.

WARRINGTON A v. OLDHAM A.—This match,which was played at Watersheddings, was looked upon by the foot- ball fraternity in the Oldham district to decide as to which was the champion A, and a large amount of inte- rest was, therefore, centred in the contest. Unfortu- nately, what with rain and, snow, the ground had the appearance of a perfect slough of despond, and correct football was at a great discount. It was considerably past the advertised time when Oldham started, and the kick being well returned by Barnes. the advantage was utilized by a grand bout of passing,started by Thornley, and a minor conceded. The venue of the warfare was quickly changed to midfield, where, owing to the state of the ground, a lot of slipping about was indulged in. From here Lawless demonstrated his abilities by a capi- tal dribble, but the advantage gained was as quickly lost, Beaver's fine kick travelling to the centre line. After some tall kicking by Jolley and Sampson, Oldham rushed away to the visitors' 25,until Davies and Knowles came away to neutral territory. A couple of grand bits of play by Mather, Jolley, and Totts were supplemented by a determined rush, and Mather pickinU up, passed with excellent judgment wide out to P. Lawless, who made no mistake, and scored a finely-executed try. Additional heavy pressure culminated in two minors to the visitors' credit, although both were near escapes. Play then set- tled in the Warlington quarters, where, unfortunately, P. Lawless sprained his ankle, and had to retire. No- thing daunted by this drawback, Joe Lawless, by a really good dribble, carried the game to the line, and Watkin, to avoid any catastrophe, touched down. Knowles returned the drop out, and Craghan, rushing up, was enabled to secure another try. Then the honaesters had a good look in, Potts making amends for , his mull by a capi- tal save, and Thornley, Teare, Lloyd, and Moly- neux quickly transferred the game to more desirable quarters. The combat still proceeded much in Warring- ton's favour, Buckley, Davies, and Knowles harassing the home defence. A rare chance for Oldham was splendidly saved by Potts, when a try seemed imminent, and Lloyd, Thornley, and Craghan counterbalanced the temporary advantages, and another minor was recorded. Eventually a minor was given to Oldham, the score at half time being 0-2--5 to 0-0-1. Restarting, Lawless was early prominent by a grand run into his opponents' lines, but the homesters were now playing a desperate game, and transferred the oval to the half way flag. A dribble by Buckley was succeeded by a lot of time being monopolized in packings, until Oldham got well away to the Warrington goal. The heavy pressure was at length relieved by Davies, Knowles, and Teare, and their efforts were of no avail, for when Beaver got his foot to the ball it went sailing back to the line, and a minor was granted. For a time the combatants vied with one another between the quarter flags, Knowles, Molyneux, and Buckley ultimately getting well up, when Jolley had a futile shot at goal. Some uninteresting play followed in the visitors' territory, until a grand combined rush took the leather to the home "25," and Mather picking up from a mis- kick, scored the final try. The remaining play was all in Warrington's favour, who retired winners by 0-3-7 to 0-0-2. Teams :—Warrington: Sampson, back; P. Lawless, Jolley, Potts, three-quarter backs; J. Law- less and Mather,half backs; Davies, Molyneux, Craghan, Thornley, Teare, Knowles, Lloyd, Barnes, and Buckley, forwards. Oldham: Watkin, back ; Bennett, Beans, and McDonnell, three-quarter backs; Gray and Kilshaw, half backs; Whittle, Tuohy, Andrews, Whitehead, Nuttall, Simpson, Darlington,Wolstenholme, and Murrell, forwards.
WARRINGTON v. OLDHAM.

The Warringtonians surprised even themselves on Saturday, when they defeated the smart combination from Oldham pointless. The representatives of spindle- , dom have done some remarkable performances this sea- son,and the introduction of the two Welsh internationals into their team has worked wonders in their play, and instead of a rapid run of ill-luck (which has attended them in seasons gone by), the present season has been , almost a series of victories. By many it was thought that Warrington would be added amongst their victories, but in many cases before, which visitors to Wilderspool are aware of, our local club has risen to any special occa- sion, and when such has been the case, the Warrington- ians have rarely failed to vanquish their opponents. Saturday's match proved no exception to the rule, and although it was acknowledged that the visitors were ex- ceptionally strong in the back division, it was thought that the Oldham combination would receive a check from the smart play of the home forwards. That this was the case was fully borne out by the play. The visi- tors brought supporters to the number of over 500, and there would n,t be far short of 6,000 present when Gwynn kicked off towards the pavilion goal. Webster punted to llurst,who tried to show his sprinting powers, but finding opponents equally fleet of foot, he handed over the charge to McCutcheon, but the pass was wild and not taken. Play was thus early on in the Oldham 25, and after Gwynn had effected a clearance, the vi,sit- ing forwards rushed the oval to the home end. Evans, as strong on the defence as ever, soon had the ball out of danger, and bein., ably backed up by Ashton, Fair Turner, and Berry, their progress was not stayed until McCutcheon got clear, when a race across the field saw Daniels effecting a splendid tackle. A free kick to War- rington was spoiled in its return by Bandies, and Old- ham had now an anxious time of it. Daniels put in some neat play, and further ground was gained, Hurst being at fault. Combination was a marked point in the home forwards, but a rash effort in the final stage only credi- ted the Warrington team with a minor. Berry made his mark from a droll out, and James Bate ran round a pack, and kicked judiciously. McCutcheon was tke sa- viour of his side repeatedly, and although Gwynn and
THE PRUDENTAL ASSU RANCE COM- PANY LIMITED.

Some extracts from the forty-second annual re- port for the year ending 30th December, 1890, of this Company will be found in our advertising columns. The figures there published give a clear insight into the enormous, always increasing busi- ness of this Company. The number of policies issued in the ordinary branch during the year was no less than 55,846, assuring the sum of £5,615,676, and producing a new annual premium income of £340,699. The premiums received during the year were £1,162,649, being an increase of £257,734 over the year 1889. The claims for the year amounted to £308,076, and the number of policies in force was 220,545. In the industrial branch the premiums re- ceived during the year were .£3.517X5, being an increase of £181,183. The increase in the premium receipts for the years 1887-90 was £606,630 giving an average increase for the first four years of the quinquennium of £1510657. The claims for the year amounted to .E 1,489,204. The number of deaths was 169,890, and 661 endowment assurances matured. Upwards of 41,000 free policies have been granted during the year to those policy holders of five years' standing who have desired to discontinue their payments, the total number now in force being 208,719. The number. of policies in force was 9,099,204; the average duration continues to in- crease and now exceeds six and a half years. The total assets of the Company have been raised during the year from £10,946,146 to £12,579,870, being an increase of £1,633,714. We may add the genial and active superintendent of this district of the "Pru- dential" is Mr. J. Lythgoe, of 69, Sankey-st.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA.t MARCH 14, lz9l.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA.t MARCH 14, lz9l.

Hurst in succession got a kick to Boscow, the latter was as cool as ever, and replied with interest. Oldham could make no headway whatever against the splendid play of the home forwards, and eventually, after Berry had been prominent on the popular side, Jolley made a des- perate effort to score, being pulled up a few yards from the line. Frank Turner got an apparently fair try from a line-out, but a moment later, a rare example was set the team when after J. T. Bate had tried to get through, Ashton tried his hand, and the home skipper did not try in vain, a loud cheer an- nouncing the point. Fair Turner took the place without succeis. Considerable ground was made by the Oldham backs by tricky work, and play was taken direct to the homelines. The stay was but temporary, and Hurst being a trifle slow in ridding himself of the oval, still further ground was gained by Warrington by the aid of a free kick, which Berry stopped in being returned. A sequence of passes be- tween the two Bates and Daniels puzzled Gwynn and Nolan, but the chance was lost by over-eagerness to score and the homesters had to be content with being on the aggressive. Fair Turner was conspicuous in a line-out, and fine cross dribbling by Povey, Donohue, and Frank Turner saw the game near the Oldham posts, Pennington saving. Daniels earned a round of applause by a fine tackle of Nolan, aud from some loose play which fol- lowed, Berry got away, but a knock forward negatived the chance. McCutcheon next ran across the field in fine style, but found a barrier in Bandies and the• elder Turner,and after Boscow and Webster had been fruitless in staying a rush of the visiting forward, James Bate in- augurated a running passing movement, which took play to near the Oldham twenty-five. Daniels and McCut- cheon exchanged kicks with advantage to the latter, and although Donohue dribbled well along touch, the Oldham right wing responded in brilliaut style. Evans who had had but little to do so far, now had a shot at goal, and a minor was recorded. Soon after James Bate put in a beautiful run down the open, but the final pass fell into the hands of an opponent,and a certain score was lost. The home quarters were once more invaded, but Ashton, the Turners, and Webster worked the leather out of danger, and half time was reached with the score as Warrington, 0-1-2; Oldham, nil. Frank Terner restarted and the home forwards early asserted their superiority. Hurst, after a monotonous attack on the Oldham citadel, raced away in fine style, but Daniels effected another brilliant tackle. Then a surprise awaited the onlookers, for Fair Turner getting clear from a line out gained con- siderable ground by his feigning to pass,the tricky play being loudly applauded. Dillon and Berry raced away at top speed with the oval at their toes, but Pennington saved in marvellous style. Gwynn seconded his efforts, but the Warrington forwards would not be denied, and another specimen of fine combination forced Hurst to 'save. This did not satisfy the homesters,as was plainly seen on the restart, and another passing display by the Bates, Evans, and Webster saw the latter failing to reach the final pass. By this means the pressure was eased,but Warrington working the oval with precision in the loose, raced away once more, and another minor was recorded. James Bate passed finely across to Daniels, but it was but poorly taken, and then Nolan and Hurst got clear in quick succession, and for the first time this . half the home quarters were invaded, Boscow tackling McCutcheon in fine style. Danger was averted when Evans raced away, and foiling Gwynn took play once more to the pavilion end, the superior play of the home ; forwards being especially manifest at this juncture. A , cross dribbling movement, in which Povey was the leader, resulted in Berry crossing the line, but the point was not allowed. Dillon and Jolley each had points dis- allowed, but after another spell of attack, in which Evans I made a sterling run half the length of the field, Ashton augmented the score with another try. MeCutcheon , made an effort near the close, but he was badly supported, and when the whistle sounded the final score read as Warrington, 0-2-4; Cldham, nil. Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscow, back; H. Webster,. J. W. Evans, and W. Daniels. three-quarter backs ; James Bate and J. T. Bate, half backs ; H. Ashton, Fair Turner' Frank Turner, J. Jolley, W. Bandies, W. Povey, W. Berry, T. Donohue, and E. Dillon, forwards. Oldham: W. L. Pennington. back; William M'Cutcheon, D. Gwynn, and John Hurst, three-quarter backs; J. Nolan and J. Thomas, half backs; A. Ashworth, H. Broome, E. Elomley, T. Holden, J. Pendlebury, F. Fitton, T. Potter, G. Ingram, and James Hurst, forwards. Referee, Mr. R. Wilcock.

far as the committee knew. The directors still said that with lf millions more they could bring ships to Manchester with 26 feet water. The com- mittee, however, did not agree with this. It was necessary that the help, if it was to be extended, should be sufficient, and that it should be extended at once. The present debenture holders were covered (said his worship) by theprofits of the Bridgewater undertaking. The loan as proposed in ' the report would be second debentures. A joint Bill would have to be promoted, and the Corporation in,pst be able to show, of course, that the ratepayers of Manchester consented to the pro- posal. The bill, however, ought not to be put forward until the consent of the Local G9vernment Board and the approbation of the Home Secretary were assured. Mr. Moulton, the barrister consulted by the Corporation, was of opinion that if these were assured the bill might pass this year. This was absolutely necessary, as the help must be extended at once. The Corporation must have control over the expenditure of the canal. The railways (his worship said) would probably not oppose. The only difference between the Committee and the directors was as to the point of continued payments of interest to shareholders. A large portion of the canal capital was subscribed on the faith of these payments*, but it was only allowed by law up to £750,000, which would not.of course, cover it up to the completion of the canal. The shareholders must sacrifice all interests. About two-thirds of the work had been done, and, so far as it was done, the work was satisfactory. In con- clusion his worship said that no question had ever en- gaged so much attention from the Corporation as the present, and moved that the report (which has been published in full, or nearly so, in several papers), be taken as read and the Committee continued with power to take action in support of the recommendations em- bodied in their report.

Alderman Sir J. J. Harwood seconded. He enlarged on the importance of the decision to be come to. There was absolutely no alternative for the canal ; if not helped now, the money sunk in it would be absolutely lost, and many unfortunate shareholders absolutely ruined. He insisted that if the canal had any possibility of getting money at 40, or even at 90 per cent., the Corporation would have no business to consider for a moment their application, but they had not. They could not possibly get the money on any terms elsewhere. They could not get rid of their present debentures. The Corporation were absolutely obliged, therefore, to interfere, or the whole thing would go to ruin. Sir John enlarged with considerable eloquence on the position of individual shareholders, saying he knew poor women who had in- vested the savings of their lives in it. Should they have no consideration for these people? Other corporations might join in their action, but there was no time to concert measures. Manchester ratepayers would allow the bill to pass without opposition, out of consideration for their fellow-townspeople who were interested. The Committee in recommending that three millions be the sum for which powers should be asked, said they were anxious to make more than sure of asking enough. There was one weak point in the project—What about the pro- fits or returns in the first or second year after the com- pletion of the canal ? They must, he thought, take the risk. It was not the choice of the Corporation; the canal had come to them. If a man was drowning he should be helped at once or he would perish. Mr. Alderman Thompson said a public trust had been suggested. He thought that as soon as Parliament gave them those powers, such a trust would be established, and trustees and others would invest in first debentures when they saw the Corporation taking secoad deben- tures.
A Councillor suggested that additions should be made to the number of directors.

Mr. Southern, in the course of some remarks, said that it was very likely the terms on which the Corporation could get money would be raised by their appearing in the market for such a large sum. They had many heavy demands themselves to make for their own purposes. They would hold the difference between the Four-and-a- Half per Cent. of the Canal Debentures and the terms which they had to pay as security against loss. The resolution was carried nein. con.

A memorial asking for the necessary public meeting of ratepayers to be convened was signed and handed to his worship. It was resolved that Salford and other cor- porations be communicated with, and copies of the re- port sent them, at the same time calling attention to the paragraphs as to assistance of public bodies. The Mayor and others left for London after the pro- ceedings, to interview the Home Secretary, the President of the Local Government Board, and others.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW c.außcn AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW c.außcn AT WARRINGTON.

A meeting of the members of the congregation and parishioners of Holy Trinity and of St. Alary's Bank Quay, was held in the Trinity Schools, Museum-st., on Monday evening, to consider whether the time had arrived for appointing a Committee to raise the necessary funds, Ad take other requisite steps, for the erection pf St. Mary's Church. Lord Winmarleigh has given £2,000 as an endowment fund, and promised £l,OOO towards the building of the church. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., nas promised to contribute £1,500 to the building fund, whilst the Hon. Leopold W. H. Fox Powys has placed an excellent site in Liverpool- road at the disposal of the Committee. There was a moderate attendance at the meeting, amongst those present being the Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. Carle- ton, the Rev. W. E. Glenn, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. and Mrs. James Fairclough, Mr. William Sharp, Mr. John Hatton, Mr. Rowson, Mr. R. Dobson, Mr. H. J. Westbrook, &c.

After some conversation in which it was stated that the church-going population in St. Mary's dis- trict would probably be 500 or 600, Mr. Jour; WHITE said a church to accommodate 500 or 600 was required. For his own part, he would rather see a small church crammed than a large church only half full. A congregation of 500 after all was a very large one, and a chnrch to accommodate that number would be all that would be required for the next 100 years. If it was decided to erect the church, he thought that a parsonage house ought to be built at the same time. The time would come during the next few years when the parish of St. Mary must be separated from the mother parish of Holy Trinity, although he was aware that the splitting of parishes was of no great advantage to the smaller church, and that he was in favour .of the mother churches working as far as possible by means of mis- sion churches. (Hear, hear.) He did not think there should be any great difficulty in raising the money. They had £2,500 to begin with, which was a very handsome sum ,and if they could raise £2,000 more, they might en- deavour to raise the church. (Applause.) He thought it was a sum that they could manage to raise Without having recourse to a bazaar.which involved so much work for the ladies. (Laughter.) He suggested that theyshould endeavour to get five people who would either give or be responsible for £5O each. He would not mind being one of those. (Applause.) They might find 150 people who would be responsible for or collect £lO, and a few more who would give or collect £5. (Applause.) After all, a bazaar was not the most credit- able means of raising money for a church. (Applause.)— Mr. Warburton (St. Mary's) said that when they at St. Mary's first heard of the intention of building a church, they initiated a plan for a number of them to subscribe so much a month, and they had been doing so for some time. (Heir, hear.)—Mr. Fairclough said he had great plsasure in moving that Mr. John White's views be car- ried out. He had been previously connEnted with the building of churches, and he had never known a better start than was being made in the present case. (Ap. p!ause.)—Mr. Sharp seconded Mr. Fairclough's proposi- tion, and thought it would be very ungrateful to the donors if something were not done. He considered that. the work ought to be taken in hand at once.—The motion was put and carried unanimously.—Mr. John Hatton proposed that all the gentlemen present form ,a General Committee, with power to add to their number.-7 Mr. Pairclough seconded, and the motion was carried.—Mr. Westbrook was elected hcn. sec., and Mr. Jas. Fairclough hon. treasurer, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
FROM BARTON LOCKS TO WARRINGTON.

It was Mr. Leader Williams, I believe, who alone amongst Manchester men fuuud cause for congratu- lation in the generous dampness that flooded the Ship Canal cuttings last November. The boss engineer, with the memory of much irritating argument rankling in him, exclaimed, " The water question is settled for ever. The canal has been filled in a single night l"

div.head: BARTON.
div.p: BARTON.

From the late site of Stickeifs Island one gazes down into a mighty thoroughfare 170 feet wide from the bottom, of which have already arisen a series of lock walls in stolid stone work, each about twice the size of the New Brighton Fort,con- structed apparently to last for ever. These are the Barton locks, one of them 600 feet by 65 feet, the other 450 feet by 45 feet; and beside them on the left bank four mighty sluices, each 30 feet wide, are nearly completed, There is a drop of 15 feet here in the bottom level. A pump that occupies the length of a small street is getting out the last few gallons of flood water from the cutting, where a throng of masons are shaping the great coping stones for the locks by means of templates and other apparatus of their craft. The locomotives and trucks hereabouts, having no more " spoil " to re- move,are engaged only in bringing sand and cement to the numerous mixing boards, each as large as the stage of a theatre, whereon gangs of a dozen or so of men and boys are mixing gruel thick and slab for the builders who swarm over the rising masonry. The track between these locks and the next series at Irlam was flooded in November, but I learn that the water along three miles and a half of this cutting was pumpeci out at the rate of two feet per day. A fact which speaks volumes— volumes of water, an it please you-,-for the magni- ficent nature of the machinery employed.
IRLAAI.

I secured an illicit -iici-e-On a locomotive to the Irlam locks, works of exactly the same gigantic character as those at Barton, with the exception that the fall is one foot deeper, and approaching as near completion. The progress here, as everywhere, is of the most encouraging character. "Deviation railway No. 5 " that of the Liverpool, Warrington, and Chester line at Irlam—shuts in the perspective like a mountain range, and the scaffolding in the canal cutting rises like a sky-sign nightmare of mammoth proportions, 110fu. upwards from the bottom in the centre. Here, again, one is liable to lose one's bearings, for, like all other railways on the track, it crosses the canal at an angle of about 45 degrees, and the face of all nature appears to have been out on the spree and got tangled some- how. The immense iron girders now being de- livered and hoisted into place, are of themselves a feature of the scene. What thrills one with supreme amazement, however, is the reflection that all these colossal operations are being carried on simultane- ously along 35 miles of country. So far as I have travelled no part of the work can be considered backward, in the sense that it is at all behind atty other portion.

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.

At Thelwall the great sheet of water, 172 feet wide, at about half its full depth, swept and curled into miniature seas by the brisk Marchabreeze, is a really handsome spectacle. A tiny steam launch, rocking and puffing along the surface, adds to the fine aquatic effect, and seems quite at home on its novel cruising ground. The company are making bricks hero from the native clay, in kilns of their own that produce half-a-million per week. The river is diverted beyond the right bank, and, as will be seen by a glance at the map, trends away up country in devious loops as far as Warrington town. The road-bridges and brook aqueducts, swept away in hideous ruin by the floods, have all been re- placed—by what means I. know not, but conjecture that the pile-drivers have been called into requisi- tion to set up their fifty odd feet of supports again ia the canal bottom. A great dam left in the cut- ting, separates the water from the Latchford cut- ting, which has been pumped completely dry, and looking down from the roadway that crosses it one gains a still more eplendid coup d'reil than either of those afforded on the upper sections of the track.

div.head: LA.TCHFORD.
div.p: LA.TCHFORD.

Here the Latchford lock-walls have arisen in majestic, almost solemn grandeur from the depths of 55ft. excavation into the solid sandstone. This is no longer a cutting; it is a great artificial valley, in the centre of which men are putting up moun- tains in a Tierra del Fuego of engine smoke, and the works for the deviation of the Warrington and Stockport Railway form a startling background to the view. Imagine a forest of straight pine trees, denuded of their branches, standing in irregular clumps to the height of over a hundred feet, across a chasm nearly two hundred'feet in width. Inter- lace amongst these uprights ten thousand giant copies of the letter X; add to them four colossal buttresses of black polished brickwork, and over- head throw a dizzy staging of timber, on which men the size of flies are at work with toylike steam cranes, hauling masses of iron girder work into position,and you will get some feeble notion of how a railway has to be carried over the mastheads of the ocean liners that will ere long make their way up country to Manchester. On each side of the cutting place an earthbank fifty feet high drifting away into mile-long perspective.on either hand,and shutting out the scenery behind it, and you will comprehend what has become of the "spoil "from the cuttings. Remember that every time you make a railway journey to these parts in the near future. you will have to be carried as high as a POrtland-st. warehouse over the canal service,and you will under- stand to what extent the traveller's outlook is going to be improved.
WILDERSPOOL.

The next stage of my journey began with a surreptitious and unlawful trespass on the railway premises at Latchford station, and an outrage on the company's fences. And once more I was lost upon what should have been familiar ground. The cutting extends to Wilderspool, to a point where the Mersey, having acquired a satisfactory acces- sion of foulness from Warrington, used to make an elegant curve across the path of the Ship Canal. When I was here last the upper stratum of fine silver sand, to a depth of 20 feet or so, was being removed by the ulaided efforts of one great German steam navvy, reaching out a series of giant claws at the end of a long beam, and literally pumping the sand up from below it into long strings of railway trucks. Now the German navvy has gone, and so has the sand. So have the railway lines on which the big excavator ran, and the path whereon our party walked. Furthermore, a bed of red rock to a depth .of twenty feet below the sand would appear to have been blasted out and removed, leaving only a few particularly bony pieces to be blown into cobbles arid shifted. in the course of the next week or so. The canal here, indeed, as everywhere, is practically made, and grass 'has already decked th e upper banks with an emerald vestment for a distance of half-a-mile. The transformation is marvellous, and the impression on the visitor's mind at once inspiring and profound. The works along the whole route, indeed,are at this moment grandiose and Weil:rating,' venture to say,beyond all previous human achievements.

I drove up to Warrington on the knifeboard of the penny 'bus, just as the god of day was paint- ing the royal mantle of the west. I watched the opalescent changing of the tender sky-tints; and on the Mersey margin, where the new Warrington docks are presently to be, I saw the crow sink softly on the swelling bosom of the dank dead cat. And as I gazed I mused upon the perverted taste of our artist,. who had abandoned all these pure and unalloyed delights for the meretricious pleasures of musical society, and had given his genius to the dressing of an operatic combination.—From the Sunday Chronicle.
MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY. ASSISTANCE TO BE GIVEN.

A special Meeting of the Manchester City Council was held on Monday to elect an alderman to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. W. T. Windsor, and to receive the report of the Special Committee recently appointed to consider the request of the Ship Canal Company for, pecuniary assistance in completing the undertaking. • The Mayor (Mr. Alderman John Mark) presided, and there was a very large attendance. Sir Joseph C. Lee and other direct Ors of the Canal Company occupied seats in the Strangers' Galleries. The Mayor (Mr. Alderman Mark), in opening the pro- ceedings explained the formation and labours of ths com- mittee; and enlarged on the lucid manner in which the report was compiled, in the face of difficulties and of pressure•of time. The directors had, he said, given the .committee every facility as to information. Mr. Hill for the engineering portion, and Mr. Thackray for the finan- cial, had gone into the matter most carefully. There was an impression abroad in some quarters that certain matters were beingikept back. That was not the case so

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

Considerably activity is at present displayed on the Ship Canal Works at Runcorn. The line of metals laid on piles in the river from the Old Quay, to No Man's Land is nearly completed, and when the Gantry is set in motion, the work of making the wall will be Much expedited. There is also an air of bustle in the river near the pumping engine,where the concrete foundations of the Bridgewater Lock are being laid.—Materials are carried to the spot from No Man's Land by means of a double line of metals in waggons drawn by a locomotive. From the Old Quay to Big Field, a number of steam navvies are now employed excavating the bed of the canal for that length. In some places ailepth of over 60 feet has to be excavated.
A SISTER CHARGED_ WITH THEFT AT RUNCORN.

Mary Doyle, an elderly woman of Mhfield-st., Liverpool, appeared at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a summons charging her with having stolen a silver watch chain worth 155., from the person of her brother, Peter Stubbs, shipwright, of Hankey-st., Runcorn. Mr. Burton represented the defendant.—lt appeared that on Monday, the 2nd inst.,the defendant called at Stubbs's house and asked him when-he was going to pay her the £3 he owed her for a watch and chain. He said he did not owe her a farthing piece,and bade her begone,as he wanted no dealings with her. Some strong language was used and the altercation drew together all the neighbours. The defendant and the complainant pushed each other and the latter alleged that his sister snatched his watch chain fr.m his breast. In answer to Mr. Burton he denied that he had struck his sister, and said that had the magistrates last week granted him a warrant and locked his sister up till next morning to teach her how to behave herself he would have been satisfied. He admitted that he turned out after dark with a candle looking for a chair in the street and also early next morning.—Elizabeth Whitting- ham, the housekeeper, said she saw the defendant snatch the chain.—Without hearing the defence,Mr. C. Reynolds said the law of larceny was very clear that where per- sons thought they had a right to claim the magistrates could not try it. They therefore Could not try the case; Stubbs's remedy was in the county court.—The complainant who had caused considerable amusement by his excited manner and emphatic gestures then left the court, saying that if there was no law he would make one.

div.head: MAINTENANCE OF PAUPER PARENTS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE MAINTENANCE OF PAUPER PARENTS AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Wigg at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Mondayi_ a flatman named James Houghton was summondtl to show cause why he should not contribute towards the maintenance Of his mother Mary Houghton, who was a poor and old person and unable to maintain herself. Mr. A. Linaker appeared on behalf of the Board of Guardians, and Mr. John Frodsham, the collector to the Union, stated that the defendant was a waterman and earned from 235. to 275. per week. Three years ago he promised to pay is. per week, but he had only paid about 15s. His brother contributed is. 9d. per week, and the Guardians asked for an order against the defendant of is. per week.—The defendant said he had had much aimless in his family and could not pay.—An order for is. per week was made.—A similar order was sought against Edward Richardson, in respect to his mother, Martha Richardson who is in receipt of 3s. per week from the Union.--2 Mr. Frodsham said the defendant was a labourer at the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Works, and his earnings were 2s. 84-d. a day. •He did not work regularly and was therefore only given odd jobs.—The defendant said his health had failed, and he could not carry on his work as fireman. His mother did not need relief. She lived rent free, and she had a brother in Tasmania from whom she had received £5O and many a five and ten pounds be- sides. He did not suppose that she was short of a hun- dred pounds, never mind getting anything from the Union. He was surprised at the Guardians bringing him there. Mr. Reynolds said the Union Committee ought toinqnire into this • surely they would not let a thing of this sort pass.—Mr. Linaker said the defendant had received notice to appear before the Committee, but he had not done so, and this was the first that had been heard of his mother having money.—The case was adjourned for a fortnight in order that inquiries might be made.—Joseph Hopley, a flatman, appeared to show cause why he should not contribute towards the main- tenance of his father who was paid 3s. per week from the Union funds. It was stated that the defendant was married and a waterman earning 255. a week. The Guardians asked fpr is. 6d. per week. It transpired that his brother unmarried was only contributing is. per week, and the Bench made an order for a similar contribution from the defendant.—James Garner, Frod- sham, and Joseph Garner Runcorn, were each ordered to pay 6d per 'Week towards the 3s. paid by the Uai2n to thei mother, Mary Garner.

The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 50 cases. 36 of which were old and 14 laew cases.

div.head: OLD BOOKS
div.p: OLD BOOKS

Mr. BLACKHURST called attention to the fact that there was a great accumulation of old books and papers, and he moved that they should be disposed of, and it was decided to dispose of them to a paper maker to be destroyed.
THE PRICE OF GAS AT PADGATE SCHOOLS,

The CLERK reported that the Warrington Gas Com- mittee had decided to reduce the price charged for the gasmsed at Padgate Industrial Schools, so that it be 6d. Per 1,000 feet in addition to what is charged in the borough.

div.head: TENDERS.
div.p: TENDERS.

div.head: WARRINGTON SLANDER ACTION.
div.p: A WARRINGTON SLANDER ACTION.

A VERDIQT FOR £5O. At the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday, before Mr. onstice Lawrence, John Cooper, a constable in the Warrington police force, proceeded against Thomas a tarmer, of Latchford Grange Farm, War- 4.fligton, to recover damages for slander, it being alleged that the.defendant stated to several persons that the plaintiff had been guilty of an abominable and indictable offence. The defendant pleaded Rriviiege. _ Mr. Horridge, instructed by Mr. A. -',3towne, appeared for the plaintiff; and Mr. Mule li_olland, instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and rershaW for the defendant. a The plaintiff stated that on December 17th he. was on mIltY near the defendant's farm, and towards midnight pe heard footsteps and saw a man go through a gate ~eading to outbuildings. Suspecting the man's intentions ne followed right into the defendant's stables,but did not And the man. His lamp was extinguished, and while he Isis in the stable yard engaged striking a match the endant and his wife came up carrying lights. When he saw the plaintiff defendant said, "I've caught you 11°w." Plaintiff went away, and on reaching the police- e_tation at twoo'clock next morning he found that the de- had been and made a serious statement against hire. The matter was investigated by the superior police oincers and the Watch Committee, who found that there was no truth in the charge. The matter had become generally known in the neighbourhood. Constable John Baxendale, Sergeant Cheney, and In- R3ector Spinks gave evidence as to the defendant lodg- ing a complaint at the Police Office. The defendant also charzed the plaintiff with being "boozed," but the wit- nesses saw no sign of drink on him. The defendant had been fined for allowing his dog to go unmuzzled. The Constable's clothing was examined after, the charge, but aothing to excite suspicion was discovered. The Inspec- tor stated that when the matter was investigated by the __Watch Committee the Mayor said the constable left the h.alayor's parlour without a tittle of suspicion against A youth named Hartley was called to prove that the defendant had spoken to him about the matter. . Mr. Mulholland, for the defence, said there was no de- re to allege that the plaintiff was guilty of the partieu- .4r offence. All the defendant wished to say was that it appeared to him upon the night in question some one 'tad been on his premises with improper intent. In the se of trying to find out the person he saw the plain- on:l his premises, and in the anxiety and annoyance tt, the moment he probably came to a hastier conclusion luan the subsequent investigation of the facts warranted. 4'4 Point of law, the defendant was entitled to take the d9tien he had done so long as there was no malice or in- tillreet motive, and if it was done in the honest belief at What he said was true. The defendant was called, and related the circurn- „,t4hces under which he saw the plaintiff, and afterwards Tadea complaint to the police. When the matter was ,:veatigated by the watch committee, the Mayor said it Os a case of suspicion, but that it would have to go "efore the magistrates. Upon that he (the defendant) aald, "Let the matter drop." He did not repeat the Zistter to any one.—Cross-examined: He believed the is_aternents he made to the police to be true. He now lielieved the man was guilty of the offence. He did not Prosecute, because he had told the inspector he did not ),..I)6sh to do the man any harm. He did not go to the v°!ice office to have the. plaintiff punished.—His Lord- 'P: Then what did you go for? Defendant: To report 11 -Mr. Ford having given evidence, the ulayor of Warrington (Alderman Francomb) was called, stated that he was chairman of the watch committee l'efore whom this mattes' was heard. When pressed Nyhether he made the charge against a policeman, the Oefendant said, "I make no charge." Witness believed tliat Ford was perfectly justified in having a strong sus- Meion. Defendant said it was somebody, but he would li.ot make the charge against the policeman. The plain- was exonerated. Witness considered Ford had a ht to have suspicion against someone, but not the viaintiff tjlis Lordship, in summing up, said that, prima facie,' 13 occasion would be privileged so long as there I iwas no malice or indirect motive. If the jury considered hat the defendant acted hastily, or unduly, or without It'asenable caution then it would be evidence of malice. tinl. any case the defendant would have no right to repeat . e statements made to the police, and he might at any 4tee have admitted that -he had made a mistake and ck°llld•not go on with the case. Although the gravity of charge was pointed out to defendant,he nevertheless teisted in going from one authority to another, and it ,6old be a question for the jury to say how far that was "I`ridence of malice. In the face of all, although the 4hefendant would not prosecute, he now came into court tsg.ti said he still believed the man was guilty of the /Chills. The statement of Hartley was not privileged. Vat' beensaid that the matter ought not to have come Iv 40re the court, but his opinion was that the plaintiff fo°„Uld have been unworthy to have remained in the police teieo if he had not thus endeavoured to clear his charac-
Th the e jury found for the plaintiff, damages £5O, and ma. foreman said they were of the same opinion as the 0343:_ee of Warrington with regard to the plaintiff's 44eter.

"WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday mottling. Alderman Harrison presided, and there were pre- sent Messrs. Blackhurst, T. Jones, Heaton, Davies, Jolley, Balharry, Dobson, Aukland, Dignum, Mather, Humphreys, Turton, Clarke. W. Houghton, Smith, Swinton, Gill, J. Houghton, Kilshall ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (Workhouse master.) , THE CHILDREN AND THEIR AMUSEMENTS. Mr, Mines reported that the children from Padgate Schools attended a performance at the Public Hall on Saturday afternoon, and at the conclusion they were each presented with an orange and a bun by Mr. Milton and other ladies, and a bunch of flowers from "Little Flossie one of the performers.—Mr. A. JOLLEY asked by whose authority the children went to the Public Hall. They had passed a resolution that the children should Rot go to any entertainment except on the authority of the Committee.—The CLERK believed the children were taken on the authority of the Chairman of the Corn- Inittee,—The CHAIRMAN said he did not suppose Mr. Jolley objected to the children going to the Public Hall, but had simply raised it as a matter of form.—Mr. tieterox said the committee passed the resolution referred tn._ because the children were going out almost every day. /de was sure the Committee would not grumble as long ?..s the children were not taken out too often.—The sub- Ject then dropped.
GRAPPENHALL IN ARREARS.

The CLERK re-portecrhaC-all the townships had paid their calls except Grappenhall, whose call was due in January. He would ask the Board to give instructions to sue Grappenhall if the call was not paid. He did not think it fair that any one parish should be allowed to fall into arrears.—Mr. DOBSON remarked that perhaps they Were badly off in Grappenhall.—The CLERK said they Should not,as the parish was one of the most moderately, assessed in the Union.—The CHAIRMAN thought the peo- Pie of Grappenhall were not badly off.—Mr. Sairrn ex- plained that it was not the fault of the overseers them- selves that Grappenhall was in arrears.—The CLERK Pointed out that the overseers would be held responsible, and they would be the persons to be summoned. The subject then dropped.
