THE AMENDED WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT.

Sir,—lf you, or some one of you readers, would give their opinion as to whether farmers can, under the above-named Act, demand that manure coming by boat shall be weighed over a maehine before being put into the boat,in lieu of, as now, being gauged, you or they, will, I feel sure, be heartily thanked. In the case of Gordon v. Warburton, as reported in your last week's Examiner, the discrepancy of 26 tons between machine and gauge weight is more than start- ling to the already over-rented and over-taxed farmer.— Yours, &c.,
EX-FARMER.
A LIVING CONTEMPORARY OF WESLEY.

Sir,—As the public mind at present is full of recollec- tions of Wesley, I thought the following item would be interesting to many of your readers. On Saturday last, in company with a friend, I visited on old gentleman in Salford who is now 110 years old. His name is William Hamson and he was born in Salford, November 1780. He has always lived there, and, despite its crowded streets and busy mart, he has managed to survive to the above ripe old age. His father, I was told, lived to be 102, and his maternal grandfather 107. He evidently belongs to a good old stock. The old gentle- man with his husky, tremulous voice narrated how he had seen John Wesley in connection with the building and opening of tho Wesleyan Chapel at Gravel-lane on a piece of land known as Salford Green. In corroboration of this, I ascertained that the Chapel, near which he resides, was erected in 1790. So he was about 10 years old when he saw and heard the vener- able founder of Methodism. Though he complained of pains in the side of the head, he seemed in fair possession of all his faculties. He says he peacefully awaits the call of his Master. I hope he will not be worried to death by the lionising interviewer and photographer.— Yours truly, 8, Chandos-st., Earlestown

div.head: WILLIAM WALTON.
div.p: WILLIAM WALTON.
THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.

Sir,—When Roman Catholics desire to lead opponents to imagine that they constitute the" Catholic Church," they appeal to the clause in the Creed," I believe in the Holy Catholic Church," although when that Creed was drawn up, not one of the articles in the Creed of Pope Pius was known or accepted by any Christian. When certain Anglican clergymen desire to enforce their special views and tenets, they, too, appeal to the Creed. This has been notably done in a sermon first preached in the Parish Church, put into print, and cir- culated. The argument from the Creed can serve neither party. What is a Creed .? A beief in things invisible, not visible. " Faith is the evidence of things not seen." The Creed speaks in its several clauses of things unseen. The clause about the "Catholic Church "comes be- twixt clauses referring to the Holy Ghost, and the Communion of Saints. Why should it refer to what is visible, a visible church, when these clauses and all the others refer to what is invisible? It cannot possibly do so ; otherwise it would not be an article of faith. It alludes to that great universal or Catholic Church com- posed of all tongues and peoples who trust savingly to the Lord Jesus Christ. As a great early Christian writer puts it, "The Catholic Church consists of the congrega- tion of the elect." Part of it is in heaven, part is milit- ant here on earth. This Church is alone the subject of the Creed ; and not any one visible church on earth.— Your obedient servant, Runcorn, March, 1891.

Sir,—The Salvation Army in Earlestown will be highly delighted at the splendid advertisement they got in yeur last issue, especially as it came from such a prominent source. A little more of a similar character from :the same quarter, and they will certainly begin to shape about building the " barracks " they have had in view for some time. "GAS VERSUS COMMON-SENSE !"

Sir,—With fear and trembling I reply to "Master of Arts "—to allay his natural curiosity—that, of course, ParnelPs accuser raised the smell (and it was a foul one!) around Parnell; but for which, as II have before humbly asserted, the latter would have been, politically, as" dead as a door nail," and Ireland and Home Rule would have been getting within measurable distance" of" a good end to be attained." Therefore, Ireland is thankful to Hugh Price Hughes, and would give him a warm 'welcome were he to venture over there.

" Veritas " asks in his second paragraph (the first has one or two assumptions in it, that, coming from a seem- ingly warped intellect, may well be treated with con- tempt) : What truer thing could Rev. H. P. Hughes say, than a "Christian who voted for a brewer at an election was a Christian humbug ?" Nothing truer could be said, if the phrase was uttered t.) exemplify what a fool even, a parson can make of himself, when he descends to ben- kum, and has :nothing else to feed his audience on. Why, sir, there are brewers living to-day who have done more real good to their fellows by a scratch of the pen, than the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes will do if he lives to be as old as Methusaleh ? And you may throw W. T. Stead into the scale with him.! " Veritas," however, deserves my thanks, and I therefore humbly render them to him, for " helping me over the style" with "Felix." The latter says, with a simplicity and "greenness" perfectly ludicrous," no consistent man ever solicits aid for Christian work from so tainted a source (as a brewer's purse), and Wesleyan ministers of all men." As if they had they had the monopoly ef all goodness and morality! Good Lord! have the Wes- leyans and other Creeds never held bazaars to help on their pious missions; and have they ever prevented, or attempted to prevent—a brewer from entering; and when there, have they 'never pestered him for his" ill- gotten gains ? " Why, 4` Felix," emerald doesn't half express your colour; no grass was ever greener than you are; and your experience has been of the very smallest. Therefore, your "pitiful patter," about mor- ality is really notworth powder and shot, and I leave it and the subject of "Drink versus Teetotalism" also, until that axiom in Scripture, which teaches me that I am accountable to a higher Power than theirs for all my actions, has been proved to be a lie; and until the masters oi their meddlesome school—have shown that they have any authority or mandate whatever for their fussy and offensive nose-poking into the matter of what their neighbours who differ from them choose---tand have a right to ch ,ose—to drink. None but the fanatical faddists of the 1.0.G.T. School would have the hardihood to assert, that a bottle of gas. blown mineral swipes is as good for the human frame as a glass ot good honest beer. But, sir, lam heartily sick of the cant and hypocrisy I hear on all sides in connec- tion with this Drink Question; and am daily morn con- vinced than ever, that sue] men as Hugh Price Hughes, W. T. Stead, and such smaller fry as " Veritas " and " Felix," are doing far more harm than good; but the subject being genial to their tastes, by enabling them to be constantly hunting for stinks and then rooting in them, it is not to be hoped that they will ever have the eommcn-sense and rightmindedness to drop it.—Yours truly,
PLUTO

div.head: IN DARKEST IGNORANCE WITH MOSES; AND
div.p: IN DARKEST IGNORANCE WITH MOSES; AND
THE WAY OUT.

Wherever Moses, as the writer of Gen. 1., makes state- ments not the result of human experience, and those statements can be tested by the facts involved, the facts discredit the statements.—SUNDAY SCHoOL MANUAL (2091 A.D.)

Sir,—ln my last, it was conclusively shown that, if we accept the results of modern scientific investigeion —notably in Biology and Geology—and reason upon these after the methods laid down by logicians, the re- sult is entirly destructive of the idea of Moses as an in- spired writer. Upon any known theory of Inspiration, it is utterly inconceivable that a duly accredited agent of the Maker could so grossly mistake His method and manner of working. The position here taken up is quite impregnable, if we adopt the first canon of literary critic- ism, i.e.—that the" text of our authority shall not be altered." But the "believer," whilst squirming im- paled upon the point of an inexorable logic, still assever- ates his "convictions "and thinks they are arguments.

I believe it is one of the fundamental items of the ,Christian's Creed that ordinary mortals—those in the carnal state as they say—must be born again ere they can appreciate and participate in the myths and mys- teries of the:sect. Now Sir, this may or may not be so; but of this I am convinced, that the average Christian needs very considerable regeneration ere he can attain to the comprehension and acceptance of a logical sequence affecting the dogmas of his faith. This, indeed, might be expected in one brought up from earliest infancy in an atmosphere of belief and imbued with the notion that to reason upon the basis of his faith was wrong, if not absolutely sinful. His faith has thus been developed at the expense of his rational faculties, which have be- come atrophied from disuse. But still he " reasons " ! But oh shades of Watts and Whately, how? Con- fronted by Moses, in the fix we found him in last com- munication, he proceeds to unfix him, adopting a line of ratiocination sufficient to clog the wheels of any Mill I ever heard of! The arguments used, if the incoherent tangle of inconsequent statements can be dignified by such a name, appear in two contradictory forms. I. He assumes that Moses was right. To this deified idea he sacrifices, with a light heart, all the rules and deductions of the eicact sciences. The rules of arith- metic and right reasoning are immolated upon the altar of his idea of Mosaic infallibility. As to the time occu- pied by the creative acts, he maintains that it matters not what Moses said about this matter—that we do not know what he meant--that he might mean Sze., &c. inde- finitely. As to the literary unfitness of any man who could write in this slipshod fashion to deal with such subjects as the commandments, heseems not to have the remotest idea. Apply the same reasoning—allow the same laxity of interpretation—to the words of Moses as to stealing,adultery, &c., and we see at once the literary and logical quagmire into which these innocents fall when they leave their " dreams and visions," to tread the narrow path of reasoning.. But mark how different is his treatment of the next stiff place in which he finds Moses!

11. As to the method of Creation. Here we have the argument reversed. In the first case the words were wrong and the science right. Here we have the science wrong and Moses right ! ! Now, does it not seem to ordinary intellect, undisturbed by the supposed imperia- tive necessity to believe—even unreasoningly—that these two modes of argument are self-destructive? If the siriter of Genisis I. is not to be accepted literally when he wrote that very circumstantial account of the Crea- tion in six days, how can we be expected to receive him /as accurate on such subjects as specific creation— much less the decalogue ? If the writer would blunder so greatly about the one, why not about the other? Has it never occurred to the zealous but indiscreet defender of the faith, that it is extremely irrational to destroy our faith in the general accuracy of an author, by con- vincing us that, in a particular case, he has used words which did not convey his meaning,or meant things other than he said? Here, then, let us pause to ask, "How are we to regard this writer who claims the possession of supernatural knowledge, and himself so utterly dis- proves the validity of his own claim? The conclusion /arrive at,as the only one warranted by the facts of the case, is that,whoever the writer was—and whatever else he knew—on this subject he was absolutely and entirely ignorant. How this conclusion affects the subsequent statements of this writer depends largely upon the per- sonal peculiarities of the reader. How it affects me I will tell in my next, if health and editorial forbearance hold out for another and a last word, this session, on this subiect.when I will endeavour to indicate "the Wayout" of this maze of Mosaic aarkness.—l am, sir, yours, &c., JOHN PEERS.
Penketh, March Bth, 1891.
THE GOSPELS AND THEIR AUTHORSHIP.

Sir,---Mr. Gandy in his last epistle asserts " that the Christian Fathers and Early Christian literature can be made to prove anything. This is certainly very judiciously put; for our modern rationalists have a re- markable faculty of making black to be white, or in other words of transforming truth into error. I don't apply this remark to my good friend,but I most assuredly do so to the class of authorities he relies so much upon. Let me ask him to drop the words I have marked with italics in his assertion, and then I give a most unqualified denial to his statement. The Christian Fathers and Early Christian literature do not prove anything, as, for instance, they do not prove that our Gospels are aught else than what we take them to be, the productions of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
My friend very needlessly observes that I make " a

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURD.VY, MARCH 14, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURD.VY, MARCH 14, 1891.

great parade of authorities." Now let me say that if I do so, it is no doubt a very inconvenient method to adopt with people who expect their own positive but in- arrect sta,tements to be accepted as the end of all con- troversy. \ They do not like to be troubled with authnrities. It is specially inconvenient to be asked for authorities, when perhaps to supply them is to utterly vitiate their own confident assertions, as, for instance, "The disciples of Christ were ignorant men,and could not write." but then as Dr. Abbott,the authority,adds "with the exception of Matthew "!

My friend, however, does not object to fly to authori- ties when they seem to answer his purpose. His very ir- relevant quotations from Mosheim, however, simply per- plex me. Mosheim distinctly repudiates any such libel up on the early fathers as that" they counted it pious to lie and cheat. On the contrary, in vol. I. p. 128 (Murdock and Soames translation—from which I quote—edited by Stubbs) he says, referring to the writers of the second century—" In these disputants there was sometning more of ingenuousness and good faith, than in those who un- dertook the support of truth in the following centuries. For the convenient wiles of sophistry, and the dis- honourable artifices of debate,had not yet gained admit- tance among Christians." Does my friend want anything more direct than that? for he must not overlook that my testimonies to the authorship of the Gospels were taken so far from the writers of the first and second centuries. But this is not all. In his quotation this week from page 87 of his copy of Mosheim—there is a remarkable omis- sion which I read on page 74 of the copy I use, touch- ing the "lives and morals of Christians" in the first century "as patterns of purity and holiness, worthy of the imitation of all subsequent ages." "This representa- tion," he says, " if it be understood of the greater part of the professed Christians,and not of all is undoubtedly true "(the italics are Mosheim's own). Now, how hap- pens it that this passage is omitted in my friend's quota- tion? Does it really not appear on page 87 of his copy ? It would be interesting to know whose edition of Mos- heim he quotes from.

Again,- I cannot grasp for what purpese Mr. Gandy introduces his quotation from page 84 of his copy. What in the world has it to do with the subject under discus- cussion ? Absolutely nothing. Matters of fanciful and silly interpretations of Scripture are one thing. Ws know that the early Christians and fathers were given to this; but their testimony as to facts is quite another thing; and their veracity on this point is no more to be questioned than I should dispute my friend's testimony to a fact, though I might feel inclined to ridicule his exposition of SOME, passage of Scripture. I am referred to Drs. Marti- neau and Abbott and Professor Carpenter; but in the respective quotations I look in vain for any reply to the historical evidence of Papias and Irenteus. There is as- sumption in abundance, but no proof. In their works, says, Mr. Gandy, statements are found "very far re- moved from those of Drs. Westcott and Lightfoot." Yes, indeed, there are. We find Dr. Martineau, for instance, setting his subjective, philosopical theories against the hard facts of history, and contending that these must be brushed aside since they don't square with his philo- sophy ; whilst Drs. Westcott and Lightfoot very reason- ably make such dreams give way to the force of histori- cal truth. Practical readers and thinkers, I imagine,will applaud this latter and truer method, and judge it wiser to make theories conform to facts, and not facts to theories.

Dr. Martineau's late work has been conclusively an- swered by Dr. Date in the" Contemporary " for Septem- ber last. Ido not know much of Dr. Abbott except for recent articles in the reviews, one of which has beak; dealt with by Professor Beet. But I reject the quota: tion made from him as only another specimen of that rationalistic assumption so often opposed to the evidence of history. The name of Carpenter is one to conjure with in the estimation of some people. But the work from which Mr.Gandy quotes is not likely to establish the reputation of its gifted author as a very high authority in that historical criticism in which as yet our English West- cott and Lightfoot are generally acknowledged to rule paramount. From a rectrit review of his hooka is like all its predecessors which I have ever seen; it fails utterly just where it ought to succeed; and that fact the re- viewer shows very conclusively. It is wisely said that the strength of a chain is only equal to the strength of its weakest link; and when rofessor Carpenter comes to the crucial test in his argument, down he goes. He can give no satisfactory explanation on his theory at all, whilst he admits the universal reception of our gospels in the latter half 'of the second century—" how the gospels came to have been thus universally re- ceived among churches so widely apart, so differ- ent from one another in temperament and mode of thought, and so ecclesiastically independent." The reviewer, whilst acknowledging "his great learning and ingenuity" further. states that he supports the "advanced "criticism by arguments "far from per- suading us of the validity of his position." (" Literary World," 23rd Jan. 1891). Now it is exactly at this point that my present argument stands—the testimony of Papias, and Irenteus especially to the fact that uni- versally the four Gospels were received in their time, as the productions of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and,John. I shall await with some curiosity to hear how Mr. Gandy disposes of this matter. I hope to have the privilege of .replying to some other items in my friend's letter. One matter I think shoutd have immediate attention. Mr. Gandy takes um- brage at my tone and style of writing. I have no desire, and no right in fact, to assume any superiority. But permit me to say that I also think that my friend would have "consulted his own dignity better " had he refrained from speaking so disrespectfully of the disciples of Christ, from classing -the Christians and Fathers of the fist centuries—a race of the Purest and noblest characters as a body that ever walked this earth—amongst "the most unprincipled liars and forgers of whom we have any record," and further bad he given a little more thought ere he had attempted to to throw redicule upon the canon of sacred Scriptures by citing a stupid monkish legend which he should have known had no truth in it whatever. He need not wonder that my "self-conscious superiority" to that sort of thing should have asserted itself in some way or other, though none the less to my sincere and deep esteem for his many excellent traits of character in other respects.—Yours, &c., JOHN DIGNUM.
Penketh, 12th March, 1891.
DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. J. B.
LORD CHARLES BERESFORD.

This gallant naval commander is the second son of the Rev. John Beresford, fourth Marquis of Waterford, and was born on lie 10th February, 1846, at 'hiliptown, Co. Dublin. Ile !ntered the Royal Navy in 1859, was appointed a lieuten- ,nt in 1868, and advanced to he rank of commander in 1875. In 1872 he was ap-
pointed Flag Lieutenant to

the Commander-in-Chief at De\ .nd he accompanied the Prince of Wales as naval aide-de-camp to India in 1875-76. His lordship received the gold medals of the Royal Humane Society, and of the Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane Society, for having on three occa- sions jumped overboard and saved lives at' sea. On one of these occasions when he rescued a marine who had fallen overboard at Port Stanley, Falkand Island, he was attired in heavy shooting clothes, and his pockets were filled with cartridges. At the time of the bombardment of the ports of Alexandria, Lord Charles Beresford was in command of the gunboat" Condor," and in the action of July 11, 1882, he greatly distinguished himself by his gallant conduct. The ironclad, " Temeraire," which got ashore at the beginning of the engagement, was safely assisted off by the "Condor." Then the for- midable Marabout batteries, which constituted the second strongest defence of the port of Alexandria, were effectually silenced. This latter success was ' chiefly due to the gallant way in which the "Condor" bore down on the port,and engaged guns immensely superior to her own. So rigorous, indeed, was the attack on the big fort, that the Admiral's ship signalled" Well done, Condor." In consequence of the conflagration and looting in Alexandria. a re,T, gular police system was organised under Lord Charles Beresford. Strong measures were necessary to subduP the looters. Several of them, detected in the very act ot setting fire to houses, were sum- marily shot in the great Square, and those caught plundering were flogged. Loid Charles Beresford afterwards served in the Soudan campaign under Lord Wolseley for the relief of General Gordon, and was in command of the naval brigade in the expedi- tion across the desert. He was elected Conservative member for Waterford in 1874,and sat till 1880, and he represented East Marylebone from 1885 to 1889. He was appointed a Lord of the Admiralty in August, 1886, and resigned his position as M.P. in order to qualify for Admiral.
ST. JOtIN'S AITBULA.NCE ASSOCIATION
At RUNCORN. Under the auspices of the Runcorn branch of the St. John's Ambulance Association, a tea party and concert were held in Bethseda Schoolroom, on Wed-.

Aesday evening. The building was suitably deco- rated with flags and mottoes. Over 300 sat down to tea, and at the entertainment afterwards the room was crowded to excess. Mr J. W. Lightburn pre- sided, and in opening the proceedings, dealt with the useful and beneficial character of the Association, and complimented Colonel Hammersley upon having been the means of establishing the Runcorn centre. Although only 15 months since that time, two thirds of the consta- bles of the district had become certified members ; and while they had to carry out the stern behests of the law, they were ready at all times to assist in minimising suffer- ing. (Applause.) He mentioned a case where Superin- tendent Large had recently saved the life of a woman who had severed a large artery, and said the members of St. John were always ready to render first aid. (Ap- plause.) During an interval in the programme, Lady Brooke presented the certificates to the successful students, Dr. McDougall remarking that 43 were presented for ex- amination and all had passed successfully. (Applause.) After this ceremony the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, on behalf of the class, presented Dr. McDougall with a handsome ebony walking stick, and a surgical bag suit- ably inscribed, the articles having been supplied by Mr. C. Dutton and Mr. S. Coventry respectively. Mr. Williams paid a high tribute to the ability and thoroughness with which he had carried out his duties as tutor; and in acknowledging the gifts, Dr. McDougall said he felt proud that he had been the instructor of the class, and convinced that every individual member would carry away with him happy reminiscences of the class at which they had acquired valuable knowledge; which he hoped would be permanent. (Applause.)—Several members of the class now gave interesting illustrations of how to render "first aid."—The Chairman proposed a vote of thanks to Lady Brooke for her presence, and said it was a pleasure to see her ladyship identifying herself with any object for the benefit of the people of Runcorn. (Applause.)—Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation, and Sir Richard Marcus Brooke responded on behalf of Lady Brooke.—Mr. Epps proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and to all who had assisted at the tea or entertainment, and the motion, having bean seconded by Mr. Reynolds, was passed.—Dr. McDou- gall passed a high eulogy on the services rendered to the class by P.C. Crowder and P.C. Bullock (the secre- tary).—The programme consisted of songs, recita- tions, &c., and was thoroughly enjoyed. Master J. Crowder recited a piece composed for the occasion, entitled "The Ambulance Class," and Mr. and Masters Outhwaite gave a couple of instrumental selections in good style ; Miss Heatherington sang, " Will you come back to me ?" ; and Miss Jones, " When the tide comes in " ; while the duet, "List to the Convent Bells," was rendered by Misses Jones and E. Wright; Mr. R. Morris, contributed " Anchored " ; Mr. Gates, " Nazareth," and "The boatswain's story " ; and Mr. J. Leathwood, "The Village Blacksmith" ; Mr. A. E. Hallam provided the humourous part of the programme, and he recited and sang and mimicked in a manner that convulsed the audience with merriment. Mr. C. Le Couteur was the accompanist. Should there be a sufficient number of ladies who express desire for instruction in ambulance work, Dr. McDougall will commence a class for their benefit early in April.
MR. T. M. HEALY, M.P.

Mr. Timothy Michael Healy, common ly called "Tim." has been described as "undeniably the cleverest man but one in the Parnellite party." His poli- tical reputation was almost as suddenly made as was that of Mr. Parnell himself, whose secretary he became on em- erging from a railway clerk- ship at Newcastle. He was boln at Bantry in 1855, first entered Parliament in 1880,

and was called to the Irish bar in 1884. _le married a daughter of Mr. T. D. Sulli- van in 1882. It was written in 1885 that" the quickness with which Mr. Healy got to know his material, in the shape of the forms of the House, was especially remarkable, and some critics of obstruction as a fine art prefer his style to that of the master himself. He has a more fiery manner, but there is an uncommonly long head be- hind his brazen front. The frank brutality which the affects does not entirely conceal a bump of ven- eration. There i no one who opposes Mr. Glad- stone more bitterly, but respects him more sincere- ly than Mr. Healy, who has been heard to say that if the" Grand Old Man" were only a less unrepent- ant political sinner, he would lick his boots and feel proud. There is, too, a tenderness about "Tim ',' which people who only know his House of Commons side would not suspect. After a bitter vituperative struggle at St. Stephen's, he will go to a friend's house where there is a little lady Ruth of ten years, whose dearest friend he is, and taking her on his knee, he will tell her the most bewitching fairy stories till it is hours past lbedtime, while the rest of the family sit round in a charmed circle." There have been great changes since this pas=age was written, including re- conciliation to Mr. Gladstone, but Mr. Healy still has a "fiery manner," and recently a good deal of his oratorical fervour has been expended on Mr. Parnell, his former leader, and his supporters. Mr. Healy, like many of his confreres in Parliament,has suffered imprisonment for his advocacy of the cause jof Ireland. In 1885 he failed to secure his return 1 for South Derry, but in 1886 he was sent to Parlia- ment unopposed for North Longford.
ADDRESS TO WIDNES. (With apologies to the slqade of Robert Burn s.

Oh! Widnes, perfume's darling seat, All hail thy chimneys and thy towers, All hail the chemic fumes that greet The stranger wandering through thy bowers; Thy pall of smoke that constant lowers Wherever one may cast a glance, Thy grateful scents, like-summer flowers, Oh ! never say they come by " Chance." One feels, in passing through thy streets, The charms thou hast are all thy own, Or if a rival, that thy sweets Are equalled only by Cologne; Thy gifts thou scatterest wide and free Unlike a selfish cunnudgeon— (What viler compound can there be Than sulphuretted hydrogen ?) Let Widnes flourish evermore, As fast the freighted years roll by, Enthroned upon fair Mersey's shore, The cherished home of alkali; While cheerful gases gaily drift, As through the town a traveller goes, The carriage window he will lift, And hold his 'k;!rchief to his nose.
C. H. L.

div.head: BANKS, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: BANKS, OF RUNCORN.

Mr. James Broyden Banks, watchmaker, and jeweller. of High-st., Runcorn,died at his residence in Leinster Gardens, on Saturday afternoon. He had been ailing for some time,but it was not until three weeks ago that he became bedfast. He was attended by Dr. Robinson and Dr. McDougall; and Dr. Glynn of Liverpool, was consulted but the complication of ailments from which he suffered resisted all their skill, and he died as stated. Mr. Banks, who had served his time with the late Mr. Handley, watch- maker, was one of the old2st and best-known trades- men in the town. In politics he was a Conservative, and in religion a churchman, and although, he took a keen interest in local affairs, he never aspired to fill any of the public offices. He had attained the age of 58 years, and leaves a widow and three daughters to mourn his loss. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon, at the Parish Church. His remains were enclosed in an oak coffin, which was borne on the shoulders of Messrs. Snowball, Thomas Lydiate, Charles Roberts, and John Ravenscroft jun. The. mourners were Messrs. Bankes, C. Pownall, law) ; John Mason, J(Ramhyels), JoChonllmiera,son ((baraopthtoenr T. Collier Helsby, Kewley (Liverpool), and Hockey (New Brighton). The last tokens of respect to the memory of the deceased were paid, by the following tradesmen and friends, who walked in procession :—Dr. Robinson, Messrs. Wm. Allan (Liverpool). John Ball, sen. (Higher Runcorn), Rowland, W. H.Chadwick,Robt. Wright, John Leicester, Arthur Riley, Frank Johnson, George Bell (Wavertree), George Shone, N. Large (super- intendent of police), J.Burton (solicitor), Harry Rhodes, Wm. Farrell, Richard Morris, J. Unsworth, Wm. Sutton, James Sutton,G. S. Wharton, and J. Bate. En route, the windows of the shops and dwellings were darkened. The burial service in the church and at the grave side was conducted by the Rev. J. Halden. Mr. R. Morris was the undertaker.

div.head: WIDNES STABBING CASE AT THE LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.
div.p: A WIDNES STABBING CASE AT THE LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. J as- tice Day, in the Crown Court, Edward Hynan, 20, labourer, was indicted for wounding Michael John Keegan, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm, at Widnes, on the 25th December. Mr. Cooper prosecuted, and Mr. Segar defended. Counsel, in opening the case, said the prosecutor and prisoner were drinking together on Christmas Eve, and at eleven o'clock they and Mrs. Keegan went to prisoner's father's house. Prosecutor had a row with his wife, and it ended in Keegan and Hynan havinga fight in the street. The prisoner then went into the house, and fetched out a jug and a knife. He threw the jug at Keegan, butit missed him and hit Mrs. Keegan. Hynan then stabbed prosecutor in the arm. Keegan ran away, and the prisoner followed him and again I stabbed him, this time in the back, inflicting a somewhat I serious wound, which incapacitated him for a consider- able time. The prosecutor said he had a couple of words with his wife at the prisoner's father's house, and the pri- soner " tupped " him twice in the mouth with his head. They took off their coats and had a fight, and the pri- soner afterwards stabbed him. Cross-examined by Mr. Segar.—Prosecutor said he was too drunk to stand, but sober enough to get up when he fell. (Laughter.) Mr. Segar, for the defence, asked the jury to convict the pri- soner of unlawful wounding only, and submitted that the prosecutor's testimony was not reliable, owing to his in- toxicated condition at the time that he received the injury. The jury found the prisoner guilty of unlawful. wounding only. —Flis Lordship said it was absolutely necessary that the use of the knife should be stamped out. The prisoner behaved in a very cowardly way, as he did not stab the prosecutor in the course of the fight, but went into the house and deliberately brought out a knife, with which he stabbed Keegan. He must go to gaol for 18 calendar months.

div.head: LIVERPOOL MURDER.
div.p: THE LIVERPOOL MURDER.
SENTENCE OF PINFOLD.

At the Liverpool Assizes yesterday, Arthur Edward Pinfold, 31, porter, of East Grinstead, Sussex, was charged with the murder of Maggie Stewart, alia3 Isabella Cowie, by stabbing her in a cab at Liverpool, in December last. The question of prisoner's sanity was raised, and although one medical witness deposed he considered the prisoner sane, another who knew pri- soner's family was called, and said the prisoner and his brother were subject to fits, whilst their mother died during an epileptic seizure. The jury returned a ver- dict of guilty after a minute's consideration without retiring from the court. His Lordship then summed up, and sentence of death was then passed in the usual form, amid death-like silence. The prisoner said nothing: he only slightly bowed. One of his brothers was greatly affected. Judge Day was deeply distressed while passing sentence, and the governor of the gaol and several occu- pants of the court could not refrain from tears.

div.head: SERIOUS CONDIT CT OF WIDNES GAS
div.p: SERIOUS CONDIT CT OF WIDNES GAS
STOKERS.

Before Mr. J. Birchall and Lieut.-Col. Gamble, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, James Cooke, a stoker in the employ of the Widnes Local Board at the Gas Works, was summoned for a breach of con- tract. Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted on behalf of the Board, and stated that the retorts at the works were worked by gangs of three men and a foreman; and on Sunday night, March Ist, one of these gangs con- sisted of the defennant, Howard, and Callaghan. Howard heard the defendant and Callaghan say they would "chuck the job" when they had put in the first draw, namely, charge the retorts. Afterwards the foreman, Threlfall, saw them leaving the works, and he called to , them to come back, but they walked on. OH Monday Callaghan went to the works in a drunken condition, and demanded his back pay from Mr. Carr, the engi- neer, - who refused it, and the defendant then used most abusive language. In conseqnence of these two ' men leaving their work without the usual week's notice, 15,000 feet of gas less than usual was made on that night, causing a loss of about 30s. to the Board. Du ring the winter the town had several times had a short supply of gas, owing to the stokers leaving their work, and the Board had suffered enormously in consequence. This statement was borne out by the evidence of the defend- ant, who pleaded that he left in consequence of illness.— Mr. Birchall said the Bench were convinced the defend- ant had committed the offence, and it was a very serious matter. The penalty they could inflict was £2O, or three months' imprisonment, and the defendant would have to pay 40s. and costs, or go to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.—Mr. Knowles said the man Callaghan had ab- sconded, and he applied for a warrant, which was granted.

At a late hour, on Wednesday night, a woman named Dorothy Sinclair. who lived with her husband, a farm servant, at Coalside, Morpeth, was arrested on a charge of murdering him. Sinclair and his wife were at Mor- peth hiring on Wednesday, and it is alleged that shortly after reaching home she stabbed him to the heart with a carving knife, and he died immediately. CRITCHLEY. div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C. BY AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C. BY AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

In the House of Commons this week, Mr. Mun- della addressed a question to the Vice-President of the Committee of the Council on Education with reference to the statement of Mr. Kynnersley, her Majesty's Inspector of Schools for the Cheshire dis- trict. The statement is that "Pit is now only in Birkenhead and Runcorn that we have really objec- tionable buildings." Mr. Mundella's question and the answer of Sir W. Hart Dyke dealt altogether with Birkenhead, but for us locally interested it would be welcome information to know which are the objectionable buildings in Runcorn. They cer- ' tainly are not the Board Schools; the denomina- tional committees, therefore, had better carefully examine their premises, and discover in what they are . lacking _

The eleCiion for the Guardians of Runcorn Union takes place early next month, and it is highly pro- bable that there will be a contest, but whether it will be productive of such incidents as on the last occasion is doubtful. Nominations must be sent in to Mr. H. a Linaker, Frodsham, the returning officer before the 25th inst. The method of voting is a most unsatisfactory one, and the sooner a change is made to' the ballot, the better. No arguments are needed to prove the necessity of a cottage hospital in Runcorn ; the number of serious accidents occurring in the district demon- strates only too clearly how useful such an institu- tion would be. Two attempts have been made to establish a hospital—in 1883 and in 1887—but on each occasion failure to raise the funds attended the efforts of the promoters.. On Monday evening a ratepayers' meeting presided over by Mr. Taylor, the Chairman of the Board of Commissioners, was held for the same purpose,and a committee was ap- pointed to draw up a scheme. After two failures one cannot help asking will the present prospect succeed. Certainly a better start might have been made by electing a more representative committee, for whether it was meant or not, the meeting acted in a way to give the; impression that it is a De- nominational movement, and unless that suspicion is removed, I fear there is no hope that the desired end will be attained.

The Runcorn Musical Society will bring their second season to a close on Tuesday evening next, when the Oratorio Elijah will be performed in the Drill Hall. A strong array of musical talent, vocal and instrumental, has been secured for the occasion, and a treat of no ordinary character is anticipated. The Rev. Dr. George Bartle, of Freshfield, near Southport will not have very pleasant memories of Widnes. On Whit Monday he arrived at the chemi- cal Metropolis by a Cheshire Lines excursion train, and he alleges that whilst descending from the compartment in which he had been travelling, the train started and he was thrown on to the platform. At first he experienced no ill effects, but afterwards he suffered from nervousness and want of sleep. His memory was defective, and lie had to call in the aid of a doctor. He had now to decline en- gagements, as when preaching he broke down in his quotations, At the Liverpool assizes this week he sought to recover damages from the railway company, and because of the contradictory evidence the jury awarded him £2O: As the Judge made no order as to costs, Dr. Bartle after he has paid his counsel will find himself considerably lighter in pocket. Widnes at the present time is in very bad odour in more senses than one. Two miles round the people are complaining of the vile smells with which their nostrils are assailed, and of the in- jury and destruction brought upon vegetation. The malodorous fumes from the chemical works are said to reach nearly to Liverpool on one side, and to cause considerable trouble and loss to the Cheshire , farmers on the other ; and if such really be the case, what must the poor Widnesians who bave to live in the very midst of it be suffering? They are not worried with a trifle in the way of chemic," but the nuisances of the past few months have caused them to grumble very loudly, and the Local Board have taken action to have the nuis- ance abated. LATEST NEWS.

EARL GRANVILLE'S ILLNESS. Earl Granville passed a good night, and his condition yesterday morning was much more satisfactory. THE SECOND DRAWING-ROOM. The Queen held the second drawing-room of the season at Buckingham Palace yesterday. It was well attended. DELTH OF AN IRISH M.P. Mr. Peter M`Donald, M.P., for North Sligo, died at Kingstown, on Thursday night. Mr. M'Donald was an anti-Parnellite. MR. W. O'BRIEN MADE BANKRUPT. In Dublin yesterday Mr. William O'Brien was adjudi- cated a bankrupt, he not having paid the law costs in- curred in his abortive libel action against Lord Salis- bury. EXECUTION IN IRELAND. Yesterday morning, at eight o'clock, John Purcell, aged 40, blacksmith, was executed at Kilmainham Gaol, for the murder of Bridget Smith, aged 60, at Nan!, county Dublin, last November. A reprieve has been refused. Berry was the executioner. THE ROMANTIC ABDUCTION CASE. MRS. JACKSON RECONCILED. All deubts as to Mrs. Jackson's satisfaction with the course pursued by her husband in forcibly taking her from the custody of her relatives were dispelled on Thursday night. Sitting at the piano, and for nearly an hour the lady played and sang in a sweet contralto voice a succession of operatic airs, to the great enjoy- ment of her fellow prisoners, as well as the crowd of sightseers and bailiffs outside, who cheered heartily. THE SNOWSTORM RENEWED. OVER 50 LIVES LOST. There was a renewal of the snowstorm on Thursday night in Cornwall, Devon, and Somerset. Altnough there is railway commtinication open between Bristol and Exeter, the drifts in country roads have been much increased, and all traffic through these channels have been blocked. Hundreds of men were employed on Tuesday and Wednesday to clear the roads in and about Taunton, and now the.work has all to be done over again. The Central News says the loss of life by Monday's blizzard is only as yet very imperfectly known. It is believed that at Start Point alone nearly fifty lives were lost during the fearful storm. The loss of life on the Devoeshire coast during this week's storm has been altogether unparalleled.; YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack at a quarter past four. Lord HERSCHELL moved the second reading of a bill enabling the trusteeo of an open space in the Leicester Vestry District to distribute the assets to the benefit of the inhabitants. Lord Hommusz moved the rejection of the Bill, as the ground and the space should remain an open space for recreation pur- poses. After a long discussion the Bill was read a second time. EDUCATION BILL—Lord MORTON called attention to the education code, and complained of alterations, since 1872, opposed to the fundamental principles of the Act. Viscount CRANBROOK said the Code was working satis- factorily. Several Bills were advanced a stage, and the House adjourned at 25 to seven. HOUSE OF COMMONS. Tho Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. SMALL HOLDINGS BILL.—In answer to Mr. Esslemont, Mr. CHAPLAIN declined to acquaint the House with the the provisions of the Government Small Holdings Bill. The assumption that the price would be placed at thirty years' purchase was entirely a gratuitous one. THE GLASGOW ACClDENT.—Answering Dr. Cameron, the Secretary said his attention hail been drawn to the extraordinary accident whick occurred at Dixon's Iron Works, Glasgow, on Tuesday. He had been in commu- nication with the Inspector of Explosives upon the sub- ject, and consideration was now being directed to the matter. SUSPENSION OF RULES.—Mr. W. H. SMITH moved a resolution suspending certain rules in order to admit of the House sitting for despatch of Government business after midnight. Discussion ensued, and on a division the motion was agreed to. THE TAXATION OF GROUND VALUES.—OR the motion for going into supply, Mr. J. STUART ROSE called atten- tion to the unfair incidence of the local taxation of graund values in London and other large towns, and moved that in opinion of the House the freeholders and owners of ground values in the metropolis ought to con- tribute directly a substantial share of local taxation. Mr. S. MONTAGUE seconded the resolution, believing the equitable taxation of ground values urgently called for.

T e dividend of the North British Railway for the first half of the year on ordinary preference stock is at th e rate of 11 per cent, per annum. The Duke of Cambridge left Cairo on Tuesday morning by special train for Ismailia. The Duke stayed two hours at Tel-el-Kebir, and intended to embark on board the Ganges at Port Said. His health is quite restored, and he has much enjoyed his visit to Egypt.
